It does not measure bytes moved, allocation peaks or elapsed time. Across 28 layers, the logical FP16 K/V payload grows from 42×28 KiB=1,176 KiB to 43×28 KiB=1,204 KiB , exactly one 28-KiB position. After this second forward chooses the comma, that comma is again only a chosen ID; it has no K/V until the next forward. The small toy deliberately does not simulate tokenizer semantics, 28 layers or GPU execution; use the recorded real shape ledger to connect its operations to inference. Use the operation map to ask a performance question Dense Q/K/V, output, gate/up/down and vocabulary projections multiply activation rows by weights. RMSNorm and softmax include reductions over different axes; RoPE, residual additions and SiLU/product operate elementwise or on pairs. Attention mixes across the growing history, and K/V remains live for later steps. Reshape/transpose changes the view/layout and can entail copies when a consumer requires a particular layout. Which operations become separate kernels or fuse together depends on the selected backend; a mathematical box is not automatically one CUDA launch. Flatten batch and new positions into M=B×S . The same 1,536-wide projection sees M=42 in our prefill and M=1 at the next step. In a constructed B8/P512 batch, it instead sees M=4096 and then M=8 . Retained history changes attention's source axis, not the number of newly projected query rows. These shapes motivate bandwidth/compute hypotheses later in the chapter; they do not by themselves predict a millisecond ratio. The first token is not a decode forward Keep a tiny ledger before writing a timer. With prompt IDs x1…x4 , prefill computes their K/V and logits for choosing y1 . Immediately after the choice, the cache contains four positions, not five: choosing an ID does not compute its hidden states. Feeding y1 back creates its K/V and permits choosing y2 ; the cache now has five positions. Feeding y2 back permits choosing y3 ; the cache has six. The lab checks this invariant at runtime: after selecting O outputs, retained length is P+O−1 . A conservative serving capacity plan may reserve P+O positions, but should say that it is a budget rather than a tensor observation. Likewise, a 128-output answer has 127 post-first gaps. If their arithmetic mean is 22 ms, their total is exactly 127×22=2,794 ms . Adding the actual first-token interval gives a larger completion interval. If 22 ms were only the median gap, multiplication would not reconstruct the total. A small set of slow gaps could leave the median unchanged while making completion much later. The lab's mean decode step interval is total decode wall time divided by O−1 ; it is not a distribution of individually timestamped token events, and it is not a client streaming ITL measurement. The serial token axis At decode step t , the model cannot choose token t+1 until logits for t exist. Work within a step can be massively parallel, and multiple sequences can be batched, but the output-token dependency remains. Prefill instead processes many known prompt positions together. Thus long input with short output and short input with long output can stress different parts of the same GPU. FlashAttention is a concrete example of optimizing attention through IO-aware tiling; it is not a claim that all service delay lives inside that kernel. Known prompt positions versus dependent output steps Prompt known 128 or 4,096 input tokens → Prefill many known positions; build KV → Decode 1 one new position → Decode 2…N each step waits for the previous token The arrows show one request's dependency, not a claim that all CUDA work is serial. Multiple live requests can contribute one step each to an iteration-level batch. Shape is a hypothesis, duration is evidence For a fixed model, prefill with more positions often increases matrix sizes and attention work, while decode adds one new position at a time and reads retained state. That suggests a qualitative prediction: increasing prompt length should primarily enlarge prefill and KV; increasing output length should multiply decode steps. It does not predict a particular wall-time ratio. Fixed launch overhead, kernel selection, sequence padding, cache behavior, compilation and measurement noise all affect the observed ratio. In the pinned five-trial table, some decode medians even decrease with longer input. The right response is to preserve raw trials and investigate, not smooth them into a monotonic curve. Ask what is held constant before comparing: model revision, tokenizer, precision, batch, generated-token count, warmup state and synchronization. A timing measured without synchronizing a CUDA device may record only kernel dispatch on the CPU, not completed device work. Conversely, a profiler can perturb execution and make an otherwise good timing unrepresentative. The course's phase exercise records synchronized measurements; its local profiler artifact is a learning tool, not a public production-latency claim. A pair-count is not a wall-time model In a simplified dense causal attention calculation, a prompt of length P has on the order of P²/2 valid query–key pairs. Increasing P from 128 to 4,096 multiplies that attention pair count by roughly (4096/128)² = 1024 . Yet the v2 1.5B/O32 prefill medians change from 22.3 to 163.7 ms, about 7.34× rather than 1024×. There is no paradox. Attention scores are one component of a transformer layer; projections and feed-forward work scale differently, fixed overheads matter, the GPU can exploit larger shapes differently, and IO-aware kernels avoid materializing the full score matrix in slow memory. Pair count is a mathematical work term, not a prediction of service milliseconds. Preserve the five-trial ranges and the unresolved identical-shape variation described below; 7.34× is an observation of this run, not a law. The first output is selected from the prefill logits, so O generated outputs require D=O−1 subsequent decode forwards. At decode query j=1…D , the current input token adds its own K/V and attends P+j positions. Summing per-head query–key pairs gives DP+D(D+1)/2 . With O=256 , D=255 : a 512-token prompt gives 255×512+255×256/2=163,200 pairs; a 4,096-token prompt gives 1,077,120 , exactly 6.6× as many. These are decode-only pair counts per head, not prefill work, HBM bytes, or a 6.6× wall-time prediction. Changing the definition of a “step” without changing the summation is an off-by-one error, not a harmless notation choice. Batching changes the effective machine problem At batch one, each decode step produces one new token for one sequence. If several sequences advance together, the same model weights may be used for multiple token computations in the iteration. That can increase useful work per weight byte moved, but it also raises live KV demand and may lengthen an individual request's decode cadence. “Higher aggregate tokens/s” and “better per-user latency” are distinct outcomes. Imagine four copies of our sequence-completion request advancing in four lanes: each iteration can choose four IDs, but no lane skips its dependency on its previous ID. That picture explains the counting; the measurements below use repeated synthetic IDs, not four measured natural-language requests. A long prompt may demand a large prefill while short decode steps are ongoing; admitting it can interfere with active streams. Separating prefill and decode across resources is one architectural response studied by DistServe , but that paper is not evidence that our one-GPU course run uses disaggregated serving. The immediate diagnostic lesson is to record phase and request shape, then test the actual scheduling policy under the intended workload. A batch size copied from a paper or a benchmark with different output lengths is not a capacity plan. Count live state before blaming compute The pinned Qwen2.5-3B configuration has 36 layers, two KV heads, and head dimension 128. At two bytes per element, logical KV payload per token is 2 (K and V) × 36 × 2 × 128 × 2 = 36,864 bytes = 36 KiB . A worked population of 64 sequences with 512 prompt and 256 generated tokens each gives a conservative budget of 64 × 768 = 49,152 token positions, or 1.6875 GiB of logical KV payload. That is not the process-memory reading. Weights, temporary activations, allocator reservation, graph buffers, block rounding, and fragmentation remain outside the formula. Nor is every token’s cache necessarily resident for the full request lifetime. The calculation is useful as a falsifiable lower-level component, not as an admission guarantee. Change the KV-head count in the KV budget explorer and observe the linear change while remembering these omissions. Derive the units before reaching for a GPU monitor One token contributes a key vector and a value vector to each transformer layer. With grouped-query attention, the number of KV heads—not the number of query heads—sets this particular payload. The pinned Qwen2.5-3B config provides 36 layers, two KV heads and 128 values per head. At FP16, each value is two bytes. Multiply 2 arrays × 36 layers × 2 KV heads × 128 values/head × 2 bytes/value . The head and value units cancel, leaving 36,864 bytes/token . Dividing by 1,024 gives 36 KiB/token . If someone substitutes decimal “36 KB,” the numerical error is small here but the habit becomes dangerous in a tight capacity budget. For the worked 64-request population, each request budgets 512 input plus 256 generated positions. This is a conservative capacity allowance, not the exact final tensor length in the lab: the last chosen output has not been fed back, so the lab retains 512+256−1=767 positions per sequence. The budget reserves 768 positions per request and 64 × 768 = 49,152 across requests. Then 49,152 × 36,864 = 1,811,939,328 bytes , and division by 2³⁰ gives 1.6875 GiB . Notice how the units and population are explicit: logical payload for this hypothetical collection of live tokens. We did not measure a 64-client Qwen2.5-3B service in this calculation. A KV budget changes with live tokens and head count Worked scenario Live tokens Payload per token Logical KV payload 32 × (512 input + 512 output), pinned two KV heads 32,768 36 KiB 1.125 GiB 64 × (512 input + 256 output), pinned two KV heads 49,152 36 KiB 1.6875 GiB Same 49,152 tokens, hypothetical four KV heads 49,152 72 KiB 3.375 GiB The first two rows use the pinned configuration as arithmetic input; the third changes a config parameter to show sensitivity, not to claim a second measured model. These are logical payloads before allocator, blocks, weights or temporary memory. A full memory ledger has more than one line For an idealized three-billion-parameter FP16 model, raw weights alone are about 3 × 10⁹ × 2 = 6 × 10⁹ bytes , or roughly 5.59 GiB. “Three billion” is rounded, and real checkpoint/module composition matters, so this is a back-of-envelope term, not a measured Qwen file size. At a particular instant, disjoint live tensors such as weights, KV, temporary activations and workspace contribute to allocated memory. Those allocated bytes are already inside the allocator's reserved pool; only its unused portion is additional pool space. Device-total accounting also includes allocations outside that pool and other processes. Do not add allocated to reserved, or assume independently observed maxima describe the same instant. A 16-GiB card showing 8 GiB apparently free at one instant is not proof that 8 GiB of additional live KV can be safely admitted: allocation granularity, peaks and concurrent work remain. Now switch explicitly from the 3B transfer calculation to the measured 1.5B model. Its 28 layers, two KV heads and 128 values per head give 2 × 28 × 2 × 128 × 2 = 28,672 bytes = 28 KiB/token at FP16. The required matrix records that value from the actual configuration. The 3B figure of 36 KiB/token would be the wrong coefficient for this run. The KV column is model/config arithmetic at final retained length, not an isolated allocator-counter measurement. Why can KV grow by (4223−4127) × 28 / 1024 = 2.625 MiB while the phase peak stays flat? The maximum occurs during a different live-object combination: in these rows, the recorded prefill peak already equals the overall peak. Extra final KV does not exceed that earlier maximum. We have not measured which particular temporary tensor caused the peak; this evidence establishes the timing boundary, not a complete allocation attribution. A peak is a maximum over time, not the size of the final cache. Allocated bytes and reserved bytes also answer different questions: live allocated tensors are inside the allocator's reserved pool, not an extra pool to add on top. In these P4096 rows, the reserved peak is 3,586 MiB; adding it to 3,349.34 MiB would double-count live allocations. A between-cell device sample after releasing models was at most 333 MiB in the v2 rehearsal, far below the in-process peak. It cannot bound live execution. An admission rule needs worst credible live state, other device users and measured headroom, not an idle snapshot. Weight compression and KV are separate levers Quantizing weights may reduce the weight term but leave FP16 KV unchanged. Quantizing KV may change a different term and has its own quality and kernel constraints. Changing attention implementation can reduce temporary IO without changing the logical persistent KV formula. Increasing batch or sequence length can make weights a smaller share of total live memory even though the model file is identical. This distinction is the bridge to Chapter 03: “the model fits” is not a single yes/no property of a filename. It depends on the complete serving workload and the implementation that actually runs. A roof is not a latency prediction In an illustrative machine model with 60 TFLOP/s compute and 600 GB/s bandwidth, the ridge point is 60,000 / 600 = 100 FLOP/byte . A workload at 20 FLOP/byte has a bandwidth ceiling of 600 × 20 / 1,000 = 12 TFLOP/s , below the compute roof. Moving a point by changing reuse or precision is meaningful only if the real implementation changes bytes or operations. Launch gaps, queueing, kernel inefficiency, and memory capacity are absent from the simple roof. The original Roofline model explains the upper-bound interpretation; the explorer lets you vary intensity. Derive the roof; then say what it cannot predict Arithmetic intensity I is operations divided by bytes moved at a chosen memory boundary. If peak compute is C and sustainable bandwidth at that boundary is BW , the simple attainable upper bound is min(C, BW × I) . The example uses decimal units consistently: 60 TFLOP/s = 60,000 GFLOP/s , 600 GB/s , so C/BW = 100 FLOP/byte . Below that ridge, doubling useful arithmetic intensity could raise the bandwidth ceiling; above it, the compute ceiling dominates in this model. Neither statement says a real kernel will reach the roof. An illustrative 60-TFLOP/s, 600-GB/s roofline Intensity Bandwidth ceiling Compute ceiling Model upper bound 5 FLOP/byte 3 TFLOP/s 60 TFLOP/s 3 TFLOP/s 20 FLOP/byte 12 TFLOP/s 60 TFLOP/s 12 TFLOP/s 100 FLOP/byte 60 TFLOP/s 60 TFLOP/s 60 TFLOP/s (ridge) 200 FLOP/byte 120 TFLOP/s 60 TFLOP/s 60 TFLOP/s Invented hardware values, not the RTX 5070 Ti specification. A roofline is a ceiling for the chosen operation and memory boundary, not a service TTFT, a utilization target, or an observed throughput. Suppose the operation count for one illustrative kernel is one tera-operation and its intensity is 20 FLOP/byte. The simple roof would give a lower bound near 1 / 12 s ≈ 83 ms of idealized device execution. The measured service might take far longer because it waits in a queue, launches many kernels, moves data at a different level, samples tokens serially, or simply runs inefficiently. If a profiler says the kernel occupies only 10% of service wall time, a 2× kernel speed-up can reduce whole-service time by at most roughly 5% under an Amdahl-style fixed-remainder approximation. This is an illustrative calculation , not a measurement of the course kernel. It teaches where not to spend the next week. Derive a decode hypothesis, then list the missing bytes Let be an approximate active dense-weight count and the bytes per stored weight. For one decode row, the dense-weight estimate is about FLOPs when a multiply and an addition count as two operations. If those weights stream once through the chosen memory boundary, traffic is about bytes. Their ratio is FLOP/byte, approximately one at FP16. For B token rows ideally sharing that weight sweep, the ratio becomes . Batch one, four and 32 then give one, four and 32 FLOP/byte. This is a useful first-order hypothesis for weight reuse; it is not measured total-kernel intensity. The cancellation of in the ratio is instructive. A larger model still does more work and moves more absolute bytes; the ratio alone does not determine its latency. At the hypothetical 600 GB/s boundary, streaming 3×10⁹ two-byte weights takes at least 10 ms if that traffic assumption holds. But cache hits reduce transferred weight bytes, while K/V, activations, normalization and attention add other work. Kernel shapes can change achieved rates. A long-context decoder can therefore leave the simple weight-only regime even with the same model and batch. Name the model's omissions before using it to select an optimization. Now interpret a batch experiment correctly. In a constructed example, B1 takes 1.0 s for 31 post-first steps; B4 takes 1.5 s for the same steps per sequence. Aggregate decode rate increases from 31/1.0=31 to 4×31/1.5≈82.7 tokens/s, while mean per-sequence cadence worsens from 32.3 to 48.4 ms. Neither result contradicts the other. The lab uses identical-length rows and a static batch, with no scheduler, queue, arrivals or padding imbalance. It isolates a shape/reuse comparison; it cannot establish a serving concurrency limit or predict p95 TTFT for mixed real requests. Efficiency is not the same as a good schedule A prefill that fills the GPU efficiently can still delay active decoders. Consider a deliberately simplified serial device schedule: three decode steps of 10 ms each would finish in 30 ms, but an 80 ms prompt operation inserted after the first step stretches that interval to 110 ms. The diagram is not a measured trace and assumes no overlap. Its purpose is to separate kernel efficiency from request scheduling: the large operation can be individually efficient while violating another request's cadence. A scheduler may split or defer it, but that changes overhead, first-token wait and fairness. Topic 05 studies those scheduling mechanisms; this topic supplies the shape and time-budget vocabulary needed to evaluate them. The corresponding measurement must include both populations. Timing the large prefill alone misses its impact on existing streams; timing only a single stream misses the arrival and admission policy. Do not use the isolated lab to claim that chunked prefill is better or worse. Use it to predict where interference might arise, then design a later mixed-workload test with client deadlines, request spans and explicit failure counts. This returns the physical model to the system boundary from Chapter 01. “Bytes moved” needs an address HBM traffic, cache traffic and host-device transfers are different boundaries with different bandwidths. A tiling method can reduce HBM reads by reusing values in faster on-chip storage without changing mathematical FLOPs. FlashAttention is an IO-aware attention design; its benefit must be evaluated at the actual sequence shape and implementation path, not inferred from the name of an installed package. A decode kernel that repeatedly reads model weights can have different reuse when many sequences share an iteration batch. The operational intensity you plot should therefore be calculated or measured for the actual kernel and boundary, not borrowed from an unrelated prefill benchmark. Capacity is another separate constraint. Even a compute-efficient kernel cannot launch if the current live request state does not fit. And a service can be slow because its GPU is idle between launches, in which case both compute and memory roofs are generous but irrelevant. A productive prediction names its possible falsifiers: if the device timeline has large launch gaps, the roofline is not the first answer; if HBM bandwidth is far below its relevant ceiling while SMs are also underused, look for shape, occupancy or launch issues before pronouncing the workload “memory-bound.” Follow a byte before optimizing an operation Device memory is relatively large and distant from arithmetic units; on-chip storage is smaller and can support much greater reuse. CPU DRAM adds another location and a host-device transfer boundary. HBM and GDDR are different implementations of device memory, not synonyms for all GPU storage. L2 is shared cache, while shared memory and registers have more local ownership and limited capacity. The exact L1/shared-memory organization varies by architecture. The diagram is a reasoning map rather than a mandatory physical route for every load. Ask whether the value is already available near the consumer, whether many threads can reuse it, and whether bringing more state close reduces the number of resident thread blocks. A tile is a block of a larger operation selected to fit and reuse data locally. If a weight tile is fetched once and used for several token rows before eviction, useful FLOPs per transferred byte increase. Merely enlarging an allocation does not create this reuse. Register pressure or shared-memory use can also reduce occupancy—the amount of simultaneously resident work—and sometimes expose latency that a smaller tile hid. “Use more on-chip memory” is therefore a design trade-off, not a universal prescription. The CUDA Best Practices Guide describes the underlying memory/access mechanisms; the course asks you to connect them to an actual shape and an observable consequence. Coalescing concerns how nearby threads' memory requests combine into transactions. Four neighboring useful elements can fall within a compact footprint, whereas four scattered elements can require fetching several segments. Both programs may perform the same arithmetic and use the same logical tensor size, yet transfer different amounts of data. The drawing intentionally does not assert a universal transaction size; alignment, dtype, architecture and cache behavior matter. Effective bandwidth based on useful payload is a useful application metric, but a hardware traffic counter may see additional fetched bytes. A discrepancy between them is a reason to inspect access patterns, not to silently change the denominator. A fusion example with bytes, not marketing language Take three elementwise functions over N values. An unfused implementation reads input X, writes intermediate A, reads A, writes intermediate B, reads B and writes output Y. Ignoring cache effects, this is six transfers of N elements. If one fused kernel keeps the intermediates local, it may need only the initial read and final write: two transfers. At N=1,048,576 FP16 elements, the useful payload is 12 MiB versus 4 MiB. The mathematical result and operation count can be essentially unchanged while the data movement and launch count shrink. That accounting does not promise a threefold time reduction. Perhaps the original intermediates already hit in cache; perhaps the fused kernel uses too many registers; perhaps arithmetic dominates; perhaps launch savings matter more than traffic. A valid experiment preserves the function, shape, precision and output check, then measures both implementations under one timing boundary. In a production service, it must also show that this region matters to the user-visible objective. Fusion describes removing boundaries, not removing required dependencies. Why FlashAttention changes IO without removing attention Dense causal attention conceptually combines a query with allowed keys, normalizes scores and uses the resulting weights to aggregate values. A straightforward implementation can materialize a large score matrix in device memory between those steps. An IO-aware tiled algorithm instead processes blocks and maintains running normalization/output state, avoiding that full intermediate materialization. The causal triangular picture still explains which positions may interact; it is not the allocation plan. The original FlashAttention paper makes IO movement central to the algorithm rather than treating memory as an afterthought. Online softmax in two blocks Consider one query/head with scores [0, ln2, ln4] and scalar values [1,3,5] . Full softmax has relative masses [1,2,4], so its weighted result is (1+6+20)/7=27/7≈3.857143 . Split the keys into blocks of two and one. Keep the current maximum m, denominator l, and unnormalized weighted numerator a. For vector values, a is a vector of head width . C is the new key block. Initialize m=−∞, l=0 and a=0; the first rescale is zero. Every exponential uses the same new maximum. Updating only the denominator, or forgetting r, changes the result. State m Rescale r l a a/l First block: 0, ln2 ln2 0 0.5+1=1.5 0.5×1+1×3=3.5 7/3 Second block: ln4 ln4 0.5 0.5×1.5+1=1.75 0.5×3.5+5=6.75 27/7 The old block's contributions become half as large because the reference maximum increased by ln2. Without rescaling, the erroneous result would be (3.5+5)/(1.5+1)=3.4 . No full score matrix needs to survive between blocks. This example explains exact normalization; it does not simulate CUDA tiling, mask handling or a performance gain. The notebook executes this example offline and checks alternate block partitions. “Exact attention” distinguishes this approach from an approximate attention rule, not from all floating-point rounding differences. It does not eliminate the model's persistent KV state, the cost of dense projections or the dependence between generated tokens. PyTorch dispatch depends on hardware, dtype, mask and shape. The lab's focused traces provide evidence about the actual operator path for the two captured cases; another shape may select something else. For 1.5B/B1/O32 its P128 and P4096 prefill medians were 27.8 and 185.6 ms; decode medians were 1,116.3 and 965.7 ms. The apparent reversal does not prove that longer prompts accelerate decode. Capacity, bandwidth, latency—and allocator behavior A capacity bottleneck means the required live objects cannot coexist in available memory, or cannot do so with safe headroom. It appears as admission rejection, allocation failure, paging or a runtime's lower-than-expected active-sequence limit. A bandwidth bottleneck means useful work is limited by the rate of moving bytes at a chosen level; the program can fit perfectly and still spend most device time waiting for data. A latency bottleneck concerns dependent fetches whose waits are not hidden by enough independent work; fitting the tensors and having high aggregate bandwidth do not remove those dependencies. A separate fragmentation or reservation problem means logical payload calculations understate allocator behavior and reusable pools. Calling all these mechanisms “VRAM bottleneck” conceals the remedy. Weight quantization could improve capacity but slow a kernel; better batching could improve weight reuse but raise KV capacity pressure; changing allocator settings could alter reservation without changing the mathematical work. Use the right observation for each claim. For capacity, collect peak allocated and reserved memory under the target live-token mix and count failures. For bandwidth, profile actual traffic and execution at the memory level in question and compare with a relevant achieved bandwidth—not only a vendor peak. For fragmentation, inspect allocation patterns over repeated arrivals/cancellations and the runtime's block management. A one-number GPU dashboard cannot identify which mechanism is responsible. This distinction sets up the quantization trade-off in Chapter 03: smaller representation is one possible lever, not a diagnosis by itself. Why a wall clock can lie to a CUDA beginner GPU calls are often asynchronous from the CPU's perspective. Timing only the Python call that launches work can measure dispatch overhead while kernels continue after the stopwatch stops. The usual teaching protocol warms the path, synchronizes before starting, launches the work, synchronizes before stopping and then repeats. This does not make the measurement perfect: synchronization changes overlap and a profiler changes execution. It makes the defined interval inspectable. Keep the request-level HTTP clock separate from the phase benchmark, and do not add independently measured medians as if they were one observed transaction. Return to the exact prompt rather than an unlabeled stopwatch. Its per-step replay records the following two intervals around the same forward/selection. The wall interval includes completion synchronization; CUDA events mark an interval on the device stream, not a sum of kernel durations. Decoding text, printing the row, loading the model and chat tokenization are outside the timed forward. Per-step barriers and inspection make this a different observation protocol from the whole-loop v2 decode timer. Two clocks on the first four actual forward/selection steps Exact replay operation Selected token text Synchronized wall, ms CUDA-event interval, ms {promptReplay.replay.steps.slice(0,4).map(step => {step.phase}, output choice {step.output_index} {JSON.stringify(step.selected_token.text)} {step.wall_ms.toFixed(3)} {step.cuda_event_ms.toFixed(3)} )} Single observations from the recorded concrete prompt . Each interval encloses forward and greedy selection; neither is an HTTP metric or a sum of kernel durations. These are actual individual observations, not medians, p95 or a warm-path target. A similar wall/event value does not prove an absence of host launch gaps: a gap may occur between the two events as well. Use a time-ordered trace to attribute time to kernels. The prompt replay record explains warmup, stop conditions and instrumentation. In the instructor rehearsal, one GPU process ran at a time under a 24-GiB memory scope, with immutable model snapshots already cached and offline mode enabled. These precautions avoid downloading on every clean run and bound host risk; they do not turn a five-trial batch-one phase timing into a fleet-level latency distribution. The record includes source revision, model revisions, versions, timestamps and per-trial arrays so a reader can scrutinize the result instead of accepting a slide label. Five trials can start a question, not finish one A median of five observations is robust to one extreme value compared with a mean, but it still has little information about tails. If the values were 25, 27, 28, 29 and 70 ms, the median would be 28 ms and the unusual 70 ms would remain operationally interesting. The published arrays let the reader inspect spread and shape order rather than accepting a lone median. For a confirmatory experiment, specify a warmup rule, interleave or randomize shapes to reduce order bias, collect enough independent runs for the decision's uncertainty, and report failures and memory peaks beside timing. The required sample size depends on the effect size and variation; an arbitrary “three runs” ritual is not a confidence argument. Do not add median prefill from one set of runs to median decode from another and label the sum an observed end-to-end request. Both medians might come from different trials, and the real API includes tokenization, queueing, transport and post-processing. If you need an end-to-end claim, time actual complete requests under a pinned interface. If you need a phase explanation, use phase timers and profiler traces. The two measurements should reconcile qualitatively, but they answer different questions. This is the same evidence discipline established in Chapter 01: a number carries its observer and denominator with it. Choose the next instrument First isolate load, warmup, prefill, decode, and service waiting. If GPU kernels occupy only a small share of wall time, a detailed kernel profile may be the wrong first instrument; inspect CPU launch gaps and request traces. If one kernel dominates device time, inspect its shapes and memory behavior. PyTorch’s profiler can capture operators and allocations; NVIDIA’s Nsight Systems locates timeline gaps, while Nsight Compute interrogates a selected kernel. Profiling perturbs timing: validate any improvement again without instrumentation. Choose the first instrument from the missing boundary Observation First question Useful instrument Premature conclusion to avoid High HTTP latency; engine duration low Where did the request wait or buffer? Request trace across gateway, queue and stream “The attention kernel is slow.” Engine wall time high; GPU has gaps Is CPU launch, tokenization or synchronization starving work? Nsight Systems timeline or PyTorch operator trace “Low GPU utilization means no bottleneck.” One kernel dominates device time What shapes, occupancy and memory traffic does it have? Nsight Compute on that selected kernel “Theoretical peak bandwidth is its measured bandwidth.” OOM at a client count; idle sample looked safe What was the peak live KV and allocator reserve? In-process peak counters plus request/KV accounting “The model file fits, so the workload fits.” This is a diagnostic routing rule, not a profiler screenshot from the pinned lab. Identify the slow boundary before choosing a more expensive instrument. What a kernel profile can and cannot say A kernel profile can reveal occupancy, memory transactions, launch configuration and instruction mix for a selected invocation. It cannot by itself tell whether the user waited in a queue for two seconds or whether the proxy buffered output. A system timeline can reveal that the GPU sat idle between decode launches, but it may not say which application decision caused the gap. A request trace can show long admission wait without explaining the later matrix-multiply efficiency. These are complementary views of a causal chain, not competing brands of one universal profiler. For an illustrative case, suppose a request takes 800 ms end-to-end, of which 500 ms is queue wait, 200 ms is engine execution and 100 ms is transport/validation. Even eliminating half the engine work saves only 100 ms: end-to-end falls to 700 ms, a 12.5% improvement. If the objective is p95 TTFT under load, admission or capacity policy may have greater leverage. Change the numbers and the decision can reverse. The arithmetic is a budget exercise, not a claim about our measured server. This is why the student's analysis should name the chosen latency population and decompose it before announcing an optimization. Make the next measurement discriminate hypotheses Suppose a trace shows long decode time for a small model. Hypothesis A says repeated weight reads at batch one make the path bandwidth-sensitive. Hypothesis B says CPU launch gaps dominate. A kernel-only optimization would help A but barely touch B. Test A by comparing measured device occupancy, memory traffic and kernel duration across batch shapes; test B by checking the system timeline's gaps and CPU thread activity. Before running either tool, predict the contrasting signatures. If both signatures appear, quantify their wall-time shares before deciding which to fix first. The pinned 1.5B phase run cannot adjudicate these two hypotheses alone. It has timing arrays and a local teaching trace, not a published, versioned per-kernel analysis with enough repeats for a production claim. A careful chapter should say “the phase data motivate profiling,” not “the phase data prove HBM saturation.” That boundary is intellectually productive: it tells students exactly which experiment they would run next. An evidence ladder for one performance claim Symptom client latency + failure population → Phase prefill vs decode → Timeline GPU work vs gaps → Kernel shape + traffic → Re-test same service contract Stop climbing when the current evidence is sufficient for the decision. A profiler result must be validated again at the user-visible boundary without instrumentation. A completed diagnosis of repeated projection work Executed CPU operation-count case, not a GPU bottleneck claim. The notebook repeats the toy's three feature rows to make a 42-position prefix and supplies nine more fixed rows. These are invented features, not tokenized text. Both paths use the same one-block weights, absolute positions, exact attention rule and requested last-position logits. We measure calls that project one row through Q, K or V; we do not time Python. Diagnostic step Evidence / decision Symptom The no-cache path projects the whole growing prefix again at every forward. Prediction 3×(42+43+…+51)=1395 Q/K/V row-projection calls. Cached path: 3×51=153. Instrument The actual linear function increments a counter at each Q/K/V row call. Intervention Retain previous K/V and project only new rows; leave inputs and weights fixed. Recheck The notebook asserts 1395 versus 153 calls and compares all ten sets of last-position logits within 10⁻¹². Conclusion 1242 redundant row projections removed, about 89%. No claim of a 9.12× latency speedup. Attention still reads all available keys. Cached state grows to 51 positions, with four values each for K and V in this one-layer/one-head toy. The counter isolates redundant projection work; it says nothing about which operation dominates a real GPU's wall time. This restricted case closes a causal loop without using the unresolved timing variation as a made-up diagnosis. Avoided arithmetic is real, but reduced rows can change kernel selection and weight reuse, while fixed and launch costs remain. The executed call is torch.allclose(reference, actual, atol=.05, rtol=.01) : its elementwise rule is |actual−reference| ≤ 0.05 + 0.01×|actual| . In PyTorch's definition , the relative term uses the second argument; this comparison is not symmetric in general. The largest absolute difference is 0.05078125, so this is not an assertion that every error is below 0.05 or that FP16 paths are bit-identical. The required lab: a small experiment with an explicit stop rule Begin without a GPU: first run the provided input verification, frozen CPU installation and worker bridge. Installation can need network access; it installs no GPU packages. Then follow the recorded concrete-prompt replay and tiny transformer example through %%lsm cells. Inspect the messages, exact chat input, token IDs, output sequence and KV ledger. Predict the next row before revealing it. The replay itself downloads no weights and performs no inference: recorded intermediates are not your own GPU evidence or completion of the required 50-trial matrix. The executable notebook is the experiment contract, not an optional illustration. Protocol topic02-phase-v2 runs two pinned models sequentially: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. Each model has four batch-one cases—input 128 or 4,096 crossed with output 32 or 128—and one batch-four case at input 128/output 32. Five trials for each of ten model/case combinations give 50 raw trials. The B1/128/32 row is the matched control for B4/128/32. Output 512 and batch eight are optional extensions after the required core, not unannounced grading requirements. The previous slides' longer matrix has been retired; all three teaching surfaces now use this one bounded contract. Before executing, write a directional prediction for prompt length, output length and batch size. Name both the held-constant quantities and an observation that could contradict the prediction. “The GPU is memory-bound” is too broad. “At fixed model, precision, input and output lengths, B4 should improve aggregate decode rate because token rows can share weight work; per-sequence cadence may worsen” is testable. It still does not assert a kernel mechanism without a trace. Freeze your prediction in the analysis file so the explanation cannot be quietly rewritten after seeing the numbers. After the recorded replay, the GPU route resolves immutable snapshots from a persistent model cache. Only a missing snapshot in an online environment permits an initial download; the instructor rehearsal is offline. A fresh output directory must not mean a fresh model download. Next comes one small-model smoke, then the core matrix, then separate two-shape profiles. Each trial is checkpointed before checking allocation recovery. A failed run retains completed rows and a failure status; the validator refuses to call it complete. It also rejects missing or duplicated trials, wrong model revisions, nonfinite timings and incorrect step/rate arithmetic. Passing this CPU checker proves structure and consistency, not that someone really ran a GPU or diagnosed the right mechanism. What v2 changes—and why it is a new protocol Version 2 requests only last-position logits during prompt processing. In the pinned model implementation, logits_to_keep=1 avoids projecting every prompt position into the full vocabulary when only the last distribution is needed to choose the next output. At P=4,096 and vocabulary size 151,936, a full two-byte logits tensor alone would contain 4096×151936×2=1,244,659,712 bytes, about 1.16 GiB. The last-position slice needs 303,872 bytes, about 297 KiB. This is tensor accounting for the vocabulary output, not a measured total-memory saving; the full prompt still passes through the decoder and creates KV. The pinned Transformers source makes this argument inspectable. Each actual shape receives a full warmup path outside the trial timer. Shapes are shuffled within each of five rounds under a fixed order seed, limiting simple “all short cases first, all long cases last” bias. Models remain sequential to bound resource use. The caching allocator is not emptied between trials; freeing unused pools is a cleanup operation between models, not an invisible cold-start condition applied to every observation. Both synchronized wall and CUDA-event intervals are recorded. Because a Python-driven decode loop can leave gaps between launches, neither interval should be relabeled “sum of kernel execution time.” A separate kernel timeline is needed for that attribution. These changes alter the experiment. The historical v1 medians remain useful for teaching uncertainty and phase interpretation, but comparing v1 with v2 cannot isolate the effect of last-position logits, warmup, ordering or any other single change. A causal speedup claim would require a matched A/B experiment changing one declared factor under a shared protocol. The course does not need another uncontrolled performance headline; it needs an experiment whose evidence can survive questions. The complete v2 instructor record is linked in the following section, with raw arrays rather than only a selected median. Resource safety is part of reproducibility Historical 30 September instructor rehearsal: complete artifacts, unresolved variability The clean-source v2 rehearsal completed the smoke, all 50 core trials and both profiles in 190.248 seconds, using cached models offline. The maximum core allocated-memory peak was 3.271 GiB; after the process exited, device use returned to its initial 14 MiB. This verifies the bounded lab path on the instructor machine. It does not establish a stable performance baseline across machines or validate the cause of every timing difference. On the instructor host, an external memory-limited scope caps host RAM at 24 GiB with no additional swap allowance, and a wall timeout limits duration. Before and after notebook cells the runner requires at least 24 GiB host RAM available and at most 12 GiB device use. Student environments have their own available capacity, so the notebook's portable checks are not a promise that every Colab instance can finish every shape. If a run fails, keep the partial artifact and record the failed model/case, error class and available resource evidence. Inspect other GPU processes and retained tensor references. Do not raise the limits, shrink the matrix or relabel a smoke as a completed lab to obtain a green result. After fixing an identified cause, use a new attempt directory and explain the change; never overwrite the only failed evidence. A new attempt should reuse cached snapshots and the matching package environment. This discipline is just as important in a weekly course workflow as in production: twenty students' repeated evaluations are not twenty excuses to redownload the same model or leave stale processes behind. Read the trace in four passes First identify the scope. The required traces use the 0.5B model at B1, prompt 128 and prompt 4,096, with eight outputs each; they capture prefill plus seven decode forwards, not the full 128-output timing case. Second locate the named topic02_prefill and topic02_decode_7_steps CPU ranges and the corresponding CUDA activity. A host range is an annotation of code execution; without an explicit completion barrier at its end, it need not enclose every last device event it launched. Do not visually add unrelated host and GPU rows as if they were sequential. Here is a specific piece of that evidence, not a generic “GPU timeline.” In the P128/O8 trace, the first selected cudaLaunchKernel API interval in this excerpt spans 0–35.809 µs on the CPU. Its correlation-matched indexSelectSmallIndex GPU kernel starts at 47.801 µs and lasts 1.440 µs. The time origin is that first CPU launch, not request arrival. These are different events on an aligned trace clock: CPU API duration is not GPU kernel duration, and a gap alone does not identify its cause. The sanitized excerpt records the deterministic selection rule, eight consecutive kernels, associated launch intervals and original trace hash. The launch intervals belong to the named decode annotation; this is the synthetic 0.5B profile, not the 1.5B natural-prompt replay. Third distinguish framework attribution from physical kernel events. A PyTorch operator can launch one or several kernels, and user annotations can enclose many operators. The notebook's compact profiler summary is a ranked set of profiler entries, including operator, kernel and user-range representations; these rows are not disjoint time buckets and must not be summed into “total GPU time.” For actual kernel occupancy on the timeline, inspect CUDA kernel events and merge overlapping intervals at the desired boundary. A long operator name proves neither bandwidth saturation nor a specific end-to-end performance share. Record the event category, phase and input shape with every observation. Fourth propose the next test. If the trace suggests launch gaps, a more detailed system timeline and CPU activity are useful; if one selected kernel dominates, inspect its shape and relevant hardware counters. If the device is fast but client first-content time is slow, return to request spans. Save both traces and two annotated observations in the private analysis. Rerun any proposed optimization without profiling before reporting an improvement. The trace is a diagnostic intervention with overhead, not the production latency oracle. Vocabulary you should be able to explain without a slide Residual stream / pre-norm The running hidden representation updated by elementwise addition / a block ordering that normalizes each branch input before attention or MLP, with an unchanged bypass feeding the addition. RMSNorm / epsilon / gain Root-mean-square normalization over one row's features / a small positive stabilizer inside the square root / learned per-feature scaling. The operation does not average tokens together. Feature axis / head axis / position axis Coordinates of one representation / independent query projections or shared KV groups / locations in a sequence. Reshaping features into heads does not create more sequence positions. Bias / projection A learned additive output-coordinate vector / a learned linear mapping between feature spaces. A shared bias is added to each position; it is not a cache or attention mask. RoPE / causal mask Rotary position embedding rotates paired Q/K coordinates / a rule preventing a query from using future positions. Position information and future-access restriction solve different problems. Softmax / logits / greedy A normalized exponential distribution along a declared axis / unnormalized scores / choosing the highest score. Attention softmax spans source positions; vocabulary softmax spans possible output IDs. MLP / SiLU / SwiGLU A multi-layer perceptron operating per position / the function x×sigmoid(x) / a gated MLP that multiplies a SiLU branch with a second linear branch before projecting down. Concatenation / elementwise product Joining head-derived feature coordinates into one wider row / multiplying matching coordinates. Neither operation should be confused with matrix multiplication or summing across positions. Autoregressive dependency The next output choice uses earlier chosen tokens; parallel arithmetic within a step does not remove that chain. Prefill / decode Processing known prompt positions and selecting the first output, versus later forwards that advance each live sequence by one new position. GEMM / GEMV General matrix–matrix / matrix–vector multiplication. The token-row dimension helps explain why prefill and small-batch decode may use different kernels. Q, K, V Query, key and value projections in attention. Retained keys/values let later queries reuse already-computed history. MHA / GQA / MQA Multi-head, grouped-query and multi-query attention: respectively equal query/KV head counts, groups of queries sharing K/V, and all queries sharing one KV head. HBM / GDDR / DRAM High-bandwidth memory and graphics double-data-rate memory are device-memory technologies; dynamic RAM also underlies host memory. Do not apply one boundary's bandwidth to another. FLOP / FLOP/s Floating-point work / work rate. “GFLOP” alone is not a throughput unit. State whether a multiply-add counts as two operations. Arithmetic intensity / ridge Work per transferred byte at a declared boundary / intensity where compute and bandwidth roofs intersect. Allocated / reserved / peak Live allocator tensor bytes / the allocator's pool including reusable space / the maximum of a specified counter since reset. These are not three disjoint memory terms. Warmup / synchronization Excluded setup executions / an explicit completion boundary. A warm path can still vary; a barrier changes the interval being measured. SDPA Scaled dot-product attention API/path. The requested API name does not uniquely identify the kernel selected for every shape. Trace / profile A time-ordered event record / attributed performance information. Categories and scope matter more than the file's name. Questions that often reveal a missing boundary “If batch four is faster than expected, did we beat the bandwidth law?” No law predicts your wall time from the weight-only approximation. Cache reuse, launch overhead, shapes and experimental variation can all matter. Preserve the raw trials and investigate the specific claimed mechanism. “Why do two identical prefill shapes have different medians when only requested output length changed?” Prefill does not know the future loop count in this lab's forward call. Differences can arise from ordering, runtime/host scheduling, allocator state and variation; future output length is not a causal explanation by itself. This is a particularly useful internal consistency check. “Why not just synchronize after every token?” That would define a different decode loop and can change overlap and launch cadence. It may be useful for a separate token-level investigation, but cannot silently replace the current whole-decode timer. “Does a flat reserved-memory line prove a leak?” Not by itself: the allocator may retain reusable pool space while live allocated bytes recover. Check tensor ownership and repeated live-state growth. “Can I infer KV bytes from the model's advertised parameter count?” No; use layers, KV heads, head dimension and cache dtype. “Can the instructor's table replace my GPU run?” No; it is a reference for reasoning and artifact structure, not your submitted experiment. Chapter 03: Model quantization for production

We have a weight matrix and several typical inputs. How can we preserve its outputs with four bits per weight? First build a quantizer and improve it; then evaluate a real FP16/NF4 model on a GPU. This chapter teaches the mechanisms before the lab: follow one matrix from rounding to input-aware choices, then return to Qwen. Derive a scale; observe the outlier Four bits permit sixteen patterns. Our signed container has codes −8 through 7. For symmetric range fitting we use magnitudes up to 7, leaving −8 unused. This deliberate convention makes the fitted positive and negative ranges equal; it is neither the only INT4 convention nor NF4. Zero point is fixed at zero, so no separate offset is stored. is weight value per integer step, not bytes; is the code. Maximum magnitude 7 gives scale 1. An all-zero group uses scale 1 and code 0. Arithmetic uses Python floats, omitting scale-storage rounding. Why divide by 7? Seven steps must cover the largest magnitude at the positive endpoint. Now .49/1 rounds to 0, .40 rounds to 0, .60 rounds to 1, and 7 stays 7. The negative row becomes [0,−1,1,−1]. Signed error always means reconstructed minus original. These are three different outcomes; the service must expose enough evidence to distinguish them. One investigation, three student-owned skills Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct receives a support ticket and replies with billing, access or bug. The operational incident is concrete: “After successful login, the Save button does nothing and my edits disappear.” The expected label is bug; a measured FP16 output was access. A well-formed response can send work to the wrong team. Admission (A): verify the served name and implement a rendered positional budget. Completion and quality (B–C): understand token selection; implement evaluation over all attempted tickets and inspect real mistakes. Diagnosis (D–F): compare two one-factor policies on calibration, inspect their baseline and class recalls, freeze an observed choice, then test it on held-out and explain the errors. What vLLM does between JSON and generated text Current execution: the notebook uses managed Python 3.11.17, vLLM distribution 0.30.0+cu129 and module 0.30.0 ; it verifies both identities. The 0.29 architecture/API references and recorded request examples below are historical context, not instructions to install 0.29. Use the current frozen setup and 0.30 serve reference for the live lab. Old measured results keep their original versions and dates. The JSON body contains messages, a served model name and generation settings. In the historical vLLM 0.29.0 architecture, the API server handles HTTP and prepares model inputs, including tokenization. The engine core manages live requests, KV state and scheduling; workers perform model forward passes using weights and retained state on the GPU. This explains why a name mismatch can fail before expensive model execution and why correct admission does not guarantee available memory. These are responsibilities, not an assertion that every deployment has exactly four processes. See the versioned architecture description . The pinned Qwen model has 24 decoder layers, hidden width 896, 14 query heads and two KV heads, with head dimension 64. Hidden states use axes [batch, positions, 896]; logical K and V at one layer use [batch, 2 KV heads, retained positions, 64]. With FP16 K/V, one retained token costs bytes across layers, or 12 KiB. The first factor counts K and V; the final factor is bytes per FP16 scalar. This payload calculation excludes allocator blocks, weights and workspaces. It connects Topic 02's tensors to a concrete service decision: longer rendered inputs leave more live KV state. The model dimensions come from the immutable config , not an invented “typical LLM.” For one sequence, input IDs have shape [1, S], where S counts the entire rendered prompt. Prefill computes prompt states and fills the retained K/V. At a subsequent decode step the model consumes one newly selected token, attends to earlier positions and appends its K/V. The last-position hidden vector has 896 components. With column-vector notation, the vocabulary projection has shape [151936, 896], giving 151936 logits. Serving engines may pack positions from different requests; these are logical axes, not a captured vLLM buffer layout. Topic 03 used Transformers FP16 and bitsandbytes NF4. Here the same checkpoint is deliberately reloaded in FP16 as an engine-integration control. Keeping the task does not mean automatically loading the earlier NF4 representation into vLLM. Format support and task behavior require separate tests. How an output setting changes a prediction A logit is an unnormalized score for a vocabulary token. For a positive temperature T, compute . With invented logits [2, 1, 0], T=1 gives approximately [0.6652, 0.2447, 0.0900]. At T=0.5 the distribution concentrates to [0.8668, 0.1173, 0.0159]; T=2 flattens it to [0.5065, 0.3072, 0.1863]. Temperature zero is the greedy branch, not division by zero. It does not guarantee identical outputs across runtimes or hardware. These toy probabilities describe one next-token choice. They are not probabilities that a ticket belongs to a class, and they are not measured Qwen logits. A class string can span several tokens; its sequence probability involves conditional probabilities at successive steps. Do not interpret one generated token's log probability as calibrated class confidence. At T=1 and top_p=0.8 , token A alone contributes 0.6652, below the target cumulative mass. A+B reaches approximately 0.9100, so both remain and C is removed. Renormalization gives [0.7311, 0.2689, 0]. The threshold applies to cumulative mass after sorting, not independently to every token. Increasing top_p does not promise higher classification accuracy. The laboratory changes one setting at a time in this numerical toy; the fresh task baseline uses temperature zero. See the historical 0.29 sampling implementation . An output cap counts model tokens, including generated stopping tokens when counted by the runtime, not characters or events. In a separate invented task with labels refund/delay, a toy tokenizer splits refund into re + fund: a one-token cap yields re, which that task rejects. This is not the actual Qwen tokenizer. For our real exact-label task, a complete capped output exactly bug can pass the format rule while still being wrong. Inspect actual tokenizer IDs before assuming a cap is sufficient; EOS and a length cap are different stopping mechanisms. The current vLLM 0.30.0 worker accepts extra_body=&#123;"structured_outputs":&#123;"choice":["billing","access","bug"]&#125;&#125; . This constrains complete strings through legal continuations. At string prefix b, billing and bug remain possible; at bi, only billing remains. This is a string-prefix illustration, not three measured token IDs. A sequence-aware grammar handles multi-token names and termination. It can suppress explanations, but a wrong allowed label remains wrong and an insufficient cap can still truncate. The versioned structured-output documentation explains the supported field; the old guided_choice field is not used. Evaluate all attempts, not only convenient outputs Keep three predicates. Protocol complete means the supported response finished without error (for raw streaming, recognized finish plus DONE). Valid task format means that its complete content, after outer whitespace removal only, is exactly one of the three lowercase names. Correct means that the valid label matches the declared gold label. The parser must not extract billing from billing because… or accept a partial access prefix. Our eight-attempt fixture contains four correct predictions, one wrong valid label, one complete non-label, one partial correct-looking prefix and one failed attempt. Six are complete; five are valid; four are correct. Accuracy is 4/8=50%, valid-label rate 5/8=62.5%, completion rate 6/8=75%. Accuracy conditional on validity is 4/5=80%: a different statistic that hides invalid or incomplete cases if reported alone. For an empty population, a rate is undefined; the notebook returns None. The confusion matrix has three true-class rows and four prediction columns: billing, access, bug and invalid/incomplete. Every attempted ticket occupies one cell. A wrong valid label moves into an off-diagonal class cell; a malformed or failed response goes into the fourth column. This preserves both model mistakes and service failures instead of dropping them from the denominator. Read the actual model mistakes The Topic 03 T4 capture measured Transformers FP16 on 12 handwritten tickets, four per class. All outputs were valid names; six were correct. In true-row/predicted-column order the matrix is [[0,3,1,0],[0,4,0,0],[0,2,2,0]]. Access appears in nine predictions. This supports investigating class confusion; it does not establish a cause without a controlled intervention or production accuracy from twelve cases. Worked ML examples and self-checks A correct format can hide a constant classifier The historical v2 vLLM task run contains 12 calibration and six held-out tickets. Calibration has four gold examples per class: always answering access gets 4/12, or 33.3%. Qwen gets 6/12, or 50%, but its billing recall is 0/4; access recall 4/4; bug recall 2/4. A single overall rate hides the unserved billing category. On held-out, Qwen outputs access on all six tickets and gets 2/6, exactly the constant-access baseline. Every answer is complete and valid. This measured result motivates error analysis; it does not prove the cause is prompt wording, GPU execution or the model itself. Six handwritten cases also cannot establish a statistically reliable quality change from 50% to 33.3%. Self-check: if a classifier outputs bug for all six balanced tickets, what are accuracy and billing recall? Accuracy is 2/6; billing recall is 0/2. Changing the constant label does not make the classifier useful. A nucleus threshold is cumulative mass At T=1, toy A/B/C probabilities are 0.6652, 0.2447 and 0.0900. With p=0.8, A alone is insufficient. A+B reaches 0.9099 with rounded inputs, or approximately 0.9100 before rounding; retain both. Divide by the retained exact mass to get 0.7311 and 0.2689. Neither retained token individually exceeds 0.8. Self-check: at p=0.6, which tokens survive? Only A: its mass already exceeds the threshold, so its renormalized probability is 1. This describes a toy next-token decision, not a calibrated probability that a ticket belongs to billing. The green port that proves too little Picture an operator who has launched a local model server. The process has not exited; port 8000 accepts connections; a monitoring page says “healthy.” A student client sends a chat request and receives 404. Another sends a long conversation and receives 400. A third sees several streaming content fragments and then a disconnect without a terminal marker. These symptoms have different owners. A listening socket proves almost none of the promised chat contract: not model-name agreement, not template rendering, not context admission, not final completion, and certainly not behavior under load. Chapter 01 taught us to separate clocks and failure populations; here we separate API, engine and GPU boundaries. The pinned Topic 04 instructor smoke on the RTX 5070 Ti lets us inspect several of those boundaries without inventing a production outage. It used one pinned Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct snapshot and vLLM 0.29.0, served locally as topic04 . Positive chat and streaming probes completed; a wrong served name returned 404; a 2,329-token rendered prompt against a 2,048-token cap returned 400. The evidence covers five single-client probes, not a 64-client capacity test. We will make the inference from each probe deliberately narrow. A chat request crosses four contracts Client model name · messages · deadline → API frontend route · validation · status → Template roles → rendered tokens → Engine admission · scheduler · GPU → Response finish reason · terminal marker Logical ownership, not a process diagram. A 404, 400, incomplete SSE stream and GPU OOM should not all trigger the same “restart the model” response. The name the client actually sends The instructor’s bounded vLLM 0.29.0 run served pinned Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct as topic04 on localhost. GET /v1/models advertised topic04 ; that was the string the SDK had to send in its model field. Sending a different served name returned HTTP 404. The cheapest discriminating probe for “model not found” is therefore the model-list route, not a GPU profile or a restart. The vLLM serve reference documents the server flags; check it against the installed version rather than assuming a current web page exactly describes an older run. Chat adds a tokenizer/template boundary. JSON role messages are rendered into model-specific tokens; template markers and history consume context. A completions route may work even when chat fails, and a model-list route says nothing about either generation path. vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible server documentation lists the supported routes and caveats. Record the tokenizer revision together with the weights and the rendered prompt-token count. The model has three names and one pinned body The source model ID is Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct . The actual weights and tokenizer came from immutable revision 7ae557604adf67be50417f59c2c2f167def9a775 in the local cache. The API-facing served name was topic04 . These strings have different jobs. The client does not need to know the local snapshot path; it does need to send the API name that GET /v1/models advertises. In the smoke record, the advertised list contained topic04 . A client that sends another model string receives 404 before a slow GPU investigation is warranted. The run record keeps the served name and revision together, so “the server was up” cannot silently mean a different checkpoint. Version pinning is not ornamental. A mutable model identifier can later resolve to changed tokenizer files or template behavior even when application code is unchanged. A reproducible deployment records weight revision, tokenizer revision, engine/runtime release, precision and launch arguments. The smoke's WSL2 environment used a V1-runner/native-sampler fallback for host compatibility; that local workaround is not a universal launch recommendation. The vLLM 0.29.0 CLI reference helps find flag semantics, but the recorded vLLM 0.29.0 run and installed help are the authority for this specific experiment. The model consumes token IDs produced after applying its chat template, including role delimiters, possible system instructions, conversation history and generation marker. A model-list route can return 200 while chat fails because the served name in the request is wrong, a template is missing or incompatible, the rendered input exceeds the configured limit, or generation fails after admission. A plain completion request may bypass some chat-template behavior. The cheapest next probe depends on the status: list models for name mismatch, inspect rendered tokens for 400, inspect server/worker logs for generation failure.
