A stream has a lifecycle, not just fragments Server-sent events (SSE) deliver a sequence of frames over one HTTP response. A client may see role or metadata frames before nonempty content; it may see several content deltas; then it expects a completion signal. In the historical 29 September raw probe, eleven JSON frames were parsed and the terminal [DONE] marker arrived. The SDK's separate streaming probe produced content with finish_reason=stop , first content at 0.053 seconds and total wall time 0.463 seconds. These are separate requests ; 0.053 is first content observed by that client, not a universal model-token TTFT. When may a client call a streamed answer complete? Open HTTP response begins → Frames metadata + content deltas → Finish reason: stop or limit → [DONE] terminal SSE marker Strict completion rule for this course's raw-SSE probe. A socket close after content but before the expected terminal marker is a partial stream, not an ordinary complete answer. Verify the exact protocol for the installed server version. A proxy can buffer or coalesce frames, changing the client's first-content time without changing engine computation. It can also time out or close a stream after several deltas. The application should distinguish an intentionally complete answer from a partial one and avoid saving partial text as if it passed the same quality check. A retry after partial delivery needs its own idempotency and user-interface policy; repeating generation may produce different text. Chapter 01's observer-clock lesson applies again: capture server emission and client receipt separately before blaming decode. One complete CPU example: bytes become text, lines and events Server-sent events, abbreviated SSE, define a text framing format. The format does not imply that each network read contains one event, that each event contains one token, or that each token corresponds to one Unicode character. Separate all four units before writing a parser. A socket supplies bytes. UTF-8 maps bytes into Unicode text. Line endings divide that text into fields. A blank line dispatches an SSE event. Only then can an application interpret the event’s data as a JSON object or the API-specific terminal string [DONE] . The WHATWG event-stream specification defines framing; the pinned vLLM chat implementation defines its chat payloads. The following request and stream are synthetic CPU fixtures . No model produced their content, timings or usage counters. Their purpose is to make every parser state inspectable without downloads, CUDA or a running service. The notebook embeds the same fixture JSON and standard-library parser. The question is deliberately different from the historical server smoke, so a reader cannot accidentally attach old GPU timings to it. {JSON.stringify(fixture.request,null,2)} The text deltas concatenate in arrival order to Café ☕. . The role event has empty content. The finish event ends generation, the usage event reports accounting, and the final data event contains [DONE] . A leading heartbeat comment is a framed record but produces no application data event. Consequently this fixture has seven records including the comment, six data events, five JSON objects, two content events and sixteen supplied byte chunks. The invented usage counter says four completion tokens. Those are five different counts with different meanings, not alternative spellings of “tokens.” Inspect the entire fixture wire text Visible \r\n below denotes the two line-ending characters. A second line ending closes each event. The actual fixture uses those bytes, not four printable backslash letters. {fixture.frames.map((frame,index)=>`Record ${index+1}\n${frame.replaceAll('\r','\\r').replaceAll('\n','\\n\n')}`).join('\n')} A chunk can end halfway through é In UTF-8, é occupies the two bytes C3 A9 , and ☕ occupies E2 98 95 . One network read can end after C3 ; the next can begin with A9 . Decoding the first read independently with strict UTF-8 fails because the sequence is incomplete. Decoding it with replacement mode may insert a replacement character and irreversibly damage the JSON string. An incremental decoder retains the unfinished byte prefix and combines it with the next read. The same reasoning applies to the three-byte coffee character, which the fixture deliberately splits after E2 . Chunk boundaries are accidental transport observations. A proxy, TLS record, OS buffer or HTTP client implementation can change them without changing the logical event stream. The classroom fixture supplies sixteen chunks to stress this fact. Joining every chunk first and parsing at EOF would recover the same final text, but would defeat streaming and make first-content measurements meaningless. A correct streaming client processes complete events as soon as enough bytes arrive while preserving every incomplete suffix for the next read. Line buffering and event dispatch SSE accepts LF, CRLF or CR line endings. CRLF may itself split between reads, so the parser needs to remember a trailing CR and avoid interpreting the following LF as an extra blank line. A line beginning with a colon is a comment. A field such as data: hello contributes hello to the event’s data buffer; the parser removes at most one optional space after the colon. Two data lines become one data value separated by newline. The next blank line dispatches the assembled event. Unknown fields do not become JSON content merely because they arrived on the same connection. For example, data: &#123;"choices":[], followed by data: "usage":&#123;"prompt_tokens":13,"completion_tokens":4,"total_tokens":17&#125;&#125; and a blank line forms one JSON document with a newline after its comma. Calling json.loads on either data line independently fails. Conversely, a single network read may contain two whole events, and a parser that stops after the first loses data. The notebook tests both split and coalesced input. At EOF, the parser must not dispatch an event that never reached its blank-line terminator. A minimal processing sketch is below. It names state rather than hiding it inside a library. The actual notebook implementation additionally validates JSON shape, choice index, byte limits, trailing input, usage fields and invalid UTF-8. Its scope is a single text choice. It does not implement browser reconnection, arbitrary event handlers, tools, audio, multimodal output or every provider’s stream dialect. {`for byte_chunk in incoming_reads: decoded_text = utf8_decoder.feed(byte_chunk) for complete_line in line_buffer.feed(decoded_text): if complete_line is a comment: continue if complete_line is a data field: event_data.append(field_value) if complete_line is blank: payload = join_data_lines_with_newline(event_data) event_data.clear() if payload == "[DONE]": mark_terminal() elif payload: update_client_state(parse_json(payload)) on_eof: reject_invalid_utf8_or_unterminated_data() classify_using_finish_done_and_error_state()`} Protocol completion, output quality and cancellation Keep at least the accumulated content, finish reason, usage object, terminal-marker flag and error state. A role event can initialize metadata without appending text. A nonempty content delta appends exactly its string; trimming every delta would turn Café plus ☕. into Café☕. . An empty choices list can carry usage and must not trigger choices[0] . A finish reason can arrive before the final accounting event, so stopping immediately at finish discards legitimate trailing metadata. Under the course’s strict one-choice text contract, normal completion requires a recognized finish reason, terminal [DONE] , valid stream shape and no recorded error. finish_reason="stop" usually indicates the generation reached its stopping condition. finish_reason="length" indicates a cap stopped it. Either can terminate a syntactically complete stream, but a length-limited answer may be unacceptable for the task. A parser should retain the reason, while the application decides whether the answer satisfies its requirements. A calculator demanding one integer can reject fluent prose after a normal stop. A summarizer can reject a sentence cut in half after a length stop. A tool-calling application requires a different success predicate from this chapter’s text-only client. The API may send an error object after HTTP headers already declared success. At that point, the server cannot revise the already transmitted status code. The pinned vLLM implementation can emit an error event and then [DONE] . Therefore the terminal marker alone cannot mean successful generation. Preserve the error even when DONE arrives afterward. A stream with plausible partial text and no DONE is likewise incomplete under this course contract. Saving that text as a fully accepted result corrupts both the user experience and the success denominator. Fixture variant Client observation Classification What it does not establish All events Content, stop, usage, DONE Complete protocol response Model quality or real server health Drop terminal event Same text, no DONE Partial That generation finished successfully Cancel after first content Café , local cancel Cancelled Engine KV state has been released Invalid JSON or error object Malformed or failed response Failed A useful complete answer The correct timestamp depends on the question For the synthetic fixture, the first data event arrives at 0.03 seconds but contains only the assistant role. First content arrives at 0.10 seconds, another content event arrives at 0.14, finish at 0.15, usage at 0.16 and DONE at 0.17. If send time is zero, first-content delay equals 0.10 − 0 = 0.10 s , or 100 ms. Terminal wall time equals 170 ms. An empty heartbeat at 10 ms does not become a first-token measurement merely because it is the first transport activity. These are illustrative client arrivals supplied by the fixture, not measurements of vLLM. The 40 ms difference between the two text events is an inter-event interval. It cannot establish token latency because the two strings may each encode multiple model tokens. Even when the server exposes token IDs, buffering may group their client arrivals. To compute a mean of known token-arrival gaps, state that there are N observed token timestamps, use (where and are the first and last token-arrival times), and retain the complete arrival sequence if studying jitter. With 40 tokens, first arrival at 0.40 s and last at 1.18 s, the illustrative mean is 0.78/39 = 0.020 s/gap . A DONE event at 1.20 s adds 20 ms of terminal processing; substituting it for the last-token timestamp mixes two quantities. Neither calculation isolates GPU decode. A client timeout does not prove engine cancellation A connection deadline limits establishing the route. A first-content deadline limits waiting for useful text. A read-inactivity timeout limits the interval without incoming transport progress. A total deadline limits the entire attempt. These clocks answer different questions and may expire at different times. An SDK timeout parameter is not automatically a whole-request wall budget; inspect its HTTP client semantics. Record the expired clock, preserve partial content with its incomplete status, and close the response in a cleanup path. Never substitute zero for an unavailable first-content time. Closing the client stream is the first step in cancellation. The frontend and any proxy must observe the disconnect, propagate an abort for the relevant request, and release live engine state. A client-only fixture can prove that the application labels an attempt cancelled, but cannot prove that a real GPU worker stopped generating or released KV blocks. That needs engine-side active-request evidence, resource recovery and, ideally, a follow-up bounded smoke. The historical course run did not contain a cancellation experiment, so cancellation cleanup remains a proposed test rather than a measured success. Browser EventSource adds automatic reconnect behavior around a GET request. This chapter uses an HTTP POST carrying a JSON generation request and reads its response as SSE. Copying EventSource’s reconnect policy blindly into this client can start another generation, duplicate text or replay tool side effects. A retry is a new attempt unless an explicitly supported application protocol proves otherwise. Keep its attempt ID and metrics separate. After partial display, decide whether to replace the old answer, offer a user-controlled retry, or visibly preserve the partial answer. Appending a regenerated answer to the first one is usually a bug. Worked incident: healthy generation, delayed delivery Consider an illustrative observation: direct loopback receives its first content at 100 ms and successive events afterward, while an external client receives all events near 900 ms. This pattern suggests buffering somewhere on the external path, but does not prove which component caused it. Compare the same prompt, model, sampling settings and request correlation fields. Inspect server emission spans and proxy configuration without subtracting unsynchronized wall clocks from different machines. Test the direct and proxied paths separately, with one bounded request each. If the proxy buffers by block, changing that policy and rerunning the paired test should change client arrival shape while leaving engine work comparable. A successful local probe does not certify remote timeouts, authentication, TLS or cancellation propagation. Equally, a slow remote first-content time does not justify increasing GPU memory utilization before inspecting the route. Write the diagnosis as a falsifiable hypothesis: “The proxy holds events until its buffer flushes.” Evidence against it could be late engine emission even on the direct route. The purpose of the service map is to find this next discriminating measurement, not to assign every delay to the nearest unfamiliar component. A useful negative test is an expected failure The wrong-model and over-context probes deliberately produce non-2xx responses. They are not “failed lab runs”; they test that invalid input is rejected at a predictable boundary. For the wrong-model request, 404 points first to the served-name contract. For the 2,329-token rendered prompt against a 2,048-token cap, 400 points to validation of a declared size limit. The latter is better than allowing impossible work to consume GPU memory until an obscure worker error occurs. A 500-class error or transport disconnect on a valid request would be a different incident and should not be merged with these expected negatives in a “failure rate” denominator. When writing automated checks, assert the status, the relevant response shape, and the reason the input should fail. Do not merely assert “not 200.” Otherwise a broken server that returns 500 for every request would pass the negative suite. Positive and negative probes belong together: model list, ordinary chat, stream completion, wrong identity and over-context jointly test a small observable contract. Their combined success is a strong smoke result and a weak capacity result—exactly the distinction the chapter intends to teach. Context is a memory policy, not merely a string length Count rendered tokens after applying the exact chat template, then add the requested output cap before judging a model-length limit. Long prompts also create KV state; a request-count cap alone cannot guarantee fit. The KV budget explorer shows the logical payload arithmetic, but it omits vLLM’s allocator and runtime reserves. The engine arguments document context and memory controls; the run record states which values this course actually used. Worked context calculation: reject before expensive work The server launch set --max-model-len 2048 . The negative probe's chat template produced 2,329 prompt tokens. The prompt alone exceeded the configured limit by 2329 − 2048 = 281 tokens, so rejecting it with HTTP 400 was a valid, inexpensive outcome; no amount of queue patience could make that request fit the declared context. A different illustrative request with 1,800 rendered prompt tokens and a 512-token output cap asks for up to 2,312 total positions, also beyond 2,048, though its input alone fits. An application should make this distinction visible instead of telling every 400 caller only “bad request.” The first pair is measured; the second is a worked example. The limit applies after rendering roles and template markers Scenario Rendered prompt Requested output cap Against 2,048 Pinned negative probe 2,329 Not needed to exceed 281 over; observed HTTP 400 Illustrative chat 1,800 512 2,312 potential; 264 over Illustrative smaller chat 1,800 128 1,928 potential; 120 spare Only the first row is a measured API response. Actual admitted-generation accounting follows the installed runtime's rules; the worked rows teach why output budget belongs in the context decision. A request-count cap is not a memory proof The launch also set --max-num-seqs 4 and --gpu-memory-utilization 0.45 . Four is an upper bound on simultaneously active sequences in that configuration, not an achieved client throughput or evidence that four maximum-length sequences were ever present. From the pinned 0.5B model config , 24 layers, two KV heads and a 64-dimensional head at two bytes per value give 2 × 24 × 2 × 64 × 2 = 12,288 bytes = 12 KiB of logical FP16 KV payload per retained token. Four hypothetical full 2,048-token sequences would hold 4 × 2048 × 12 KiB = 96 MiB of logical KV payload. This is not the service's allocated VRAM: model weights, runtime reservation, block accounting, graph buffers and other tensors remain. The arithmetic also does not imply that a 45% memory-utilization target is “mostly unused GPU.” Engine flags control an allocator budget and runtime behavior; memory visible in a device monitor may include reserved pools. A cap of four sequences can prevent the instructor smoke from overcommitting a host but tells us little about a different model or a 64-client workload. To design a real admission envelope, measure peak live and reserved memory across the intended context distribution and check failures as clients increase. Chapter 02's KV calculation is a component ledger, not a license to set request count by division alone. The course’s public submission example carries only student-facing artifacts. Weekly repetition should reuse assets, not stale processes A repeatable lab has two different kinds of state. The Topic 04 smoke used loopback-only host 127.0.0.1 , port 8000 , FP16, a 2,048-token model length, at most four active sequences, a 0.45 GPU-memory-utilization target and eager execution. The launch command as a reproducibility record {launch} &lt;PINNED_LOCAL_SNAPSHOT&gt; is an explanatory placeholder, not a literal shell path. The notebook resolves the verified local snapshot and passes arguments as a list, avoiding shell interpretation of a path. --served-model-name fixes the API identity. --host 127.0.0.1 binds to the loopback interface. --dtype float16 declares the model compute/storage choice supported by this run. --max-model-len 2048 establishes the context cap. --max-num-seqs 4 limits sequences processed in one iteration according to the vLLM 0.29.0 CLI reference ; it is not four requests per second or a cap on every connected client. --gpu-memory-utilization 0.45 controls an executor memory budget. --enforce-eager chooses the eager execution path for this bounded teaching run. The rendering/tokenizer/template boundary is implicated after frontend identity and basic engine checks. Avoid subtracting unsynchronized host clocks. Terms used in this chapter Logit An unnormalized vocabulary-token score at a generation step. It is neither a probability nor automatically a class score. Nucleus / top_p The smallest descending prefix of next-token probabilities reaching the specified cumulative mass, followed by renormalization. All-attempt accuracy Correct accepted labels divided by every attempted ticket, retaining failed, malformed and incomplete outputs. Per-class recall Correct predictions for one gold class divided by all attempted examples of that class. Baseline A declared simple control; here a constant access prediction exposes whether a classifier adds useful discrimination. Calibration The development cases used to compare and choose a configuration. This means configuration selection here, not probability calibration. Held-out Cases excluded from configuration choice and evaluated only after freeze. Public classroom examples are not a secret production benchmark. Token probability and class confidence A next-token distribution describes one vocabulary decision; interpreting it as calibrated confidence in a whole class string needs a separate method and validation. Served model name The API-facing identifier advertised to clients, independent of a local filesystem path. Chat template The model-specific rendering rule that places roles, message content and generation delimiters before tokenization. UTF-8 A variable-width encoding of Unicode text into bytes. One character can cross network-read boundaries. SSE event A dispatched event assembled from text fields and a blank-line boundary. Its data is not inherently a model token. Delta An incremental update, such as a fragment of content or metadata. Append content exactly, preserving spaces. Finish reason The generation-level reason an output ended, distinct from the terminal transport marker. First-content delay The client interval from sending the request to the first nonempty generated text delta. Readiness An operational decision that this deployment can serve the declared client contract, supported by appropriate probes. Cancellation A request to stop an in-flight attempt. Client classification and actual server resource release require different evidence. Smoke test A small bounded test of a declared path. It can reveal broken integration without estimating capacity or quality over a population. The next topic opens the engine boundary: how live sequences share KV blocks and how the scheduler admits work at iteration boundaries. Here the deliverable is the observable client and lifecycle contract that makes those later measurements interpretable.

Chapter 05: PagedAttention & continuous batching

This chapter and its lab form one engineering investigation. The corrected notebook code passed its own two full instructor browser rehearsals on 13 October 2026 (UTC), Tesla T4 / standard RAM. That does not certify learner understanding, free GPU quota or deployment quality. Results and instructor solutions stay private;{' '} the topic page separates the acceptance states . One classifier and several unfinished requests The application is the support-ticket router from Topic 04. “I forgot my password and cannot sign in to my account.” should go to access . “I can log in, but clicking Export crashes the application.” should go to bug . These are handwritten teaching cases, not a representative customer population. The gold label describes the desired answer; it does not establish what Qwen will predict. A useful serving change must preserve evidence about wrong answers rather than counting any completed string as a successful classification. Suppose a short ticket arrives while another request has a longer context or continues generating. The weights are shared, but the requests have different histories, stopping conditions and arrival times. Three questions follow. Where does each request's computed history live? Which request can execute next? What measurement could support a claim that the complete service improved? Paged KV placement, iteration scheduling and comparative measurement answer those questions separately. None, by itself, improves the classifier's understanding of the ticket. The required engineering actions are deliberately small: account for independently rounded KV capacity; select arrived requests for available decode slots; inspect a controlled pipeline/vLLM comparison. A driver, server launcher or timing utility is supplied infrastructure, not the student's primary intellectual work. The supplied GPU comparison passed technical rehearsal with instructor solutions; this chapter does not publish new speed results. A local vocabulary for the investigation Prefill is a forward computation over the rendered prompt positions.{' '} Decode consumes the latest selected ID to compute the next prediction.{' '} A forward is one evaluation of model operations, not necessarily one client request.{' '} EOS is a configured end-of-sequence ID that can stop generation before the cap.{' '} A backend is the implementation executing attention or the larger inference stack. A pool is reserved reusable storage. A token budget limits scheduled positions in an iteration, not users or bytes. Preemption suspends some work when resources are needed elsewhere; recomputation rebuilds lost intermediate history from retained IDs. Topic 02 explains K/V and autoregression in more detail; Topic 04 explains the distinction between model output quality and service execution. What the named model stores The pinned Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct configuration {' '} has 24 decoder layers, hidden width 896, 14 query heads, 2 KV heads and head width 64. Grouped-query attention lets seven query heads use each KV head. The cache stores the keys and values, not fourteen independent copies just because fourteen query heads exist. For one layer and one request, a logical key tensor has axes [KV head, retained position, head feature], with lengths [2, S, 64]. The value tensor has the same logical shape. “Position” is a place in the actual rendered model input or computed generation history; it is not a word, character, client or vocabulary index. During ordinary decode one new input position produces new K/V at each layer. These logical shapes do not specify whether a backend stores physical memory in head-major or position-major order. The first generated ID is selected from the prompt's forward pass. That selected ID acquires its own KV only when a later forward consumes it. A stop token may never be consumed in another forward. Consequently prompt length plus output cap is a conservative planning quantity, not necessarily the exact live cache length at a chosen instant. Allocator lookahead and block rounding are additional implementation choices. With FP16 keys and values, multiply two objects, 24 layers, 2 KV heads, 64 features and 2 bytes per element. The result is 12,288 bytes, or 12 KiB, per retained position across all layers. The first factor 2 counts K and V; the final factor 2 counts bytes per scalar. Confusing those factors makes later calculations hard to audit. Using fourteen query heads instead of two KV heads overcounts this payload by seven. means bytes per position across all layers; is layers; is KV heads; is features per head; is bytes per scalar. The leading 2 counts K and V. This configuration gives 12 KiB, excluding metadata and weights. This is not the total memory of a running model. It excludes weights, temporary tensors, block tables, alignment, allocator reservations and any extra precision metadata. Changing the weight representation to four bits does not automatically change this FP16 KV formula. Model weights and per-request state are different objects. A physical block is a storage unit For the main arithmetic example, one block has sixteen position slots. Request lengths 17, 31 and 33 therefore need 2, 2 and 3 independent blocks. Total capacity is 7 × 16 = 112 positions for 81 live positions. There are 31 unused tail positions: 15 for the first request, 1 for the second and 15 for the third. At 12 KiB per position the live payload is 972 KiB, while ideal block capacity is 1,344 KiB. The difference, 372 KiB, is unused tail capacity under these assumptions, not a measured change in nvidia-smi . Why not round the total 81 positions once? That would produce six blocks with 96 slots. It assumes that one request can fill another request's unfinished tail. That is a different ownership policy from the independent block tables in this example. The accounting function must round each independent request first, then sum. A zero-length request uses zero blocks in the toy. Empty input produces zero totals, not an exception or an invented placeholder page. is retained positions of request i; is positions per block; is total blocks. Sum after per-request rounding: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7. Shared-prefix blocks are excluded. For simple growing full-attention sequences without sharing, at most one block per request is partly live. That observation explains why unused capacity is bounded in this model. It is not a statement that all serving memory is fragmentation-free. Metadata, reserved pools, prefix sharing, sliding-window attention, speculative lookahead and hybrid cache groups need their own accounting. A KV page is also not a CUDA thread block: one concerns stored positions, the other groups GPU execution threads. How attention finds noncontiguous history A request presents a logically ordered sequence, but its storage need not occupy one contiguous run of physical blocks. The block table maps each logical block index to a physical block in the pool. In the separate tiny diagram below, block size is four, not sixteen. A has six positions: logical block 0 maps to physical 3 and logical block 1 to physical 0. B has three positions in physical 2. Physical IDs are invented pool indices, not token IDs, device addresses or observations of a real allocation. For logical position 5 and block size 4, integer division identifies logical block 1; the remainder identifies offset 1. A's table maps that block to physical 0, so the read uses offset 1 in physical 0 for A's corresponding K/V head and feature. The unused offsets must not become extra context. The live length and causal/mask policy determine which positions are legal. The physical memory layout within a block is backend dependent. Finishing A can release its references while B continues. If a physical page has another live owner, it must not be overwritten. Prefix caching introduces an additional distinction: an unreferenced cached page may be evictable while still retaining useful bytes. An engine can keep the whole pool allocated and reuse free blocks internally. Logical release need not reduce device-level allocated memory. This is why a flat nvidia-smi curve cannot prove that completed requests were never released. Paged storage cannot change the attention equation Consider a deliberately tiny head with one feature. Query is 1; keys are 1, 2, 3, 4 and the paired values are 10, 20, 30, 40. All four keys are legal for this final query. The usual square-root head-width factor is 1 because the toy dimension is 1. Real Qwen heads have width 64 and retain positional and masking rules. The scalar helper applies a stable softmax by subtracting the maximum score before exponentiating. Scalar query , keys and values define this invented D=1 final-query example. All retained keys are legal. It omits real head scaling and positional/mask details. The global weights are approximately 0.032059, 0.087144, 0.236883 and 0.643914. They sum to 1; their weighted value sum is 34.926527. Suppose the first two K/V pairs occupy one page and the last two another. Normalizing each page separately produces 17.310586 and 37.310586. Averaging those outputs gives 27.310586, not 34.926527. The failure is the denominator. The correct attention gives pages different total probability mass according to all scores together; the wrong average gives each page half the mass regardless of its scores. Implementations may compute partial statistics and combine them stably without materializing the whole attention matrix, but their combined result must preserve global normalization. “The values are stored on separate pages” is not a license to define separate attentions. Here is the missing merge step. Let a page's stable unnormalized mass be{' '} , with the same {' '} global score maximum . Its local output is{' '} . Then{' '} . For this example the normalized page masses are 0.119203 and 0.880797. The merge is 0.119203 × 17.310586 + 0.880797 × 37.310586 ≈ 34.926527. Equal masses 0.5/0.5 instead produce 27.310586. A teaching diagram must identify which error it actually demonstrates. Change the block size without changing the population Keep lengths 17, 31 and 33 and the same scalar dtype. The batch can outlive its short member Now hold memory placement aside and examine scheduling. Two decode slots are available. A, B and C arrive at tick 0 with 5, 1 and 1 decode steps. D arrives at tick 2 with 2 steps. Each active request executes one step during [t,t+1), and any completion releases its slot at t+1. At 5, C and D enter the next cohort; C completes at 6 and D at 7. A request-level batch can finish its short member early without admitting a new member. That distinction is lost when “static batching” is described as if every member completed simultaneously. Continuous mode evaluates membership at each iteration boundary. After B finishes, C enters at 1 and finishes at 2. D is then eligible by arrival time and enters at 2; it finishes at 4. A still finishes at 5. Independent requests share work; A's five dependent decode steps are not predicted simultaneously. Continuous batching changes membership, not autoregression. Read the trace without inventing milliseconds The completion ticks for A/B/C/D are 5/1/6/7 in static mode and 5/1/2/4 in continuous mode. Residence time subtracts arrival. D's static residence is 7 − 2 = 5, not 7; its continuous residence is 4 − 2 = 2. Averaging all four requests gives 4.25 versus 2.5 ticks. Makespan is 7 versus 5 ticks. Idle slot-ticks are 5 versus 1: two slots times total elapsed ticks, minus the same 9 useful request steps. None of these numbers is a measured GPU metric. Completion here means the end of the request's invented decode work, not the arrival of a client-visible response from the pipeline API. The unit-time assumption does essential work. Actual iteration duration depends on active tensor shapes, prompt/decode work, memory traffic, kernels and framework overhead. A hypothetical continuous iteration cost twice as high would make 5 × 2 exceed 7 × 1. That counterexample is not an observed vLLM slowdown; it demonstrates why the shortest logical trace alone cannot establish a wall-time improvement. Nor are active slots equal to measured GPU SM utilization. A useful prediction is consequently conditional: replacing empty cohort slots can admit work earlier, but the resulting task completion and cost must be measured under a specified workload. The lab asks for that prediction before the observation. It does not force the student to declare that vLLM must win. Where the real V1 scheduler differs The pinned 0.30.0 tuning guide {' '} describes chunked prefill and a scheduled-token budget. A sequence limit, client concurrency, token budget and KV capacity constrain different objects. For simple arithmetic, three ordinary decode positions consume 3 of a 256-token budget, leaving 253 for a 300-position prefill. This is an explanatory budget example, not a logged execution of the current scheduler. Inspect the actual scheduler source {' '} and KV manager {' '} when interpreting behavior. Already-running work, chunk eligibility, capacity and recomputation make the decode-only model incomplete. A waiting request can be blocked by one limit even if another resource appears available. Increasing a sequence limit is not equivalent to increasing the token budget or allocating more KV capacity. The Paged Attention design page {' '} explicitly labels its kernel description historical. It is valuable for learning the original mechanism, not a claim that every current attention backend executes that exact kernel. Likewise the original paper's speed ratios belong to its evaluated systems and workloads, not a guaranteed multiplier for this notebook. A versioned explanation preserves that boundary. Chapter 06: High concurrency: the saturation knee

This chapter follows the approved saturation-knee arc. The notebook mock profile validates the analysis pipeline on a declared synthetic queue; the measured T4 runs of 18 and 21 October 2026 are published with their limits. Teacher materials and raw run evidence stay private;{' '} the topic page separates the acceptance states . One service, many simultaneous clients The support-ticket classifier from Topics 04–05 answers one request well. This chapter asks what happens when many arrive at once: where throughput stops growing, which resource runs out first, what errors and tail latency do at that boundary, and how to defend one operating point under a service-level objective. The course leaderboard already scores the geometric mean of output throughput at 32 and 64 concurrent clients — this chapter teaches you to read the curve you are being graded on. Begin with the incident. The service is healthy at 8 users: replies arrive in fractions of a second, every deadline met. At the rush hour, 128 simultaneous clients arrive, and three things happen at once: requests start dying at their wall-clock budgets (the client, not the server, gives up); users refresh their tabs, silently doubling the offered demand; and the replies that do arrive are late enough to miss product deadlines even though their content is correct. Nothing about the model changed — same weights, same GPU, same code. The question "what ran out?" has exactly two prime suspects, and the whole chapter is a disciplined investigation of which one, when, and what honest evidence looks like. Three habits carry the whole investigation. Errors are data: a timed-out request is a record with a terminal outcome, never a number to drop. The tail speaks before the mean: p95 crosses product deadlines while the average still looks healthy. And a prediction frozen before measurement beats a good story written after it. A note on scope, because the topic is deliberately narrow in one dimension: concurrency changes the time and memory behavior of the service, not the quality of the model's answers. We will not re-litigate classification accuracy here; Topics 03 and 04 own that question. What changes with load is whether an answer arrives at all, how late it is, and how many simultaneous askers the box can honestly sustain. Keeping those axes separate is what makes the investigation tractable — and it is also operationally realistic: in production, the person debugging saturation is rarely the person debugging prompt quality, and conflating the two dashboards wastes both teams' time. When you finish this chapter you should be able to say of any latency incident: "this is a queueing story, a scheduler story, or a model story" — and be right, with evidence. Finally, a word to the grading contract. The course leaderboard scores the geometric mean of output throughput at exactly 32 and 64 concurrent clients, with a p95 TTFT gate at 64. Those two points sit deliberately in the region where saturation begins for this workload. Understanding why those numbers were chosen — and what a submission optimizes when it chases them — is not exam trivia; it is the difference between tuning blindly and tuning against a declared target. Everything in the next sections builds toward making that target legible. Anatomy of the incident: three simultaneous failures It is worth slowing down on what "the service broke" actually means, because three distinct failures hide inside that phrase, and each is measured differently. The first is starvation : a request waits so long in queue that its wall-clock budget expires. The journal sees this as a timeout — a record that terminates without ever reaching first content. The second is silent demand amplification : a human user who times out refreshes the page, and the client sends a second, identical request. To the service this is new demand; to the product, the first request still failed. A driver that retries quietly makes every measurement lie — which is why the lab driver never retries, and why "no retries" is a rule you carry into any production load test. The third is soft degradation : answers keep arriving, but late — late enough to break a promise to a user even though the HTTP status is 200 and the label is correct. Throughput dashboards look fine under soft degradation; tail-latency dashboards do not. A useful saturation study reports all three: outcome shares, offered versus completed rates, and tail percentiles. Notice what is not on this list: the model getting worse. Classification quality is upstream of this chapter. If the model mislabels tickets at one client, it mislabels them at 128 clients too. Concurrency changes time and memory, not semantics — and one of the disciplines of this topic is keeping those measurements separate. What a request is made of Before any queue forms, understand what each arriving request carries, because the prefill work of a request is proportional to its full rendered size — not just to the human text inside it. Every request to the classifier is a rendered prompt: a system instruction ("Choose ONE label for the current unresolved support issue…"), the user's ticket text, and the chat-template wrapper that binds them. On the frozen teaching corpus, application A's tickets cluster around a hundred rendered tokens, while application B's documents run five times longer. The lab visualizes this anatomy directly: a stacked bar per application splits each rendered prompt into the system instruction and chat wrapper before the user text, the user text itself, and the wrapper tail after it. For A, nearly the whole bar is user text — the "payload" dominates the envelope. For B, the envelope takes visible share: a five-hundred-token document still carries its wrapper, and the scheduler processes every token of it during prefill. The numbers are in characters — an honest proxy — because exact tokenization belongs to the engine run; the proportions are what teach. The anatomy matters for two reasons. First, prefill cost scales with the whole rendered prompt: B pays five times the prefill of A even when its "useful" text is what you care about. Second, the wrapper is not free noise — it is part of what the scheduler must process, and in the stretch section two applications with very different length profiles will share one server, competing for the same prefill steps. When you later read a waterfall chart and wonder why one request's service segment is longer than another's, the answer often starts here, in the anatomy of what arrived. Where request time goes A request has several client-side clocks on one monotonic origin: logical arrival, admission to the client call, first content byte, terminal. First-token time (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT) are defined on these clocks. Waiting before the first token is not service; a missing first-content timestamp is not zero seconds. is queue wait before this request is first attended to; is the prefill: one full forward pass over the prompt; counts generated tokens after the first; is per-token decode time under load. Under load, and move first; which of them doubled decides the diagnosis. Run the diagnosis game on this decomposition. If TTFT doubles but TPOT holds, the request waited longer in queue — an admission or capacity problem upstream of compute. If TPOT doubles but TTFT holds, the decode steps themselves got slower — interference inside the batch, most often someone else's prefill stealing a step (the next section explains why). If both double, you are approaching a boundary where neither queue nor service can absorb the load. This reading is the single most transferable skill of the topic: latency numbers are not adjectives ("slow") but sentences with subjects (which stage) and verbs (grew). Why throughput grows before anything saturates Every forward pass reads all model weights once, no matter how many requests share that pass. With FP16 weights of the pinned 3B model at about 6.2 GiB and 32 generated tokens per request, one lone request moves roughly 198 MiB of weights per generated token; sixty-four requests sharing their passes move about 3.1 MiB per token. Nothing got faster — the same read served more work. is bytes of weights read per forward pass; is the number of requests sharing the pass; is weight traffic per generated token. This is arithmetic on declared facts — bandwidth, kernel efficiency and KV costs are not modeled, so it explains the rising part of the curve, not a measured speedup. The deeper way to read the formula: batching converts idle memory bandwidth into throughput. A single request leaves the GPU's weight-reading capacity almost entirely wasted — you pay the full 6.2 GiB of traffic to produce one tiny classification. As concurrency rises, each weight byte fetched does proportionally more useful work, and throughput climbs. The curve cannot rise forever, though, because batching does not multiply the other finite resources: KV memory grows per request (not per batch), and every step of compute — including the prefill of each newly admitted request — still costs a full forward pass. The rising part of the saturation curve is amortization; the flattening part is everything amortization cannot touch. Two finite resources The rising curve ends at a ceiling made of two resources. Compute: prefill of a newly admitted request is a full extra pass that competes with every resident decode. KV memory: each retained position costs 2 (K and V) × 36 layers × 2 KV heads × 128 features × 2 bytes = 36 KiB (axes from the pinned configuration ) — GQA is why this number is small; 16 query heads share 2 KV heads. A 2048-token context therefore bills about 72 MiB per request. On a 15.36 GiB T4 with 6.2 GiB (6350 MiB) of weights, the arithmetic ceiling is (15360 − 6350) ÷ 72 ≈ 125 simultaneous full-context requests. That is an upper bound, not a scheduler promise: fragmentation, activation memory and admission policy each take a share. The lab freezes this prediction before measuring and returns to the gap afterward — the gap is the lesson, and each missing request has a name. There is also a fundamentally different answer: KV compression . Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), open-sourced by DeepSeek in their FlashMLA kernels, compresses K and V into a shared latent representation that reduces the per-position cost by roughly an order of magnitude. The arithmetic ceiling we computed (125 requests) assumes standard multi-head attention; an MLA-based model on the same GPU holds far more resident contexts because each one bills less. The knobs of Topic 07 move the ceiling; MLA removes it by changing what is stored. Both approaches answer the same observation: KV memory is the binding resource for long-context workloads. Practice turning the two-resource frame into predictions. A workload of long prompts and one-token answers (a search reranker) will hit the KV wall first: memory is billed by context, not by output. A workload of short prompts and long generations (a story writer) will hit compute first: decode steps dominate, and the KV bill accrues slowly. The ticket classifier sits closer to the first case — which is why the memory ceiling is the right back-of-envelope for this chapter, and why the measured T4 run (short prompts, natural-EOS answers of about two tokens) never approached it. When your workload changes shape, redo this paragraph from scratch; the arithmetic is cheap, and it is the difference between a tuned guess and a prediction. Continuous batching under load Continuous batching runs one compute step at a time for all resident requests. The timeline below holds this chapter's central mechanism: when a new request is admitted, its prefill needs a whole step, and every resident request waits that step — TPOT jumps although nothing failed. When KV runs short, the scheduler preempts a request and later recomputes its early tokens: work is repeated, not free. Walk one hypothetical minute to make the mechanism concrete. Suppose four requests are residents, each earning one token per step, and a fifth arrives. Step 1: the scheduler must build the newcomer's KV — a full forward pass over its prompt — so all five requests are scheduled but only the newcomer actually advances (its prefill completes). Steps 2 through 60: all five decode together, and amortization resumes. The newcomer's arrival cost each resident exactly one token-step of delay — invisible in any per-request error count, visible as a one-step TPOT blip in the journal, and visible on the waterfall as a brief widening of every grey band at that moment. Now suppose KV memory runs short at some later step: the scheduler preempts the request with the least progress, discards its computed KV, and lets the freed memory serve the others. When the victim is re-admitted, its prompt is prefetched again — recomputed from scratch. The victim's latency doubles for a reason that never touches its own output quality. These two events — insertion stall and preemption recompute — are the entire "hidden" cost of mixing arriving work with ongoing work, and both are purely scheduler-level: no kernel is slower, no weight is different. Read latency curves through this mechanism. Latency growing without errors is prefill interference. Completions stopping is admission control. Duplicated early tokens are preemption recompute. Same graph, three different mechanisms, three different fixes — and only the journal, with per-request timestamps, can tell you which one you are looking at. It is worth stressing the counterintuitive part: the scheduler is not "slow" when these events happen. It is making locally reasonable trade-offs under contention — finish the newly admitted prefill now so the request can start earning tokens; evict a victim so a promising request fits. Production engines push this further with an async scheduler : the CPU prepares the next batch while the GPU computes the current one, eliminating the dead time between steps. DeepInfer (DeepSeek's open-source engine, Apache-2.0, October 2026) made this the default; vLLM is moving the same direction. On the waterfall, the effect is visible as uniformly narrower grey bands — the scheduler is never idle waiting for the GPU to finish before deciding what runs next. Saturation is not a malfunction of the scheduler but the consequence of requests whose combined demand no longer fits the step budget. That is why the remedies of this topic are measurement and choice of operating point, not "fixing" the engine — engine knobs arrive in Topic 07. Queues and tails A closed-loop client sends its next request only after the previous one terminates. With clients, mean residence and think time , offered demand is — Little's law in closed form. A fixed client count therefore delivers falling demand as the service slows: the system throttles itself. This is why the lab defines waves by concurrency and reports offered and completed rates together; their divergence is the queue. The tail deserves its own paragraph, because it is where product reality lives. Under queueing near capacity, the distribution of wait times stretches: most requests still do fine (the median barely moves) while an unlucky minority waits many times longer than before. Percentiles like p95 exist precisely to make that minority visible. A product promise of "every ticket classified within a second" is a p100 promise — the strictest possible — and near saturation it is the first casualty. When you choose an operating point later in this chapter, you are really choosing how much tail you are willing to sell: every notch of extra throughput buys queue position, and the buyers of that queue position are your p95 requests. Notice also the asymmetry of trust: users forgive a consistently slow service more readily than an unpredictably fast one. A p50 of 400 ms with p95 of 900 ms feels worse in production than a steady 600 ms, even though the means are identical — one more reason the mean alone is not a service description. Little's law also gives you a quick honesty check on any load test you did not run yourself. If a report claims 128 concurrent clients sustaining, say, 40 requests per second, then mean residence is at least 128 ÷ 40 = 3.2 seconds — and every latency number in that report must be consistent with at least that much residence for the population as a whole. When the claimed "average latency" is far below what the concurrency-to-throughput ratio implies, one of three things happened: clients were not actually closed-loop (they slept between requests), the latency was measured only over a surviving subset, or the numbers came from different runs. You now have the arithmetic to catch all three from a paragraph of marketing text — use it. One more property of closed loops deserves words because students meet it as a surprise: a closed-loop system is self-stabilizing in a way an open-loop one is not. If the service slows down, offered demand falls, which relieves pressure, which lets the service speed back up — the loop dampens oscillation. An open-loop generator (fixed requests per second regardless of response) does the opposite: slowdown causes queue growth causes further slowdown, with no natural brake until budgets expire. Production traffic is usually a mixture: human users are closed loops with think time; cron jobs and batch workers are open loops. The lab uses the closed form because it makes concurrency the single honest dial, but when you interpret results, remember which kind of world you were modeling. One experiment, everything else frozen The lab runs waves of 8, 32, 64 and 128 concurrent closed-loop clients. Exactly one factor varies. Held fixed: the pinned model and revision, frozen public corpus texts, max tokens, temperature, seed, timeout budget, and a driver that never retries — a retry silently doubles demand and hides the failure it retried. Every terminated attempt writes one journal record with client-side monotonic timestamps and a terminal outcome: completed, timeout, server error, connection error or truncation. The design principle generalizes beyond this lab: a curve is only about its varied factor if everything else is pinned. The moment two things drift between your measurement points — different prompts, a warmed-up cache here and a cold one there — the shape you draw is a composite of your drift, not of your factor. This is also why the wave order is fixed and why each wave's journal is kept whole: any later suspicion ("was wave 64 unusual?") can be answered from records, not from memory. And the audit habits belong here, before any analysis: a trusted journal has no missing terminals, no duplicate request IDs, no foreign wave tags, no impossible timestamps (terminal before arrival). The lab's audit_records classifies such damage and never repairs it — an unaudited number is an unowned number. The figure above is the chapter's memento about denominators: three completed replies and two correct labels among six arrivals give both 2/3 (conditional accuracy) and 1/6 (useful arrivals), and both are honest answers to different questions. Choosing which question you are answering — before looking at the data — is most of the intellectual work of reporting. Reading the request waterfall The lab's most direct picture is the waterfall: one horizontal bar per request, drawn from the journal you just produced. Each bar starts when the request arrived, shows a light-grey segment while it waited for its first token, a dark-blue segment while it was served, and — if the request never made it — a red bar ending at the moment the client's wall budget expired. A vertical dotted line marks that budget; bars that touch it are the timeouts. Read a waterfall in three passes. First the population: are you looking at all requests of the wave or a sample, and does the title say which? (The lab samples evenly across arrival time so both survivors and casualties stay visible — a sample of "the first forty arrivals" would show mostly the lucky ones.) Second the texture: on a small wave, grey segments are thin and blue work dominates — waiting is not yet a cost. As concurrency grows, grey creeps rightward: the queue is eating the budget before service even begins. Third the red: bars that die before any blue at all are requests that never started being served — starvation in the plain sense. The waterfall is also your best cross-check on the clock decomposition from earlier: TTFT is exactly the light-grey width, and a TPOT jump that looked mysterious in a table becomes, on the waterfall, a visible step where someone else's prefill occupied the machine. One warning about the medium: a waterfall is a sample of individual stories, not an aggregate. It convinces; it does not summarize. Use it to explain a mechanism you already measured with curves, never as a substitute for the outcome shares and percentiles that count every request. Reading the curves A saturation curve has three zones. Rise: batching amortizes weight traffic and tokens get cheaper per client. Flatten: compute and KV fill; extra clients mostly buy queue position. Collapse: wall budgets turn into timeouts and errors absorb the demand. Three ways these plots lie: dropped-error denominators, mean-only latency, silent retries — each has a required lab defense. Learn to narrate a specific curve, not just the archetype. For each wave, the reading order is: outcome shares first (what fraction even completed?), then throughput (at what price in tokens per second?), then p50 and p95 together (who waited, and how unevenly?). A curve that flattens with clean outcomes is a capacity boundary politely reached. A curve that stays high while errors climb is collapse wearing a disguise — the graph of survivors. The lab makes the disguise impossible by construction: failed requests keep their wall-clock share of the denominator, so collapsing waves lose throughput even when the survivors, measured alone, would look excellent. is completed throughput at wave ; the superscript minus marks the previous wave; is the minimum relative gain that still counts (the lab uses 0.5). A different threshold can move the knee by one wave — the definition is operational, and the lab says so. Compare the measured knee with the arithmetic ceiling from the budget section and name what ate the difference. The gain rule rewards a habit worth naming: never report a "knee" without its γ. Two teams comparing knees measured under different thresholds are comparing nothing. The same applies to percentile choice (p95 versus p99), timeout budget, and wave spacing — every operational definition is part of the result, and the memo template in the lab forces you to state the ones that matter. What the measured run said Theory gives the shape; only a measured run gives the position. The published T4 run of 21 October 2026 (owner-executed on the current notebook, single run, burst waves of three requests per client, natural-EOS replies of about two tokens — read the limits before quoting) produced the numbers this course now uses as its measured anchor. Throughput rose 29 → 208 → 306 → 311 tok/s across the four waves with zero timeouts at every wave, and then flattened: the last doubling (64 → 128 clients) bought +2%. The knee lands at wave 32 by the gain rule — and this matched the frozen arithmetic prediction exactly, the rare benchmarking day when the sentence written before the run survives contact with the measurement. Two details earn their own sentences. First, wave 8 is warmup data: its wall time (1.66 s, the longest of all four waves) and its p95 TTFT (1270 ms) are first-wave CUDA-graph capture, not steady-state behaviour — a cold-start wave inside your measurement is a confound to name, not an outlier to drop. Second, after warmup the tail tells the real story: p95 TTFT went 324 → 478 → 1076 ms while throughput went flat. Throughput alone said "nothing changed after 64"; the tail said the box was filling up. Any throughput curve that plateaus hides exactly this — which is why the lab plots outcomes, throughput and percentiles as three separate pictures before it lets you speak. The honest postscript: this workload now has three runs, and the knee came out 64 → 32 → 64 across them (18 October, 21 October anchor, 21 October replicate). The reason is not mystery noise: the 32 → 64 doubling gained 47 percent in one run and 56 percent in another — the gain sits exactly at the fifty-percent bar of the gain rule, so single-run jitter flips the verdict by one wave. All three runs agree on what matters (zero timeouts, no collapse inside the tested range, the tail rising into wave 128). The knee itself is an operational definition sitting on a threshold — quote the threshold, the bar and the run count with every knee claim, and treat a knee that flips between adjacent waves under replication as a finding about the workload, not a failure of the method. The general lesson compounds with the two-resource frame: predict first (which resource, given the shape of this workload?), then measure, then explain any gap in the direction the anatomy points — long-prompt workloads die by memory, long-generation workloads by compute, and short-everything workloads may not die inside your tested range, only plateau while the tail grows. The corollary for practice: before you benchmark anything, write the sentence "this workload is long in [prompts/outputs/neither]" and compute the corresponding budget — it takes one minute and it predicts which curve shape you are about to draw. Teams that skip the sentence end up benchmarking the wrong resource and tuning knobs that cannot help. Choose an operating point under an SLO The leaderboard is exactly this question. The judge scores with a p95 TTFT gate at 64 clients; the current round bars live on the leaderboard page, not in this chapter, so they cannot drift out of date here. The lab rule is the same shape: the largest wave whose p95 TTFT and error rate both clear the SLO, with the binding constraint named in writing, compared against your frozen prediction, plus one alternative explanation the run cannot exclude. Three honest verdicts exist. Accept : the chosen point meets the SLO on evidence you would show a stranger. Reject : no point qualifies — the product needs a smaller promise or a bigger machine, and saying so is the job. Inconclusive : the run cannot distinguish "healthy" from "lucky" — a single burst wave with clean outcomes and near-SLO tails is exactly this, and the professional answer is another run, not a hopeful sentence in the memo. The lab grades the freeze, not the fortune: a falsifiable choice with a written forecast is full marks even when the held-out answer disappoints. It helps to see the memo as a contract with three named parties. The product owner reads the SLO line and the chosen wave: this is what we promise users, at this load. The capacity planner reads the knee and the ceiling: this is where the curve bends and why, in the language of the two resources. The skeptic — every good memo is written for one — reads the alternative-explanation line: the single most plausible story under which this choice is wrong, stated before anyone can accuse the author of cherry-picking. A memo that cannot name its skeptic's best argument is not a decision; it is a hope with formatting. The three-sentence template in the lab notebook is deliberately minimal — chosen wave versus prediction, binding resource with evidence, unexcluded alternative — because every real postmortem you will ever write contains exactly those three parts, buried under more prose. And a final connection to the round you are actually graded on: the judge's score is the geometric mean at 32 and 64 clients precisely so that neither point can be sacrificed for the other. A submission tuned to look brilliant at 32 and collapse at 64 scores poorly; so does the reverse. Geometric means punish imbalance — which is, in miniature, the whole lesson of choosing operating points under an SLO rather than chasing a single maximum. Stretch: a second application arrives The document classifier from the interference study now shares the server: same weights, a different system prompt — which is not tenant isolation and not two replicas. Interference is measured honestly on each application separately, never averaged into one bar. The protection under test is an in-flight cap K ∈ &#123;1, 2, 4, 8, 16&#125; limiting the second application's concurrency. The protocol is the discipline: compare A-only against A+B at each K on a development pair, freeze one K with a written forecast, then run a distinct held-out pair once. Why a cap and not a faster queue? Because interference here has a specific mechanism: B's long prefills occupy scheduler steps that A's decodes were using. Limiting how many B requests may be in flight simultaneously bounds how many steps per unit time B can claim — a blunt, predictable, cheap instrument. The trade is equally direct: smaller K protects A's tails but starves B's throughput (K = 0 is forbidden — refusing all B work fails the second product). The dev table shows the frontier; the frozen K picks a point on it; held-out asks whether the point generalizes to texts the choice never saw. Every idea here — separate measurements, predeclared choice, held-out validation — is the Topic 03 calibration discipline returning at the systems level, which is the quiet thesis of the whole course: the experimental method scales from tensors to services. A practical detail that decides whether the stretch teaches or misleads: the dev pair and the held-out pair must differ in texts , not in protocol. Same waves, same cap candidates, same journal fields — new documents and new tickets. If the protocol also changes (different wave size, different budget), a failed held-out tells you nothing about the freeze: it might be the texts, it might be the new conditions, and you have spent your one honest validation run to learn neither. This is the same discipline as Topic 03's calibration-versus-test split, and it fails the same way in the wild: teams "validate" against a run whose load shape quietly differs from development, then ship a policy that was never tested under its real conditions. Read the dev table as a frontier, not a ranking. Each row (one K) buys B throughput at an A-latency price; there is no row that is best at both, and the interesting rows are where the exchange rate changes steeply. A cap of 1 buys A near-perfect tails at the cost of B crawling; 16 lets B sprint while A's p95 triples. The knee logic from the main lab reappears here in a second costume: choose the last cheap step before the price spikes, write down what you expect, and let held-out arbitrate. Two cost curves, one method — which is, again, the quiet thesis. What this run does and does not establish The run record for the measured figure is public (seminars/runs/2026-10-18-topic06-t4-saturation); the raw journal stays private. The owner-run GPU profile on the pinned service and the frozen public corpus produced the measured figure; the remaining teaching curves stay labelled illustrative, and the measured one carries its own limits on its face. To be complete about the boundary of claims: the mock profile validates plumbing only — its formula is declared, not discovered. The measured run is a single run on one device under burst windows; it is an anchor, not a distribution. Free-GPU quota on Colab is not guaranteed, learner validation has not happened, no classroom rehearsal has been observed, and nothing here certifies the judge, whose contract lives elsewhere and changes only through its own governance. When you quote a number from this chapter in any professional setting, quote its provenance clause in the same breath — that habit, more than any formula, is what this course is for. For the student who wants one paragraph to remember from the whole chapter, let it be this: saturation is not a wall you hit, it is a trade you choose. The curve tells you the prices; the journal tells you who paid them; the SLO tells you which price you may charge. Everything else — the budgets, the waterfalls, the percentiles — exists to make that one choice defensible to someone who was not in the room. Topic 07 hands you the knobs that move the curve itself; the reading skills you built here are what will tell you, later, whether any knob actually helped. Check understanding and transfer Answer before opening the explanations. Questions 1, 6 and 8 change one condition: reproducing the notebook is not enough unless you can predict what changes next. {exercises.map(({id,title,question})=> {title}. {question} )} Reveal eight answers and their limits {exercises.map(({id,title,answer})=> {title}. {answer} )}
