Chapter 07: vLLM tuning: moving the curve

This chapter follows the approved Topic07 arc. The notebook mock profile validates the search pipeline on a declared synthetic model; only an owner-run GPU profile on the pinned service produces measured evidence. Teacher materials stay private;{' '} the topic page separates the acceptance states . From reading the curve to moving it Topic 06 left you standing on the saturation curve with a defended operating point. This chapter hands you the knobs that move the curve itself. The same model, the same GPU, the same workload — but four named parameters of the serving engine that control which mechanism binds first, how sharply the tail grows, and where the knee lands. The course milestone says it plainly: "Configuration table + chosen production profile." The engineering virtue is not finding a magic number — it is a bounded, predeclared search : enumerate a small space, fix the measurement protocol before touching the engine, keep every failed configuration as data, freeze one production profile with a forecast, and let a distinct held-out load judge the freeze. When you finish, "tuning" will mean a discipline, not a superstition. Three habits carry over from Topic 06 and gain new meaning. Errors are data: a configuration that produces timeouts is a row in the table, not a discarded attempt. The tail speaks before the mean: a faster configuration with a worse tail is not an improvement. And a frozen prediction beats a post-hoc story — now applied to the search plan itself, not just the knee. The Round 03 precedent Before any knob is introduced, anchor on what the course itself did. In Round 03, the owner raised the speed bar by 2.3 percent with one change: FLASH_ATTN attention backend plus --max-num-seqs 64 . This was not the first candidate tried. A Triton variant had been tested first: it was faster on speed, but failed the quality floor (MMLU-Pro score below the gate). The Triton candidate was rejected and stayed rejected. Two lessons from this single real event, and a third that is easy to miss. First, knobs interact with gates you may not be watching: a speed knob can silently break a quality floor that lives elsewhere in the judge contract. Second, the discipline of keeping rejected candidates as evidence — rather than quietly moving on — is what separates a search from a fishing expedition. The third lesson: the Triton candidate was not a bad idea — it was a reasonable hypothesis that failed a gate the proponent did not know existed. This is normal and will happen to you. The professional response is not to stop having ideas; it is to know which gates exist and to check them before shipping. The gates in this course are documented in the thresholds file and in the judge contract; in your production system, they live in the SLO, the quality suite, and the canary metrics. Knowing where the gates are is table stakes; checking them before shipping is the discipline. When your own search table has a configuration that looked promising but failed, that row is your Triton. Write it down; explain why it failed; do not rerun it hoping for a different answer. The precedent also frames the budget reality. The owner did not try fifty configurations; they tried a handful, learned from each, and froze one. The search space in this chapter is deliberately small — five configurations, not five hundred — because that is what an honest budget allows, and because the skill being taught is the method, not the coverage. Four knobs, four mechanisms Each maps to a mechanism explained in Topic 06. The pinned model configuration defines the axes these knobs operate on. Each knob maps to a mechanism you already explained in Topic 06. The mapping is the whole point: you are not turning dials blindly, you are adjusting the parameters of equations you have already derived. --max-num-seqs is the ceiling on the decode batch size. Recall the batching economy from Topic 06: weight traffic per token falls as grows, because more requests share each forward pass. This knob caps . A smaller cap (e.g. 32) means each step serves fewer requests — TPOT ticks are shorter (less contention per step), but admission blocking arrives sooner because the scheduler cannot accept new work until slots free up. A larger cap (e.g. 256) lets the batch grow — amortization is stronger, but each step takes longer because more requests compete for the same compute, and the tail grows. --gpu-memory-utilization is the fraction of VRAM the engine may use for the KV pool (the remainder stays for activations, workspace, and the operating system). This knob directly scales the Topic 06 KV budget: the arithmetic ceiling of 125 simultaneous full-context requests was computed at a specific utilization. Change the share, and the ceiling moves. More pool means more resident requests before preemption — but less headroom for everything else that lives in VRAM. --max-model-len is the declared maximum context length. This is a planning parameter, not a hard limit on what the model can process: it tells the scheduler the worst-case prompt it must accommodate. A generous value (e.g. 4096) means any client may arrive with a long prompt and the scheduler reserves for it — possibly wasting capacity that shorter workloads never use. A tight value (e.g. 1024) plans for what actually arrives, but a legitimate long prompt gets rejected, which is a product decision, not a tuning one. Chunked prefill controls whether a large prompt's prefill is processed in one step or sliced across multiple smaller pieces. Without chunking, a new request's prefill takes the whole compute step — every resident request waits, and the Topic 06 waterfall showed exactly this as a grey band widening. With chunking, the prefill is split: each slice takes a fraction of a step, and decode keeps earning tokens at a slightly slower rate instead of stopping completely. The trade: total prefill latency is slightly longer (more scheduling overhead), but the interference with ongoing work is smoother. Predict before you measure The lab's first deliverable is a table: for each knob, the mechanism it controls and the expected effect on the saturation curve. This table is written and frozen before any measurement — the same prediction discipline as Topic 06's frozen knee forecast, now applied to the parameter space. is the effective batch size (capped by max-num-seqs); is weight bytes per pass; is weight traffic per generated token. As grows toward the cap, each weight byte serves more work — but beyond the cap, extra clients only queue. The knob places the amortization ceiling. The prediction exercise is not busywork, and the table is not a formality. When the measurement disagrees with your prediction, that gap is the most interesting data you have — it means a mechanism is at work that you did not anticipate, and the follow-up question writes itself. But the exercise has a second, quieter value: it slows you down at exactly the moment when speed is most dangerous. The temptation when tuning is to turn a knob, see a number improve, and immediately turn it further — a gradient-descent loop with a human as the optimizer. The prediction table interrupts this loop by forcing you to articulate why before measuring what . The articulation is where understanding happens; the measurement is where it is tested. A tuning session without predictions is a random walk with confirmation bias. In the mock profile, for example, chunked prefill may show lower throughput than predicted: the model's scheduling overhead (slicing, context switching between slices) consumes more than the smoother interference saves. In a real engine, the balance could tip either way depending on kernel efficiency and prompt length distribution. The prediction is falsifiable; the measurement is the test. Designing the bounded search Why not try everything? Four knobs, each with three or more reasonable values, four waves to run, and three repeats for honesty: the combinatorics reach hundreds of GPU-hours. The budget is finite — five configurations is what an honest lab session supports, and it is enough. The method is one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT), followed by one confirmatory pair. Start from the default configuration (one run). Change exactly one knob at a time to its most promising alternative (three more runs). Then combine the two changes that helped most independently (one more run). Total: five. The confirmatory pair matters because knobs can interact: individually helpful changes may cancel or compound when combined, and only the pair reveals this. Write the reason for each configuration before running it. The sentence is not decoration — it is the falsifiable core of the search. "seqs-32: sacrifice amortization for tail latency" is a hypothesis with named mechanisms and a predicted direction. "Let's see what happens" is not a hypothesis; it is a coin flip with extra steps. The reason sentence serves three audiences simultaneously: you (the engineer who must later explain the choice), your team (reviewers who need to check the logic), and the held-out run (which tests the aggregate of all your reasons). When a configuration fails, the reason sentence tells you which mechanism disappointed — was the mechanism wrong, or was the magnitude wrong? Without the sentence, a failure is just a number that was bad, and you learn nothing that transfers to the next decision. The search plan is frozen into a JSON file with a timestamp — the same hash-before-run discipline as the Topic 06 prediction — and any configuration not in the plan does not get run. If mid-search you realize you need a different configuration, you version the plan; you do not silently add rows. Failed configurations stay in the table. A config that OOMs, that produces timeouts at wave 32, or that clears speed but fails a quality gate — each is a row with its numbers and a one-sentence explanation. The Triton precedent operationalized: rejected candidates remain as evidence. Running the search: the config table The lab executes the plan on the mock profile (CPU, minutes). Each configuration runs the same four waves — 8, 32, 64, 128 closed-loop clients — with the same frozen corpus, timeout budget, and journal protocol as Topic 06. The output is a table: one row per configuration, with throughput at wave 64, p95 TTFT at wave 64, and error rate at wave 64 as the primary comparison columns. Why wave 64 as the primary comparison point? Because the judge scores the geometric mean at 32 and 64, and because wave 64 is where the interesting behavior lives for this workload — near the knee but not past it. Wave 128 is retained for completeness (does the config change where collapse begins?), but the decision is made on the 64-client evidence. The honest reading of the table requires the same outcome-first discipline as Topic 06. A configuration with higher throughput but 3 percent timeouts at wave 64 is not "faster" — it is trading errors for speed, and the SLO has an opinion about that trade. The error column is not a footnote; it is a gate. The Pareto front: speed against tail After the sweep, each configuration is a point in a two-dimensional space: throughput (higher is better) and p95 TTFT (lower is better). The Pareto front is the set of configurations where no other is simultaneously faster and gentler. Config dominates iff A is at least as fast and at least as gentle, with at least one strict inequality. The front is what survives: the set of undominated configurations. There is no "best on everything" unless a single point dominates all others. The front makes the trade visible. One configuration is fastest but has the longest tail; another is gentlest but slowest; the front traces the boundary between them. The SLO then picks the point: among front members that clear the SLO, choose the fastest. This is not "highest throughput" as a blind maximization — it is "highest throughput that still meets the promise ." The difference is the difference between an engineer and a gambler. Students implement pareto_front() — a filter that keeps only the undominated rows. The function is short; the concept is the deliverable. In a professional setting, Pareto thinking changes how you read every benchmark chart. When a vendor shows you a single "best" configuration, you should immediately ask what it cost: what was the tail? What was the error rate? What did it give up to win on the metric being shown? A single-point benchmark is a one-dimensional Pareto front with the other dimensions hidden — and the hidden dimensions are usually where the product lives. In practice, the hidden dimension that bites hardest is the tail: vendors benchmark on mean throughput (a flattering metric under mild load) and bury p95 in an appendix or omit it entirely. The multi-objective frame (speed, tail, error, quality, cost) is not academic sophistication; it is the minimum honesty required to make a tuning decision that a product owner can sign. A useful exercise when reading any benchmark: draw the implicit Pareto front. If the chart shows one point, imagine where the other configurations would sit — and what dimension the vendor chose not to plot. If you cannot draw the front, you do not have enough information to make a decision, and you should ask for it., you should immediately ask what it cost: what was the tail? What was the error rate? What did it give up to win on the metric being shown? A single-point benchmark is a one-dimensional Pareto front with the other dimensions hidden — and the hidden dimensions are usually where the product lives. The multi-objective frame (speed, tail, error, quality, cost) is not academic sophistication; it is the minimum honesty required to make a tuning decision that a product owner can sign. When a colleague shows you a benchmark chart with a single "winner," you should now ask: "Where is the front? What did the winner sacrifice?" Freeze the production profile Among SLO-eligible front members, pick the fastest. Write a one-sentence forecast of what the held-out pair will show. Freeze. The profile file is written with a timestamp and a hash — the same freeze discipline as Topic 06's prediction and Topic 03's calibration choice. After the freeze, the policy does not change. The freeze is the deliverable because it is falsifiable. A configuration chosen without a forecast cannot be wrong — it can only be lucky or unlucky, and you learn nothing from either. This is not a philosophical point; it is operational. A lucky configuration that clears the SLO on one run may fail on the next, and without a forecast you have no way to distinguish "the profile is marginal" from "the run was noisy." A forecast converts the held-out from a pass/fail lottery into a measurement of your understanding. If the forecast says "p95 will be about 600ms" and the held-out shows 610ms, you understand the system. If it shows 950ms, you do not — and the gap tells you where to look. The forecast is not required to be correct; it is required to be specific enough to be wrong. A configuration chosen with a written expectation can be tested : the held-out either confirms the forecast or it does not, and either way you know something you did not know before. Three honest verdicts exist. Accept : the frozen profile clears the SLO on held-out texts. Reject : it fails — the memo says the product needs a smaller promise or a bigger machine. Inconclusive : the run cannot distinguish healthy from lucky — the professional answer is another run, not a hopeful paragraph. The lab grades the freeze, not the fortune. Held-out: the profile meets new texts The held-out pair must differ from the development pair in load only — on the GPU profile, new documents and tickets from the corpus V-split; on the mock, a declared synthetic V-set with a different seed and a different length mix. Same waves, same SLO, same journal fields, same timeout budget. One run. No policy change. The discipline is Topic 03's calibration-versus-test split returning at the systems level, and it fails the same way in the wild. The most common failure mode is not malice but convenience: the team validates against a copy of production that is three months stale, or against a synthetic benchmark whose prompt length distribution quietly drifted from reality. The policy ships, the real traffic arrives, and the tail crosses the SLO on day one. The team is surprised because the validation "passed" — but the validation tested a world that no longer exists. The held-out protocol in this lab is deliberately simple (new texts, same everything else) because simplicity is what makes the boundary between development and validation visible. In production, the boundary is harder to see and easier to erode; the habit of naming what changed between dev and validation is your defense. If the held-out also changes the protocol (different wave size, different budget), a failure tells you nothing: it might be the texts, it might be the conditions. You have spent your one honest validation run to learn neither. Teams that "validate" against a run whose load shape quietly differs from development ship policies that were never tested under their real conditions — this chapter exists to make you the person who catches that. Stretch: the edge risk and the rollback plan Every chosen profile has a boundary where it stops being safe. The stretch asks you to name yours and test it deliberately. Common edges: the longest prompt in the corpus against the smallest KV pool (does the request get rejected or does the server crash?); the highest concurrent load you expect in production (does the frozen profile still clear the SLO, or does the tail cross the line?); a sudden doubling of load (does the service degrade gracefully or collapse?). In production, the edge test you ran in the stretch becomes a canary: a small percentage of real traffic routed to the new profile, monitored against the SLO, before the full rollout. The lab's edge test (longest prompt, smallest pool, highest load) maps to production's canary (longest real requests, peak hours, worst-case burst). The scale differs by orders of magnitude; the logic is identical. A profile that has survived the lab's edge test has earned the right to a production canary — not to a full rollout. The rollback plan has three parts: the trigger (what metric crosses what threshold for how long — "p95 > SLO for 5 consecutive minutes" is specific; "it gets slow" is not), the action (revert to default, halve the load, page the on-call — something a human or automation can actually execute), and the evidence needed (which dashboard, which query, which threshold — so the person executing the rollback at 3 AM does not have to figure out what "slow" means). A rollback plan that names all three is an operational artifact. A plan that names none is a wish. The deliverable is not the test result — it is the rollback plan : one paragraph naming the condition under which you would revert to the default configuration, and what evidence would trigger that decision. "If p95 exceeds the SLO for five consecutive minutes in production, revert to default and investigate" is a plan. "We'll monitor it" is not. The mock model: honest about what it is The mock tuning model is a declared synthetic queue with the same knobs. It is not a measurement of vLLM — every figure produced by the mock profile says so. The distinction matters because the mock is deliberately simple enough to reason about analytically: the queue delay is a quadratic in effective batch size, the prefill is linear in prompt length, and the decode is linear in output tokens. These choices capture the qualitative shape of contention without pretending to model the actual CUDA kernel scheduling, memory coalescing, or stream parallelism that determines real vLLM performance. When the mock shows that seqs-32 improves p95 at wave 64, the mechanism is transparent: fewer requests competing per step. When real vLLM shows the same, the mechanism is the same but the magnitude differs because the real engine has additional costs the mock does not model. The mock is a teaching tool that makes the mechanism visible; the measurement is the evidence that makes it real. What the mock validates is the pipeline : the search plan, the sweep, the Pareto front, the freeze, the held-out protocol. When the gpu profile runs the same notebook, the pipeline is already debugged and only the numbers change. The first measured owner-run (28 October 2026, T4, vLLM 0.30.0 serving Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct — seminars/runs/2026-10-28-topic07-gpu/README.md ) is the rule "when the mock and the gpu profile disagree, the gpu wins" caught in the act. The mock-calibrated search froze pair-seqs32-chunked and its forecast promised a p95 well under the 800 ms SLO. The real engine disagreed twice: the judge gain against default was ×0.63 — the profile was slower — and the held-out run on the real corpus V-split texts came back at p95 1585 ms, double the SLO. The memo recorded verdict: reject . Nothing was quietly re-tuned: the falsified forecast, the red badge, and the refusal are the pipeline working. A mock that had been tuned until it "agreed" with the engine would have been worthless here; a mock that is honestly wrong teaches you exactly which costs it fails to model. Being explicit about what the mock is not is part of the course contract. The mock's queue delay formula (0.08 × effective-batch² ÷ utilization) is a declared approximation of the real engine's behavior under contention. It captures the qualitative shape — more parallel decode work means more contention — without pretending to model kernel scheduling, memory bandwidth, or CUDA stream parallelism. When the mock and the gpu profile disagree, the gpu wins. The mock exists so that the pipeline can be tested in minutes on a free CPU. Knob interactions: why OFAT is not enough One-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) is efficient — five configurations instead of dozens — but it has a known blind spot: knob interactions. If max-num-seqs and gpu-memory-utilization interact (they do: a larger KV pool means the batch ceiling is reached differently), OFAT may miss the best combination. This is why the search plan includes one confirmatory pair: the two individually most promising changes, combined. If the pair is better than either alone, the interaction is positive (compounding). If it is worse, the knobs are fighting each other — you learned something OFAT alone would not have revealed. If it is the same as the better individual, the knobs are independent. Each outcome is information. The full solution to interactions is a factorial design or response surface methodology — topics in a statistics course, not a serving lab. The honest compromise is OFAT plus one pair, with the caveat stated: "interactions beyond the tested pair are unmeasured." A search that does not name its blind spot is not a search; it is a tour. Speed knobs and quality gates The Round 03 Triton precedent deserves its own section because it teaches a lesson that is easy to forget in the excitement of tuning: speed knobs can break quality . The Triton kernel was faster — it won on throughput — but it silently changed the model's numerical behavior enough to fail the MMLU-Pro floor. The speed gate said yes; the quality gate said no. In this chapter's lab, the quality floors are upstream: the model, the corpus, and the scoring are frozen from Topic 06. Changing a serving knob does not change the model's weights — but in production, some knobs can affect quality indirectly. A tighter max-model-len may truncate long prompts (changing the input the model sees). A very small max-num-seqs may cause preemption and recomputation, which should be numerically identical but is worth verifying for sensitive applications. The professional habit: when you present a tuning result, state which gates you checked and which you did not — and check the ones that are cheap to check. In this lab, verifying that the model still produces the same labels on a sample of the corpus costs one minute and catches the most obvious regressions. The Triton precedent was caught because the quality gate was part of the round contract; in a lab without that gate, the same candidate would have shipped. Make the quality check part of your tuning loop, not an afterthought. A useful heuristic: for every knob you turn, ask "could this change what the model computes?" If the answer is yes or maybe, add a quality probe to the sweep — even a simple one (same predictions on a fixed sample?) is better than none. you checked and which you did not. "Throughput improved 8 percent; quality gates not re-run in this lab" is honest. Presenting the speed number without mentioning quality implies the quality was verified — and if it was not, the implication is false. From lab to production The frozen profile is a lab artifact. Production adds four realities this chapter deliberately does not model, and naming them is half the preparation for Topic 08. Cancellation : a user closes the tab mid-generation, and the server should stop computing — but a cancelled request still holds its KV allocation until the engine notices, and the freed capacity is not instantly available to the next arrival. The frozen profile was measured without cancellations; production with a 5 percent cancel rate has slightly more headroom than measured, but the mechanism is not free. Quotas : per-client rate limits mean the effective concurrency is not the nominal concurrency — a client that is rate-limited sends fewer requests per second than an unconstrained one, changing the offered load in ways the closed-loop waves did not model. Backpressure : upstream systems (an API gateway, a message queue) may slow down or buffer, changing the arrival pattern from the steady closed-loop of the lab to bursty, correlated arrivals that stress different parts of the scheduler. Observation : the metrics pipeline that tells you the profile is still working — and whose own latency and completeness determine whether you learn about a regression in minutes or in hours. cancellation (users close tabs; the service should stop generating), quotas (per-client limits that change the effective concurrency), backpressure (upstream systems that slow down or fail), and observation (the dashboard that tells you the profile is still working). Topic 08 addresses these directly. What this chapter provides for that transition is the rollback plan from the stretch: the condition under which the profile is abandoned, and the evidence that triggers it. A profile without a rollback plan is a bet without an exit. The plan does not need to be elaborate — "if p95 exceeds SLO for five minutes, revert to default" is sufficient — but it must exist before the profile ships. The second gift to production is the search method itself. When the workload changes (new users, new prompt lengths, a model upgrade), the same five-step cycle runs again: predict, declare, measure, freeze, validate. The knobs may be different; the discipline is the same. That is the real deliverable of this chapter — not a magic number, but a repeatable process for finding one. What this chapter does and does not establish The mock profile validates the search pipeline — the plan, the sweep, the front, the freeze, the held-out protocol — on a declared synthetic model. Its numbers are not measurements of vLLM. One gpu owner-run exists ( seminars/runs/2026-10-28-topic07-gpu/README.md ): a single T4 pass serving Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct that measured the frozen profile against default (×0.63) and held-out p95 (1585 ms, SLO failed, verdict reject) — measured evidence, one engine, one run, not a benchmark. The search space is small by design: five configurations is a method demonstration, not a coverage claim. Learner validation has not happened, no classroom rehearsal has been observed, and nothing here certifies the judge. The quiet thesis of the whole course is now explicit: the experimental method — predict, measure, compare, freeze, validate — scales from tensors (Topic 03) to services (Topic 06) to configurations (this chapter). Topic 08 will take the frozen profile and put it behind a production API where cancellation, quotas, and backpressure try to undo it. The profile you learned to build here is the artifact you will learn to protect there. The quiet thesis: method scales Step back and notice what has happened across the course. In Topic 03, you froze a calibration choice before opening the held-out set. In Topic 06, you froze a knee prediction before running the waves. In this chapter, you froze a search plan before touching the engine, and a profile before the held-out pair. The pattern is always the same: make a falsifiable commitment, then let data judge it . This pattern is not a course convention — it is the experimental method, and it scales. It worked when the artifact was a quantization scale factor (a tensor-level decision). It worked when the artifact was an operating point on a saturation curve (a service-level decision). It works now when the artifact is a production profile (a configuration-level decision). The knobs change; the discipline does not. When Topic 08 puts the profile behind a production API, you will freeze again — this time a rollback plan — and validate against real traffic. The method is the only thing that transfers unchanged across all these levels. The second thing that scales is the multi-objective frame. In Topic 03 it was weight error versus output error versus task quality. In Topic 06 it was throughput versus tail latency versus error rate. Here it is throughput versus p95 versus quality floors. In production it will be all of those plus cost, plus reliability, plus developer velocity. The Pareto front grows dimensions, but the reading skill is the same: no single number describes a system; the front shows the trade; the SLO picks the point. A colleague who shows you one number without naming the front is either hiding something or has not looked. The knobs you learned here are conceptual — they exist in every serving engine, but the names and trade-offs differ. vLLM is the community default with broad model support. SGLang specializes in prefix caching and structured generation. TensorRT-LLM optimizes for NVIDIA hardware. DeepInfer (DeepSeek, Apache-2.0, October 2026) is the newest open-source entrant: custom MLA attention kernels, FP8 GEMM, an async scheduler that prepares the next batch while the GPU computes the current one, and batch-invariant determinism — same input, same output, regardless of batch composition. It targets SM100 GPUs and is offline-only, but its design choices (async as default, MLA as default) signal where the industry is heading. When you evaluate an engine for your own workload, the search method from this chapter transfers: declare the space, measure, freeze, validate — the knobs are different, the discipline is not. For the student who wants one paragraph from this chapter: a profile is a hypothesis with evidence. Declare the space. Keep the failures. Freeze the choice. Let held-out judge. The profile you build this way survives contact with production not because it is lucky, but because you know exactly what it claims and what it does not. And when the workload changes — as it always does — you know how to run the cycle again: predict, declare, measure, freeze, validate. The profile is disposable; the method is permanent. Check understanding and transfer Answer before opening the explanations. Questions 3, 5 and 8 change one condition: reproducing the notebook is not enough unless you can predict what changes next. {exercises.map(({id,title,question})=> {title}. {question} )} Reveal eight answers and their limits {exercises.map(({id,title,answer})=> {title}. {answer} )}

Chapter 08: Production inference APIs: FastAPI + vLLM

This chapter follows the approved Topic08 arc. The notebook core runs on a free CPU against a MockEngine whose latency knobs are declared synthetic; a live vLLM backend behind the gateway is an owner-run demonstration. Teacher materials stay private;{' '} the topic page separates the acceptance states . From a Python profile to a public promise Topic 07 left you with a frozen production profile: --max-num-seqs 32 , a saturation curve, a tail, a rollback plan. It is a good profile. It is also an internal component — a stranger with an HTTP client cannot import it, cannot call it, and does not care that it exists. The moment your engine accepts work from someone else's code, a new kind of question appears: what stands between a request you did not write and a profile you froze? The answer is one thin gateway, and this chapter builds it in front of the pinned engine. The engineering virtues are the course virtues in a new uniform. Predict before you build: the contract prediction table is frozen before any gateway code runs. A working artifact early: by the fifth executable cell a real HTTP round trip answers, on a mock engine whose knobs are declared on their face. Errors are data: two failure drills fire on demand and leave journal proof. And a frozen promise beats a post-hoc story: the gateway's SLO and rejection policy are written down before the waves arrive to test them. The course motif for the topic is the pass — order, receipt, serving window. A request enters, gets a name, is either being cooked or honestly refused, and every stage of that journey leaves a receipt you can read later. HTTP 200 is not success; it is only an answer that was sent. A cancelled generation still costs tokens. An unbounded queue is not capacity — it is latency hidden from the pager. Each of these sentences becomes a mechanism you build, drill, and journal in this chapter. The profile behind the door Nothing in this chapter re-opens the Topic 07 decision. The engine behind the gateway runs the frozen profile, and the gateway treats the engine as an opaque queue: it does not tune knobs, it does not inspect batches, it admits, forwards, and maps outcomes. This division of labor is deliberate. Tuning is a laboratory activity with a frozen workload; serving is a contract with strangers. Mixing them is how teams end up re-deriving the saturation knee in production traffic at 3 a.m. The pass also inherits the course taxonomy. Validation at the door is the planning discipline from Topic 06 — reject what you cannot serve before it occupies capacity. Admission control is the bounded queue from the saturation lab. A client disconnect is the preemption story: abandoned work must stop consuming. Honest errors are the terminal-outcome taxonomy wearing status codes. You have built each mechanism once already; the gateway is where they learn to speak HTTP. One boundary is declared up front. The core lab runs on free CPU against a MockEngine — an async in-process worker with declared latency knobs (0.15 s to the first token, 0.02 s per token, a concurrency ceiling mirroring the frozen profile). Its numbers are synthetic by construction, and every figure that carries them says so. A live vLLM behind the same gateway is an owner-run demonstration with retained evidence, never a student requirement, and no mock number is ever quoted as an engine measurement. One pass, four decisions The gateway is small enough to draw and should be. A request arrives; the gateway mints an id; validation checks the public caps; admission decides between a service slot, a bounded wait, and a refusal; the engine generates; the error map turns whatever happened into one honest code; the journal keeps the receipt. Five stages, four decisions that a human designed. The map is the review artifact of the topic. Any proposed gateway change — a new header, a retry policy, a queue resize — must name the stage it touches and the decision it changes. A change that cannot name its stage is decoration, and decoration in front of a GPU budget is how incidents are born. The figure also carries the second half of the contract: the request id travels the whole pass and reappears in all four records a human may read at night — the reply header, the engine journal, the error body, the metrics. The contract: caps at the door The request schema is a promise with named ceilings: a required prompt of at most 512 characters, a max_tokens between 1 and 64, an optional schema for structured replies. The ceilings are public — documented, versioned, and quoted in every refusal. This is not bureaucracy. A client that knows the ceiling can fix its own request without burning a round trip; a client that discovers the ceiling by experiment is paying for your documentation in GPU time. Validation at the door is admission control performed before the queue. A malformed or oversized request must not consume even a waiting slot, because the slot it would consume is capacity that an admissible request — one the gateway could actually serve on time — now cannot. The lab's first student function is the frozen contract prediction, and the gate itself — admission — is its first coded mechanism; the frozen prediction table asks for the refusal code of each probe before any of it runs. The same block introduces /health : liveness plus in-flight count, read by probes, by the daemon, and by the on-call. There is no private health route and no hidden truth. A service whose health endpoint lies is a service whose pager lies, one incident later. The id that travels Every request gets an id at the door — before validation, before admission, before anything can go wrong. The id then appears in four places: the reply header the client correlates, the engine journal that proves what the generation did, the body of every error, and the metrics snapshot. Four places is not generosity; it is the minimum set that makes the other promises checkable. Without the journal id, a cancellation claim is unprovable — you cannot show the generation stopped. Without the id in error bodies, a 3 a.m. failure is a stack trace with no request attached. Without ids in metrics, waste and refusal patterns cannot be attributed to clients at all. Identity is what converts logs into evidence, and evidence is the currency every later section pays in. The queue economy An unbounded queue is latency you promised to nobody. Every arrival is accepted, depth grows without a declared ceiling, and the delay is paid by clients who never consented to wait — invisible to capacity planning until client-side timeouts fire all at once. The bounded queue replaces the silent wait with three named outcomes: a service slot, a bounded seat, or an honest refusal. is the mean number of requests in flight (queue plus service); is the arrival rate; is the mean residence per request. With the declared mock residence of 0.47 s, ten arrivals per second already buy — past the admit ceiling of four. The law locates the knee; percentiles come from the journal, not from the law. With service slots and bounded waiting seats, the total depth the gateway is willing to hold is , and the knee — the arrival rate where refusals begin — is: At the declared depth is fully bought by the arrival rate. With the mock arithmetic (residence 0.47 s, four slots, four seats) the knee sits at 8 ÷ 0.47 ≈ 17.0 requests per second. Every arrival past the knee gets 429 with Retry-After — a designed answer, not a failure. The figure is declared arithmetic, and it says so on its face. What matters is the shape: depth is bought with arrival rate at a price set by residence, and the gateway chooses where the purchase ends. The lab drill fires 24 clients at the 4+4 pool and checks the observed share against the frozen envelope — 8 served, 16 refused. A mismatch is the most interesting data of the block: it means a mechanism you did not name is acting, and the drill asks for the name, not for a tweak to the mock. Refusal is an answer 429 with Retry-After is the most misunderstood success in the API world. To the client it is a decision with a declared pause and its request id attached — the retry becomes computable instead of hopeful. To the operator it is a designed signal: a rising rejected counter says the offered load crossed the declared knee, which is exactly what capacity planning needs to know and exactly what an endless queue conceals. The discipline extends to the client's side. The correct response to 429 is to wait the declared pause and retry the same logical request with the same id, backing off exponentially if refusals repeat. Immediate retries turn one refused request into a storm of refused attempts; the rejected counter climbs, and the gateway can see the storm only because refusals are counted. An unbounded queue hides the same storm as latency. A leaving client stops paying A closed socket is a decision by the client, and the gateway must honor it: stop the generation, journal the outcome as cancelled, and count the tokens that were produced for a reader who no longer exists. This is the Topic 06 preemption story in HTTP clothing — abandoned work must stop consuming — and it is the last, freest student function in the lab: a disconnect watcher specified by contract alone. The lab shows the bug before the fix. Without the watcher, an abandoned generation runs to completion; the journal optimistically records a completed request; the waste is invisible. With it, cancellation lands within a declared instant and the waste is a number: is the set of cancelled requests; is what request produced before its cancel landed. In the mock drill a disconnect at 0.30 s with cancellation at 0.35 s wastes (0.35 − 0.15) ÷ 0.02 = 10 tokens; without the watcher the same request burns all 64 — for nobody. The timeline makes the economics visible: the same disconnect, with and without the watcher. The declared mock accounting is stated on the figure — real engines add scheduler notice delay, and freed KV state re-enters service only after the engine notices. The direction is the lesson: cancellation is not free, and a service that does not count it will never know what abandonment costs. Streaming: the same mechanism, one frame later Server-sent events deliver text while the engine decodes, and they change nothing about the pass. Admission, deadline, error map and identity hold frame by frame: a streamed response is still one request with one id and one journal row. What streaming tempts teams into is bypassing the queue — frames feel free, so admission feels optional. It is not. A frame delivered past the declared deadline is a promise broken in slow motion. Mid-stream cancellation is the Episode 5 mechanism one frame later. A client gone at frame k triggers the same watcher, the same journal entry, the same waste count. No new machinery should be invented for streaming, and if your design grows one, that is a signal the pass was never really in charge. Honest errors: the outcome map Every terminal outcome maps to exactly one code with one next action. Invalid requests get 400, because the caps are public and the fix is known. Overload gets 429 with Retry-After , because the refusal is temporary and computable. An engine with no healthy worker gets 503, and the owner gets paged. A deadline gets 504 with the request id, because the client is owed both the verdict and the evidence. Everything else gets 500 without internal details — the client does not need your stack trace, and your stack trace does not belong on the wire. The map is the terminal-outcome taxonomy of Topic 06 wearing status codes. The lab triggers two of the modes on demand — an invalid request and a flagged-down engine — and checks the observed status against the student's own map, with the journal as proof. Two drills cover the named modes, not the whole fault catalogue; the limitation is stated in the notebook and repeated here. The negative rule does the heavy lifting: never 200-with-error-body. A 200 envelope around a failure passes shallow health checks, poisons the client's success path, and corrupts its retry logic silently. The status code is the first truth a client reads; the body explains what the code already decided. Teams that blur this split do not save work — they move the failure into someone else's monitoring, where it costs more to find. Structured outputs: schema in, validated JSON out Guided completion rides in the same contract: the request may carry a response schema, the engine constrains decoding toward it, and the gateway validates the reply against the same schema before answering. The validator is deliberately yours to write — a small checker for named fields, types and enums — because the validation failure is part of the product: a visible 422 with the exact violation path. The drill's fixture breaks the schema on purpose: an enum value outside the declared set, a number shipped as a string. The honest answers are paths — $.priority , $.score — not a silent cast. Coercion would be a double lie: the gateway would claim a reply matches the contract the client programs against, and it would hide a model behavior problem the product team needs to see. The violation path is how a contract stays true under a model that occasionally improvises. Counters you planned Five numbers run the gateway: accepted, rejected, cancelled, in-flight, and waste tokens. Each exists because a named decision needs it — capacity against arrival, backpressure health, abandonment accounting, live saturation, the price of leaving clients. The course rule is blunt: a metric you did not plan is a metric you will fake. So the metrics block plans the counters in the same block that plans the contract, and the snapshot is frozen into the journal with a feeds column: which decision each number informs. The honest zero is part of the design. At snapshot time the cancelled counter reads zero — cancellations arrive only after the cancellation block runs. A zero with a known reason is data; a number decorated to look busy is noise. When you read any gateway dashboard, ask which zeros are explained and which are painted over. Loading the pass The Topic 06 closed-loop wave driver now knocks on the student's own gateway over real HTTP. Two waves — 8 and 24 clients — with every fourth client disconnecting mid-generation. The point is not the throughput number; it is reading your own admission decisions out of the journal: served, refused, cancelled shares per wave, compared against the Block-0 envelope that was frozen before any of it ran. In the declared mock run the shape lands exactly where the arithmetic said: wave 24 shows roughly two thirds refused at the knee, cancellations only where the watcher runs, and the rest served. The table says mock on its face, and the exact percentages live in the run journal. When the wave table disagrees with the envelope, the follow-up is a named mechanism — a slow client start, a queue promotion race — not a silent re-roll. That is the same reading discipline as every freeze in this course. Freeze the API contract The chapter closes the way Topics 06 and 07 closed: with a frozen promise. The gateway SLO card declares the tail the gateway promises inside itself, the error budget, the rejection policy — who gets 429, with what pause, at which pool size — and the cancellation accounting. The memo is one paragraph a product owner and an on-call engineer can both read in thirty seconds, and both must be willing to sign. The refusal clause is part of the promise, not an apology appended to it. A client reading the contract knows that refusals carry Retry-After and the request id, that cancellations are journaled with waste, and that no failure will ever arrive dressed as success. The deliverable is the signature discipline: named clauses, named owners, and a declared bridge — Topic 09 ships this gateway as an immutable image so the contract survives machine drift. What the mock does and does not establish The MockEngine is a declared synthetic worker: its latency knobs are written in the notebook, quoted on every figure, and never compared to vLLM. It exists so the whole gateway contract — validation, admission, refusal, cancellation, error mapping, structured outputs, waves — is exercisable in minutes on a free CPU. What it validates is the pipeline and the reading discipline, not engine magnitudes. The limitations are stated, not hidden. Disconnect detection on the mock is best-case; real networks are noisier and detection latency varies. Two failure drills cover the named modes, not an exhaustive fault catalogue. The gateway is a single instance — horizontal scaling is a later topic. And the live vLLM behind this gateway is an owner-run demonstration with retained evidence; its numbers enter course materials only with that provenance. Worked example: sizing the pass from Little's law The queue is not a guess; it is arithmetic you can defend line by line. The mock engine behind the lab declares a time-in-system of W = 0.47 s for a completion at the frozen seqs-32 profile — that number is written in the notebook, not measured. Little's law from Topic 06 says the queue depth L equals the arrival rate λ times W. The gateway runs four engine slots plus a four-deep waiting row: eight requests can be inside the pass at once, so the queue is full exactly when L reaches 8, which happens at λ = 8 / 0.47 ≈ 17.0 requests per second. That is the 429 knee: below it, refusals are a bug; above it, refusals are the design working. The overload drill checks that this envelope is real. Twenty-four closed-loop clients arrive against eight slots; the journal shows exactly 8 completed and 16 rejected with 429 plus Retry-After — the arithmetic and the wire behavior agree. A junior engineer reads the 16 refusals as an outage. You should read them as the pass refusing orders it cannot cook on time, each refusal carrying the request id and a bounded wait suggestion. The alternative — admitting all twenty-four — would have hidden the same failure inside a two-second queue with no honest signal at all. This is also why the mean lies. Average latency across the drill looks acceptable even while one request in three is refused, because the refused ones return instantly and drag the average down. The Topic 06 lesson — the tail speaks before the mean — becomes an API design rule here: the SLO is written per outcome class (completed p95, refusal share, cancellation waste), never as one blended average. The illustrative tails figure above is the shape students already know from Topic 06: near capacity the mean barely moves while p95 explodes. The gateway turns that curve into a decision made at the door, in milliseconds, per request — which is the only place a decision can actually be made. The curve behind the SLO The gateway inherits its engine from Topic 07: the frozen seqs-32 profile that won the bounded search. It is worth remembering what that profile sits on. The measured T4 run of Topic 06 pushed the pinned 3B model through 29 → 208 → 306 → 311 tok/s across waves of 8/32/64/128 clients with zero timeouts; the gain rule put the knee at wave 32 in the anchor run, and the replicate flipped it back to 64 — the 32→64 doubling sat exactly on the fifty-percent bar. Three runs, one finding: quote the threshold and the run count. The gateway does not change that curve — it stands in front of it. Validation decides who reaches the curve; admission decides how many ride it at once; the error map tells the client which part of the curve refused them. When the SLO memo says "p95 inside 2 s at up to 17 req/s", the number is defensible because the curve behind it has been measured, published with its limits, and argued about in the open. And the profile itself was not the first fast option — it was the only SLO-eligible point on the Pareto front. The search table behind it is frozen, hashed, and inspectable. A contract is defensible when every layer under it — curve, front, freeze — is defensible in the same way. The drills, line by line Read the overload journal one row at a time. Rows r5 through r8: status 200, outcome completed — the four engine slots, each inside the declared 0.47 s. Row r18 arrives when all eight positions are taken: status 429, outcome rejected, Retry-After: 1 . Rows r11, r13 and the rest interleave completions and refusals as slots free up — the pattern of a working admission policy, not of a overloaded machine. The one thing that must never appear in this journal is a 200 carrying an error body: that row would mean the pass cooked nothing but told the client dinner was served. The cancellation drill is two runs of the same leaving client. Without the disconnect watcher, the orphan probe shows the generation running to its full sixty-four tokens — one client, one request at its 64-token cap: sixty-four token-slots of compute spent on a response nobody will read. With the watcher, the journal shows outcome cancelled and a wasted-token count of eight — the tokens between the disconnect and the cancel taking effect. The lesson is arithmetic, not morality: the watcher pays for itself the moment leaving clients outnumber patient ones. The error drills each trip one clause of the map. An overlong body (a 600-character prompt against the declared cap) is refused at the door with 400 before it reaches the queue — validation is admission control. A stopped engine produces 503 with the request id, so the on-call can find the exact failed request in the journal. Both drills are triggered on demand in the lab; both prove the map, not the exception handler that happened to be written first. One request, end to end, twice Happy path. A client posts a completion with a prompt and max_tokens . The schema layer checks the caps — prompt within the declared limit, output cap at most 64 — and rejects anything else with 400 before a slot is touched. The request receives its id at the door; the id is stamped into the journal, the log line, and eventually the response header. The admission queue has a free slot, so the request is admitted immediately. The engine streams tokens; the gateway forwards them; the final frame carries usage. Total gateway time inside the declared envelope; one journal row; counters move by one. Overload path. Same request, but all eight positions are already held. The queue is full, so admission refuses with 429, Retry-After: 1 , and the request id — in that order, because the id is what makes the refusal auditable. The client retries after the pause or backs off; the gateway has spent no engine time on a request it could not serve. Compare the two paths and the design statement of the whole topic appears: the only difference is one decision at the door, made honestly, with evidence either way. Run both paths through the wave driver and the shares land inside the frozen envelope: 75/0/25 percent completed/rejected/cancelled at wave 8; at wave 24 roughly a third completed and two-thirds refused, with the cancelled share jittering between runs. The envelope, not the individual numbers, is the contract — single-run jitter is expected, and the memo says so explicitly. Sources, evidence status and provenance Primary sources for this chapter: the FastAPI documentation (path-operation contracts, background tasks, streaming responses), the uvicorn deployment guide (server lifecycle behind the lab's start_gateway helper), and RFC 9110 for the status-code semantics the error map relies on — 400 for a bad request the client must fix, 429 for overload the client should wait out, 503 for an engine the operators must fix. The structured-output clause follows the schema-constrained generation interface of vLLM ; the lab exercises it against the mock, never quoting mock timing as engine behavior. Evidence status. The gateway mock run of 26 October 2026 — the teacher reference executed end to end on free CPU, 23 code cells, zero errors, artifacts seminars/runs/2026-10-26-topic08-gateway-mock/README.md — is the run record this chapter's drill numbers come from. It is a mock run: declared synthetic timing, not a vLLM measurement, and labelled as such everywhere it appears. The instructor materials — the solved reference, the per-slide script and the owner's GPU demonstration plan — stay in the private repository under instructor/ and never appear on public pages. The live-engine demonstration behind this gateway is an owner-run record that has not happened yet; when it exists, its numbers enter these pages with the same provenance discipline as the Topic 06 saturation run. Until then, this chapter claims a contract and a pipeline, not engine magnitudes. What each lab block proves — and what it deliberately does not The lab is sequenced so that every block owns exactly one claim, and every claim has a falsifiable artifact. Block 0 owns the prediction: the contract table and the queue arithmetic are frozen into api-contract.json before any gateway code runs, which is what makes the later drill results comparisons rather than vibes. If the overload drill had come first, the envelope would have been fitted to whatever happened; written down first, it can lose — and a prediction that can lose is the only kind worth making. Block 1 owns the build. The first working artifact arrives early: a bare pass-through gateway answering /health and one completion over real HTTP, long before validation, queues or error maps exist. That ordering is deliberate — students debug a known-simple system first, then add mechanisms one at a time, each behind a named function. By the time the admission queue lands, the difference between "the engine is slow" and "the queue made it look slow" is something they have already seen from both sides. Block 2 owns the breaks. The disconnect drill, the overload drill and the two error drills are not demonstrations; they are attempts to falsify the Block 0 claims. Each drill ends with a journal comparison against the frozen envelope, and each has one deliberately wrong predecessor — the orphan probe runs without the watcher precisely so students can measure what the watcher saves. Errors as data is the course-wide rule; here it wears status codes. Block 3 owns the measurement discipline: the same wave driver students met in Topic 06, now pointed at their own HTTP surface, with the journal classified into completed/rejected/cancelled shares per wave. The comparison against the envelope — not against a feeling — is the deliverable. The stretch block adds /metrics and the memo, and the memo is graded for named clauses, not for optimism: what the gateway promises, what it refuses, and what it will never dress up as success. What the blocks deliberately do not prove: engine performance (the mock's timing knobs are declared, not measured), multi-instance behavior (one gateway process throughout), and security beyond identity (no authentication surface in scope). Saying what a lab does not establish is part of establishing anything at all — the same honesty rule the saturation curve, the Pareto front and the frozen profile were held to. Reading the counters like the on-call engineer The /metrics snapshot is short on purpose: accepted, rejected-429, cancelled, in-flight, and latency buckets. Each counter answers one operational question. Accepted counts the pass actually cooking; rejected-429 counts the door working; cancelled counts clients that left mid-order; in-flight is the live occupancy of the eight positions; the latency buckets show where completed requests land relative to the declared 0.47 s per-token envelope. A counter that answers no question is decoration, and decoration drifts out of truth silently. Three readings from the snapshot deserve rehearsal. If rejected-429 climbs while in-flight stays at eight, the arrival rate crossed the 17 req/s knee — the system is healthy, the demand is past capacity, and the honest answers are scale up or say no faster. If cancelled climbs while accepted stays flat, clients are giving up before the first token — look at time-to-first-admission, not at generation speed. If in-flight sits below eight while rejected-429 climbs, something is leaking slots — an admission that never released is the gateway's own bug, and the journal's request ids are how you find it. None of these readings require engine expertise; all of them require the counters to exist. That is why observability is designed before the incident, in the same block as the contract, and why the stretch memo ends the topic by defending the SLO the counters are measured against. Streaming, cancelation and the last frame Streaming changes when the client learns things, not what the contract means. The server-sent-event frames forward tokens as the engine earns them, so perceived latency drops to the first token rather than the last. But the frames also move the cancellation problem one frame later: a client that closes the connection mid-stream is the same leaving customer as the one who vanished before the first token, and the same watcher must catch both. The lab proves the symmetry — the mid-stream cancel lands in the journal as cancelled with its waste counted, exactly like the pre-stream one, and the frame stream terminates with an honest terminal event instead of silence. The last frame carries more than text. Usage — prompt tokens, output tokens, the request id — lets the client reconcile its own accounting against the journal, which is how billing disputes and bug reports become lookups instead of arguments. And because the frames are the contract's surface too, a structured-output request validates the assembled object before the terminal frame: a schema violation arrives as a visible error with the violation path, never as a confident wrong answer with status 200. The rule from the error map survives streaming unchanged: every terminal state the client can observe is either the promised payload or an honest refusal — nothing in between.
