Chapter 09: Docker for LLM inference

This chapter follows the owner-approved Topic09 vision v2 (7 November 2026). The lab runtime is the student's local Docker; a real tiny LLM runs inside the container — Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Q4_K_M, 491 MB of weights) served by llama.cpp llama-server . The GPU variant of the image stays an owner demonstration. Every measured byte and second in your journal belongs to your machine; course-record numbers are labelled as such. From a gateway to a production unit Topic 08 left you with a gateway worth trusting: it validated inputs, refused overload with honest 429s, cancelled what clients abandoned. But the service lived in "works on my machine" land: whatever Python the host happened to have, pip installs at runtime, the cwd deciding what the app sees. In production this is not an inconvenience — it is an incident: a pod that behaves differently on different nodes has no contract. This chapter turns the service into a production unit and answers four questions that cost real money in production. Speed: what does a rebuild cost after an edit, and why does a good build measure rebuilds in seconds. Size: what the megabytes of an image are made of, and which price you pay for each way of delivering model weights. Contract: does it survive the container boundary without a single change. And recovery: the pod died of memory — what the journal shows and how fast it comes back. The course motif stays the same: the image is the blueprint of a mobile kitchen, the container is the kitchen at work, layers are its modules. V2 adds the fleet: a park of identical kitchens where one fell over, repaired itself, and was back in a second. The lab reproduces this cycle for real — with a tiny but genuine LLM in the container, on an ordinary laptop, no GPU. Your first five minutes with Docker If Docker is new to you, the lab starts with one command: docker run hello-world . It pulls a tiny image from a registry and runs it — the first artifact appears before any theory. Then the four daily commands: docker ps (what runs), docker logs (what it says), docker inspect (what it is), docker images (what you built). The whole lab journal is built on these commands: inside the notebook a guarded helper calls them, so every number lands in the journal instead of terminal history. Agree on the words early. An image is an immutable blueprint: the application's filesystem with dependencies, stacked in layers. A container is an ordinary process on your machine, launched from that blueprint in isolation: its own filesystem, its own name, bounded resources — the same Linux kernel, no "little virtual machine". That is exactly where the seconds of start and restart this chapter measures come from. Production calls these blueprints pods and their failures CrashLoopBackOff; by the end of the chapter that vocabulary is yours. An image is ordered layers Every Dockerfile instruction produces a layer: a diff over the layer below, frozen into the image. An image is an ordered stack of these layers plus a manifest. This is not an implementation detail — it is the mechanism behind three behaviors you use daily: how builds become fast, how pulls become cheap, and how edits stay cheap. A layer's build cache is valid only if that layer and every layer below it are unchanged. Change one file an early layer copied, and everything above rebuilds. The working rule: order instructions from most stable to most frequently changing. The lab freezes this order and three invalidation predictions into build-plan.json before the first build — the same predict-before-measure discipline as Topics 06–07, now about bytes instead of tokens. The cache-hit condition The block formalizes into one condition. Layer survives a rebuild if and only if it and all layers beneath it are byte-identical. From it follow both the "which edit rebuilds what" table and the pinning discipline: changing the source pin invalidates the fetch layer; changing the base, the whole stack. Read it as: a cache hit for layer k means "neither it nor any ancestor changed". A well-written Dockerfile is therefore a schedule of events: what changes daily goes above what changes monthly, which goes above what changes twice a year. In the lab you verify the condition with a live docker history after editing a file: the build-plan.json prediction against the build fact. Two build caches: layers and content Compiling llama.cpp from sources takes minutes even on a fast machine, and it is the perfect proving ground for build speed. Two caches are often confused. The layer cache remembers instructions: a layer does not re-run while its inputs are unchanged. The content cache (a cache mount; ccache in the lab) remembers bytes: object files live outside the layers and survive compile-layer invalidation. The lab measures three runs of one real compilation: a cold build with an empty ccache, a rebuild with zero edits, and a one-line patch with a warm compiler cache. Course records for this chapter: 142 s cold (10 vCPU), 0.4 s unchanged rebuild, 44 s one-line patch with warm ccache. The order of magnitude is the lesson: seconds versus minutes versus the full compile; on your machine you will record your own numbers and compare the magnitudes, not the exact values. This block caught a genuinely live trap. The first Dockerfile draft omitted ca-certificates : apt worked fine — it speaks plain HTTP to Ubuntu mirrors — while git fetch died with server certificate verification failed. CAfile: none ; GitHub requires TLS. The tooling layer is a contract with the network: list everything the build will touch. The story became a level-B student exercise: find the three packages without which the tooling layer breaks its promises. What ccache actually remembers Why does a one-line patch cost 44 seconds — not 0.4 and not the full 165? The answer is in the compiler cache's design. Before compiling each translation unit, ccache hashes everything that affects the result: the compiler version, the flags, the preprocessed text of the file — including every header it pulls. Hash match: the object file comes from the cache. Miss: the file recompiles. src/llama.cpp is a heavy hub in the llama.cpp tree: its preprocessed text changes on an edit, and so does everything that includes it. So 44 seconds is the recompilation of affected units plus linking — not "everything again" (that would be ~165) and not "nothing" (the layer cache path would be ~0.5). Three working rules follow. The compiler cache does not replace layer order: it speeds up the rebuild AFTER invalidation, while the layer cache avoids the invalidation entirely; they work on different events. The cache is environment-sensitive: changing the compiler or flags in the tooling layer empties it — which is why the tooling layer is pinned together with the base. And the cache is not an artifact: object files keep traces of build paths, so what ships in the runtime image is the linked binary, never the cache itself. All of this is testable in the lab: the third build run with a warm mount is an experiment over exactly these rules. Frequently asked questions Why not vLLM? The lab engine is chosen by one criterion: it must fit on a student laptop and come up in seconds. vLLM with its torch and CUDA stack is a 10.4 GB compressed image and minutes to start; llama.cpp with 0.5B Q4 is 1.18 GB and a second to /health. The production patterns — limits, OOM, backoff, restart economics — are identical; the scale is not, and the chapter says so honestly. The GPU image variant stays an owner demonstration. Why a 400 m limit rather than, say, 700 m? Because the incident must be deterministic. At 700 m, a replica with ~760 MB resident sits in a gray zone: the outcome depends on how many pages were already touched, and on another machine it may never fire. 400 m is below any resident configuration — the kernel fires reliably, and the crash-loop curve is recorded the same way everywhere. The production lesson is the same: a limit that sometimes fires is worse than a limit you can reason about. Why --memory-swap equal to --memory? The pair disables swap: without it, a container hitting the limit starts paging to disk — the incident becomes not an OOM but endless, slow breathing through swap. The incident's determinism costs one flag line. Where is the GPU? Nowhere — and that is stated honestly. Layers, caches, sizes, the contract, limits, OOM and restarts know nothing about the accelerator. The GPU version of this topic is the same blueprint with a CUDA base, a vLLM pin and --gpus , and it is demonstrated by the owner with preserved evidence rather than executed by students. What if a student has no Docker at all? The notebook stays green: every docker cell is guarded and prints an honest skip. Plan mode covers predictions, transcripts, journals and diagnoses; live numbers are collected on any Docker machine — in class, at home, or on any cloud runtime. Lean means pinned, not pretty The naive v0 of the lab works: a floating :server tag, root, no health declaration. It exists to become the baseline. Your v1 fixes four things, one line each. The digest pin: FROM ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp@sha256:… — a tag floats, a digest is exact bytes. A non-root user: a smaller attack surface. A HEALTHCHECK on /health: the daemon knows whether the service lives. And a deliberate choice of weight delivery — the next section. The pin is not pedantry, and the lab proves it with a live fact: fresh llama.cpp builds replaced the --mlock and --no-mmap flags with --load-mode … . "It worked yesterday" breaks not only in image bytes but in the CLI underneath. Metadata layers (LABEL, HEALTHCHECK, USER) weigh zero bytes — pins and probes cost nothing in size and change everything in reproducibility. In the lab v0 and v1 build back-to-back and docker images shows identical sizes — the cleanest proof that security and pins are free. Model artifacts: bake, mount, or download For an LLM image the size accounting is brutal: the llama-server binary is single-digit megabytes, the Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4_K_M weights are 491 400 032 bytes. No matter what you do to the Dockerfile, the weights dictate the size — so the real question is not "how to shrink" but which price you accept for delivering the weights. Bake (COPY into the image) gives a self-sufficient artifact, but every pull pays half a gigabyte extra. Mount ( -v from the host) keeps the image lean but ties the fleet to one host disk. Download at start makes the network the dominant recovery term — the worst choice for the crash-loop scenario. The lab mounts by default (the fleet lives on one machine) and offers bake as an optional measurement: course record, the COPY layer adds ~491 MB, 1.18 GB → ~1.67 GB. The third option — download at start — deserves an honest read, because it looks free and is not. The weights arrive at the moment the pod must already answer: the network becomes the dominant restart term, and in a crash-loop scenario it is paid on every bring-up. Its honest home is ephemeral nodes with a shared weight cache — where the first start on a node is expensive and the rest are nearly free. Choosing a delivery method is choosing WHERE the bill lands: in the pull (bake), in host dependence (mount), or at recovery time (download). Read the price table together with the restart curve of the incident block — it is one economics seen from two sides. The size ledger: three orders of magnitude docker history is the ledger, and it proves the arithmetic: an image's size is the sum of its layers. Course records line up the contrast this chapter exists for. Our from-source runtime image: 150 MB — only llama-server and runtime libraries; the compilers stayed in the builder stage. The upstream llama.cpp:server image: 1.18 GB unpacked. The published vllm/vllm-openai: ~10.4 GB compressed — the full torch and CUDA stack. The lab does not build vLLM; the number is the contrast. Multi-stage is the difference between seconds and minutes on every pull of every fleet machine. The same ledger answers "what if we bake". The COPY layer with weights reads as +491 MB in history, and the price shows up twice: on every pull and on every start's extraction. In the crash-loop scenario of the next section that price becomes seconds of downtime — the size ledger and the recovery economics are one table. Launch and probes across the boundary The container lives in its own network spaces, and the road from the laptop is three flags. -p host:container — the port; -v host-path:/models/model.gguf:ro — the weights, mounted read-only; --memory — the wall the pod lives behind. Inside is a real tiny LLM: llama-server with Qwen2.5-0.5B, a 1024-token context, CPU. The contract we verify was born in Topic 08: the gateway map — validation, the bounded queue, timeouts — remains the reference point against which "nothing changed" is measured. The verification probe repeats the course contract from Topics 04/08: GET /health → 200; POST /v1/chat/completions → non-empty reply text; usage.total_tokens → a number above zero. Nothing in this contract changed because the server moved into a container — that is the entire point of an image: behavior no longer depends on the host. Course records: start-to-first-/health about one second, an "OK" reply to a one-word prompt in 0.15 s on CPU. Your numbers go into your machine's contract-journal.json. Each probe maps to a failure class you will meet in production. /health returning anything but 200 means the process inside is not listening — wrong flags, wrong port mapping, or a crash loop in progress. A completion that returns but carries empty content means the contract's happy path broke — usually a rendering or template issue, which Topics 04/08 taught you to catch by reading actual bytes. Usage reporting zero tokens means accounting broke upstream of the reply. Three probes, three different suspects — and none of them care that the server sits in a container: across the boundary the contract is the only thing you can see, which is exactly why it must be strong. The production incident: a pod with a wrong limit Now the culmination — a production scenario, reproduced on your laptop. A replica runs with --memory 400m against a resident appetite of ~760 MB (491 MB of weights plus KV cache and buffers). The prediction is frozen before the run: what will the kernel do when the process touches a page past the wall? You know the answer from Topic 08 — except this time it is not the queue refusing, it is the cgroup. Two facts are visible from outside: exit code 137 and the "OOMKilled": true field in docker inspect . 137 is 128 + 9: the kernel delivered SIGKILL, the strongest possible termination, delivered from outside the process. No traceback, no Python exception: the decision to kill was the kernel's, not the application's. The journal tail breaks off mid-model-load — the evidence of where the process crossed the wall. The lab's determinism comes from --load-mode mmap+mlock : mmap file pages are evictable, and the container could keep living by breathing through eviction; mlock pins the pages in RAM, so the limit fires reliably. It is the same mechanism by which a production pod that ate its requests pays for its limit. Crash loop and backoff: how the orchestrator refuses to finish you off One OOM is half the story. The lab's pod runs with --restart=on-failure , and real production morphology begins: restart → OOM again → restart. The lab observation (course record): 5 restarts by 6.2 s, 7 by 12.3 s, 8 by 18.4 s, then a pause — the intervals grow . The orchestrator applies exponential backoff: docker from 100 ms to a 1-minute ceiling, Kubernetes from 10 s to 5 minutes, and calls it CrashLoopBackOff . The point is identical: do not hammer a dying pod, do not burn resources, do not flood the logs. The measured restart curve is a diagnosis of configuration, not flakiness. It reads: the pod dies the same death every time (OOMKilled=true each time), so the cause is not transient but structural — the limit is below residency. The corresponding fix is not "restart it again" but recompute the limit. Restart economics, term by term After the fix — sizing: limit = resident memory with headroom (~1.5×; in the lab 762 MB measured → 1200 m). Then the "down → answering again" time is measured, and it itemizes into named terms — the same decomposition as cold-start economics, applied to an incident. Read left to right: extract the layers, load the weights, init the server, answer the first /health. This is where the size and delivery decisions are paid back: a lean image makes extraction cheap; a mount over a warm page cache makes weight loading nearly free; init of a 0.5B model on CPU is hundreds of milliseconds. Course record: restart-to-ready 1.07–1.08 s across two runs on a warm machine. Size minimization IS recovery speed; the size accountant and the reliability engineer read one table. Distinguish the two restarts the lab measures separately. docker restart on a live node is the warm path: the page cache is hot, weights are barely read from disk, and the count is in seconds (course record 1.07–1.08 s). A node failure is the cold path: a fresh node pulls the image from the registry, warms the page cache from zero, and the bill adds pull and a full extraction. The difference between the two numbers is the price of losing a node — worth knowing before the incident, not during. In k8s that difference is hidden behind the replica factor and PodDisruptionBudgets — but the arithmetic underneath stays the same. This chapter's vocabulary is the direct bridge to Topic 11: a container with a restart policy ≈ a pod with a controller; exit 137 with OOMKilled ≈ the pod's OOMKilled status; exponential backoff ≈ CrashLoopBackOff; --memory ≈ resources.limits; HEALTHCHECK ≈ liveness/readiness probes. Today you measured each of these mechanics on bare Docker — in Kubernetes you will read them as native. How we caught the port ghost: debugging as part of the plot The first draft of the lab carried a defect that became a lesson. The recovery cell attached to the same port 8099 where the Block-3 container was still living, and wait_healthy instantly caught a stranger's replica answering. The journal recorded "0.0 s to ready", "0 B resident memory" and restarts that never happened. No magic: a health probe does not know WHO answers on the port — only that someone answered 200. The diagnosis took one check: comparing artifact timestamps, the executed notebook version and live docker processes. The fix is three lines: the repaired replica gets its own port ( port_host + 1 ), a warm-up call precedes docker stats sampling, and time-to-ready is recorded as measured — zero seconds is a valid measurement when it is yours. The student's moral: port isolation is not bureaucracy but the condition of honest measurement; and an "instant success" probe is a reason for suspicion, not celebration. The same evening left two more entries in the "failures as data" collection. kill -9 1 from inside a container does not kill PID 1: the kernel blocks fatal signals to a namespace's init from processes of the same namespace — simulating a crash "from inside" is pointless, a real OOM will do it properly. And a manual docker kill experiment showed something else: manually stopping a container disables its restart policy until the daemon restarts — the orchestrator distinguishes "it fell" from "someone stopped it by hand". Both traps now live in the diagnosis cell's transcripts. The fleet memory budget: requests-and-limits arithmetic A three-replica fleet on a laptop is already capacity planning — the same work production does with requests and limits. The lab's arithmetic: one replica with a 1024-token context eats ~760 MiB resident (course record; your machine — your docker stats ). Three replicas: about 2.3 GiB, plus the weights' page cache, plus the daemon itself. A 3.8 GiB Docker Desktop VM fits this fleet without maneuvering room; at 6 GiB it is comfortable. Two sizing rules follow, and they transfer to k8s verbatim. First: limit = resident × headroom . The headroom exists for named events, not superstition: context peaks (more tokens in a batch — more KV cache), allocator fragmentation, concurrent load spikes. The lab uses ×1.5: 760 MB → 1200 m. Less headroom — the crash loop returns; more — dead reserve nobody can occupy. Second: request ≈ observed resident, limit = request × headroom — in k8s, the difference between request and limit is exactly this: what the scheduler is guaranteed and what the kernel is allowed to take. The honesty check: if your limit never approaches peak residency, you do not know your load profile; if it has ever crossed it, you know it too well. Security defaults, not security options The economics of refusal are shared between Topic 08's queue and this topic's limit: an honest refusal beats silent degradation, whether it is a 429 in user space or a SIGKILL from the kernel. Every v1 default is one Dockerfile line, and the whole fleet inherits each: the digest pin (byte-exact reproducibility), the non-root uid (a smaller blast radius), the HEALTHCHECK (the daemon knows the truth about liveness), the memory limit (admission control). The lab's live log adds the server's own honest warning: "no API key is set and CORS allows all origins" — production adds authentication, TLS and network policy, but those are policies around the image, not replacements for the defaults inside. Limits are Topic 08's admission control, moved from the gateway's queue into the kernel: an honest wall beats silent degradation. Note the gradation of responsibility. The image is responsible for defaults being right and host-independent: uid, pin, healthcheck, limit. The orchestrator is responsible for limits being filled meaningfully: requests from measurements, limits with justified headroom. The application is responsible for reporting overload honestly before it gets stopped: the 429 queue from T08 is the first line of defense, the cgroup the last. Three levels, three different files in the repository, one philosophy: a declared refusal is cheaper than a surprise. SBOM and the supply chain An SBOM is the inventory of everything inside the image: OS packages, binaries, versions. One image — one document. Three questions it makes explicit. A floating base tag: :server today and in six months are different bytes; the digest is the antidote. Dependencies without boundaries: the source pin (LLAMACPP_SHA) and the weight pin (file name plus exact size) are versions with borders. Layers remember everything: a file deleted by a later instruction still lives in the earlier layer; a secret in a layer is a secret forever. docker history reads what you "erased". The diagnostic ladder: a full post-mortem of one death Walk the incident the way an on-call engineer does — down the ladder from symptom to fix, skipping no rung. Symptom: monitoring shows one of the fleet's three endpoints flapping, and docker ps shows the t09-inc container constantly restarting. The first reflex is not "restart it again" but a question: how many times has it already restarted? docker inspect answers with RestartCount — and watched over two minutes, the counter grows while the intervals between restarts double. Diagnosis one: crash loop. Cause: not yet. Second rung — the process's last sortie. docker logs --tail 20 shows a short life: the server started, began loading the model, and went silent mid-load. The tail contains no exception and no traceback — there never were any: the application did not live long enough to understand anything. In parallel, docker inspect returns the two fields that together read as a verdict: "ExitCode": 137 and "OOMKilled": true . 137 is 128 + 9: shells encode signal deaths as 128 plus the signal number; signal 9 is SIGKILL, the one signal that cannot be caught. The sender is neither the application nor the runtime: it is the kernel's cgroup mechanism, protecting the node's memory from a process that crossed a declared wall. Third rung — reconstructing the arithmetic. Why did the process cross the wall at all? The limit is 400 m; the 491 MB of weights load with mmap+mlock , meaning pinned in RAM; the context KV cache and engine buffers sit on top. Resident memory must exceed the limit before the first answer — death mid-load reproduces on every start. Not "sometimes", not "under load": the configuration guarantees the outcome. Such incidents are the cheapest to diagnose and the most annoying to operate: they fire on every deploy and read as flakiness until someone does the arithmetic. Fourth rung — the fix and its proof. The limit is recomputed from a measurement, not a hope: docker stats on a healthy replica shows 760 MiB; headroom ×1.5 gives 1200 m. The container restarts with the new limit — and now the second half of the fix matters: the proof that the crash loop has ended. RestartCount stops growing; /health answers; repeat restarts settle in ~1.3 seconds. The journal records both numbers — before and after — with the named mechanism between them: "the limit was below residency; it is now above with headroom; the cgroup no longer fires". The four-rung post-mortem — symptom, evidence, arithmetic, proven fix — transfers to k8s without a single change: only the commands that pull each rung are different. The backoff constants differ between docker and k8s, and the difference is telling. Docker grows from 100 ms to a one-minute ceiling: it assumes a local context, where a restarted process either recovers quickly or is visibly broken. Kubernetes grows from 10 seconds to five minutes: it assumes a cluster, where every dead cycle costs scheduler resources and shows in fleet-wide metrics. The morphology is identical — exponential growth with a ceiling; the constants express the price of a wrong restart in each environment. When reading an unfamiliar monitoring system, remember both orders of magnitude: intervals in fractions of a second are docker-like policy; intervals in tens of seconds and minutes are k8s. And the mount that delivers the lab's weights carries two deliberate details: an absolute path (a relative one is "works on my machine" land, the very ground this topic moves the service out of) and :ro — a container with write access to the weights is a container able to silently corrupt the shared cache every replica on the node divides. The topic glossary Image — an immutable artifact: ordered layers plus a manifest. Layer — the filesystem delta of one Dockerfile instruction. Layer cache — reusing a layer while neither it nor anything below changed. Cache mount — a directory outside the layers (ccache in the lab) that survives layer invalidation. Multi-stage — build in a builder stage; only artifacts are copied into runtime. Digest — the sha256 of the image's exact bytes; a tag floats, a digest does not. .dockerignore — what never enters the build context and is therefore never remembered by layers. HEALTHCHECK — the liveness declaration the daemon polls; in k8s, liveness/readiness probes. Non-root — the process runs under an unprivileged uid. The container boundary — port mappings, mounts and limits through which the laptop reaches the isolated process. Resident memory — what the process holds in RAM right now; read it with docker stats . Limit (--memory) — the cgroup wall; the kernel's admission control. OOMKill / exit 137 — the kernel's SIGKILL on limit violation; 128 plus the signal number. Crash loop — a pod dying repeatedly; backoff — the growing pause between restarts; in k8s, CrashLoopBackOff. Restart-to-ready — the time from "down" to "answering /health", itemized into extraction, weight loading, init and the first reply. Bake / mount / download — three ways of delivering weights, three prices. SBOM — the inventory of an image's contents. Pin — fixing a source version (commit, digest, file size) against floating tags. What this chapter establishes — and what it does not Establishes. A deployment unit that builds fast (layer cache plus cache mount), weighs honestly (a per-layer ledger, a deliberate weight-delivery price), keeps its contract across the boundary, and recovers in seconds after an honest production incident — with a journal tying every number to your machine and your build. Does not prove. Seconds and megabytes are local and machine-dependent; the course never quotes them as engine benchmarks. llama.cpp with 0.5B Q4 shows production patterns, not production scale. No real Kubernetes was launched — only its vocabulary on Docker primitives. GPU images and the vLLM fleet remain owner demonstrations. One SBOM of one image is not a security certificate. Sources, evidence status and provenance The live run record of the whole lab: seminars/runs/2026-11-07-topic09-fleet-mac/README.md (Docker Desktop on the owner's MacBook, 7 November 2026). Image mechanics: the official Docker documentation — layers, build cache, multi-stage, healthcheck. The lab engine: llama.cpp llama-server , course source pin commit fd27b2034… , base image ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server at digest sha256:6d581c78… . Weights: Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-GGUF, qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf , 491 400 032 bytes. Course records were measured on the owner's MacBook (Docker Desktop, ~3.8 GiB VM, 10 vCPU) on 7 November 2026 and are labelled as records; the live run of the whole lab is seminars/runs/2026-11-07-topic09-fleet-mac/ . The published vllm/vllm-openai size is a Docker Hub record dated 2 November 2026. The student notebook is canonical and generated by scripts/build-topic09-notebook.py ; every docker cell is guarded and prints an honest skip on a machine without the daemon. Plan mode runs everywhere; the live run needs a Docker machine. Check understanding and transfer Answer before opening the explanations. The two-caches, restart-curve and recovery-terms questions each test transfer: reproducing the notebook is not enough if you cannot predict what changes under a different limit or a different delivery choice. {exercises.map(({id,title,question})=> {title}. {question} )} Show the nine answers and their limits {exercises.map(({id,title,answer})=> {title}. {answer} )}

Chapter 10: Multi-GPU inference: tensor parallelism

This chapter follows the approved Topic10 arc. The lab runtime is the DECLARED CPU SIMULATION: the NumPy split mechanics are real (column/row-parallel shards joined by an all-reduce equal the full matmul within floating-point tolerance — max-abs error 8.9e-16 at tp = 2 in the teacher run), and every wall-clock beyond them is declared arithmetic with named knobs (C = 800 ms, B = 120, b = 25 ms). The real multi-GPU vLLM route ( tensor_parallel_size = 2 ) is an owner-run demonstration with retained evidence; no student GPU numbers exist, and every number you quote is either that declared arithmetic or your own journal row. One GPU ends twice Topic 09 handed you a contract: one immutable image that runs the same way on every machine with a container runtime. But everything that image served lived on a single GPU, and a single GPU ends twice. The first ending is memory. An 8B model at fp16 is about 16 GB of weights alone, and the KV cache must live in the same memory — against roughly 15 GiB of usable budget on a common accelerator. When the ledger does not fit, the service does not start; there is no graceful version of an out-of-memory start. The second ending is the latency floor. Even when the model fits, autoregression is a chain: each token depends on the previous one, and one stream on one device cannot buy a shorter token step by batching alone once the engine is memory-bound. Batching multiplies throughput; it does not shorten the chain. A bigger GPU is one answer, but a bigger GPU is not always available — and it is not the only axis. Topic 10 opens the first scaling axis inside one machine: tensor parallelism, the practice of splitting the weight matrices of a layer across several GPUs, running the pieces in lockstep, and paying a synchronisation beat for every join. The engineering virtues are concrete, and the lab makes you exercise each of them. The split is exact , and you prove it numerically before any economics. The economics are predicted before they are measured : the knee of the step-time curve is frozen into a plan file before the sweep runs, the same predict-before-measure discipline as the Topic 06 forecast and the Topic 09 build plan. The memory ledger is itemised , so the "which degree fits" decision is a row in a table, not folklore. And the failure modes are deliberate data : two transcripts, diagnosed cause → evidence → fix, in the same genre as the Topic 09 tag-drift and OOM drills. The course motif for the topic is a grand piano carried by four. Each bearer carries a part; the piano moves only when all four step together; and every step begins with the same "one-two-lift" beat. More bearers make each part lighter — but no bearer moves alone, and the beat is paid at every step, at every layer. Hold that image: it is nearly literal, and by the end of the chapter you will be able to compute where the extra bearers stop helping. Four axes, one first choice Tensor parallelism is not the only way to spread a model over devices, and part of the skill is knowing which axis a given problem asks for. The map has four rows, and the lab asks you to write exactly one sentence per row — the deep mechanics of the other axes belong to later topics. TP — tensor parallelism — splits the weight matrices of one layer across GPUs. Every device holds a shard of the same layer, every token passes through all of them, and the join is an all-reduce per block. It pays for the split with synchronisation beats, which is why it demands a fast bus. It is the first candidate inside one node when the model does not fit one GPU or when a shorter step is the goal. PP — pipeline parallelism — splits the layers across devices: it tolerates slower links but pays with pipeline bubbles. DP — data parallelism at the serving level — replicates the whole engine : near-zero communication, and the answer when the model fits and throughput, not step time, is the goal. EP — expert parallelism — splits the experts of a mixture-of-experts model, one expert per device. The map keeps the topic honest in both directions. When someone proposes "just add GPUs", the map asks: add them along which axis, and what does that axis charge? And when TP is proposed, the map names its precondition — a fast interconnect inside one node — so that the failure mode you will meet later in this chapter (a comm-bound regression on a slow bus) is predictable from the configuration, not discovered in production. Placement is a decision with stated costs; the lab freezes yours as paragraphs before the stretch card of the real vLLM flag appears. Split the weight matrices, join with all-reduce There are two canonical ways to cut a matrix multiplication across GPUs, and the lab makes you implement both from scratch. Column-parallel cuts the weight matrix by output features : each GPU sees all of the input X but computes only its own columns of Y . Attention heads and MLP up-projections are natural column-parallel: the outputs are independent feature groups, so no join is needed inside the block. Row-parallel cuts the weight by input features , slicing the input the same way: each GPU computes a partial product , and an all-reduce — an exact element-wise sum on every participant — joins the partials into the full output. MLP down-projections are the natural row-parallel partner. The pairing rule follows from the shapes: up-projection column-parallel, down-projection row-parallel, and one all-reduce beat at the seam. A transformer block carries two such beats — one after the attention projections, one after the MLP — and that count is a declared constant of the model you will price in the next sections. What must stay whole: LayerNorm, residuals and the softmax over the full vocabulary do not split for free; they are replicated or re-joined at the beats. The figure above is the declared mechanism, not a hardware measurement — its value is that every box in it is something you will build and check in NumPy before you price anything. Notice what the split does not change: the mathematics. Each shard computes a genuine piece of the same multiplication; the join reconstructs the full result exactly, in exact arithmetic. Whether it reconstructs it exactly in floating point is an empirical question — and that is the next section, because the whole economics of the topic stands on that one property. The split is exact — proved, not asserted The lab's first working artifact arrives early, by the same convention as every topic before: a small seeded transformer block — an input X of shape 8 × 24, an up-projection of 24 × 96, a down-projection of 96 × 24 — and a full single-GPU reference pass of it. You write the shard helpers yourself: column_parallel , row_parallel , and allreduce_sum , with shape checks at the seams. Then you assemble the block the Megatron way — column-parallel up, row-parallel down, all-reduce at the seam — and compare the result to the reference element-wise. The assembly sums the per-shard partials into the exact full output; the lab proves it numerically: the element-wise max-abs error against the single-GPU reference must stay under . The teacher run measured 8.9e-16 at tp = 2 and 6.7e-16 at tp = 4 — floating-point dust, not approximation. The teacher run of 1 November 2026 journaled the proof rows: max-abs error 0.0 at tp = 1 (the identity split), 8.9e-16 at tp = 2 and 6.7e-16 at tp = 4 — every row within the 1e-10 tolerance, frozen into split-proof.json . Those numbers are real NumPy on a CPU: the only part of this lab that is measurement rather than declaration, and deliberately the part that carries the correctness invariant. "Разбитое равно целому" — the split equals the whole — is a property the journal demonstrates, not a slogan. Why insist on the proof before any economics? Because everything downstream trusts the sum. If the all-reduce were approximate, every layer of every token would drift, and no step-time model would matter — the answers would be wrong at any speed. The exactness proof is also your first diagnostic instrument: it turns silent mechanical failures (a lost join, an empty shard) into loud verdicts, which is exactly the property the drills section will rely on. Mechanics before economics is not a stylistic order; it is the order in which claims become checkable. Step time: compute falls, the beat stays With the mechanics proven, the topic allows itself one formula. The declared step-time model has three named knobs, printed on the deck and in the notebook, with no hidden measurements behind them: , the compute of one step on a single GPU (declared 800 ms); , the all-reduce byte share billed at fraction (declared 120); and , the price of one synchronisation beat (declared 25 ms). The compute term falls ~1/tp — the work is genuinely divided. The byte share approaches B as the degree grows: every additional participant adds bytes to the same join. The beat term grows linearly: two beats per block, at every layer, and one more beat-price unit per added GPU. Declared values: C = 800 ms, B = 120, b = 25 ms. Without the beat term the curve would fall forever and the answer to "how many GPUs" would always be "more". With it, the total develops a minimum — the knee — and the whole discipline of this chapter is that the knee is predictable before the sweep . The figure shows the three terms against the degree for the declared knobs: compute falling as 800 → 400 → 267 → 200 → 160 → 133 → 114 → 100 ms, the sync terms rising to 280 ms at tp = 8, and the total dipping to 356 ms at p = 5 before climbing again. A note on honesty, in the same breath as Topic 07's mock and Topic 08's gateway: these are declared milliseconds, teaching-grade arithmetic with named knobs. The structure of the model — compute divided, bytes shared, beats added — is the honest part; the values are chosen so the arithmetic is checkable by hand. Nothing in this chapter is a hardware benchmark, and no number in it transfers to your GPU. What transfers is the reading discipline: name the terms, predict the shape, then measure. Freeze the prediction before the sweep The Topic 06 discipline — predict before you measure — makes its third outing here, and the lab enforces it mechanically. Before any sweep runs, you freeze tp-plan.json with two predictions. The first is the knee of the clean model — the step-time model without the beat term and without stragglers. Written out, the clean model is : for C = 800 and B = 120 it is 680/tp + 120, monotonically decreasing — 800, 460, 346.7, 290, 256, 233.3, 217.1, down to 205 ms at tp = 8. A monotone model makes an honest prediction: take more GPUs , the knee sits at the edge of the sweep, p = 8. That prediction is written down before you know what the full model will say, which is exactly what makes the later comparison evidence rather than memory. The second frozen number comes from the memory ledger, and the lab asks for it in the same plan on purpose: the minimal degree that fits the declared budget — 16/tp + 4/tp + 1.5 ≤ 15 , which resolves to p ≥ 20/13.5, that is, degree 2. You will meet the full ledger in a later section; the plan only needs the verdict, and the verdict is frozen before anything runs. A prediction written after the measurement is a recollection, and recollections agree with results at a suspicious rate. This is the quiet reason the plan file exists as an artifact and not as a paragraph: it is timestamped by the journal, it cannot be edited after the sweep without the edit being visible, and it converts your understanding into something a grader — or you, in three weeks — can check. If the prediction misses, the miss is the most valuable row in the journal: it points at a term you did not model, which is the next section's whole subject. The sweep and the honest verdict The full declared model adds the two terms the clean plan omitted. First, the per-beat price: b·(tp−1) milliseconds, two beats per block at every layer. Second, straggler multipliers : each shard's compute is scaled by drawn as 1 + U(−0.10, 0.15), seeded by (2026, degree) , so every run replays the same "hardware" and every journal row is reproducible. The step is the max over shards, not the mean — the beat waits for everyone. The sweep runs degrees 1 through 8 through the declared engine and journals one row per degree. In the teacher run the totals read: 818.0, 471.2, 412.6, 392.2, 354.6, 375.8, 380.5, 394.0 ms. The observed knee is p = 5 at 354.6 ms . Compare with the frozen plan: the clean model called for "take more" and named p = 8; the full model bends at p = 5. The gap is the lesson, and the lab requires you to name the mechanism in verdict.json : the per-beat price and the straggler exposure — the exact terms the plan did not pay. Why does the knee land precisely there? Differentiate the full model. Collecting terms gives , whose minimum satisfies a one-line condition: The falling harmonic term (C − B)/tp and the rising linear beat term b·tp balance when . For the declared knobs: √(680/25) = √27.2 ≈ 5.2 — the integer knee lands on p = 5. A wider bus (smaller b) pushes the knee right; a narrow one drags it toward tp = 1. The verdict ritual deserves respect beyond this lab. The plan said one thing, the sweep said another, and the difference resolved into named terms rather than shrugs — that sequence (plan → observation → mechanism) is what an honest engineering claim looks like at any scale. A student who "predicts" after the sweep has failed the reading, not the arithmetic; a team that skips the plan accumulates changes it cannot reason about. And note what is being compared: the shape of the curve against the frozen prediction — the numbers themselves are declared, so shape agreement and mechanism attribution are the only honest currencies here. The memory ledger: what divides and what does not The step-time model answers "how fast"; a second question decides "does it even start". At degree , each GPU holds its share of the weights and of the KV cache — heads and layers are partitioned, so both genuinely divide — plus costs that do not divide : activations and framework overhead, declared at 1.5 GB per GPU at every degree. The declared budget of one accelerator is 15 GiB usable, and the budget judges the whole per-GPU bar, not the weights row alone. Declared values for the teaching-grade 8B model: |W| = 16 GB, KV = 4 GB, M_fixed = 1.5 GB, M_budget = 15 GiB. The minimal fitting degree is a ledger decision: pick the smallest tp whose whole bar stays under the budget line with KV headroom left. The rows, for degrees 1, 2, 4 and 8: 16 + 4 + 1.5 = 21.5 GB — over the line by 6.5 GB, does not fit, does not start; 8 + 2 + 1.5 = 11.5 GB — fits, with 3.5 GB of headroom for KV growth; 4 + 1 + 1.5 = 6.5 GB ; and 2 + 0.5 + 1.5 = 4.0 GB . The minimal fitting degree is 2 — and notice what the rows beyond it buy: KV room, not necessity, while every added degree keeps paying beats the fit decision never asked for. This is the section where the piano metaphor earns its wage twice. Splitting the weight is carrying the piano by four bearers instead of one — but the sheet music, the metronome and the bearers' own kit do not split, and the hallway has a width. The "does it fit" decision is a row in a table with named terms; when a colleague proposes a deployment, the transferable habit is to ask for that row — which terms divide, which do not, and where the line is — and to distrust any answer that fits by hope. What breaks, on purpose Four failures are staged in this topic, and none of them is a Python exception. The first two are mechanical , caught by the exactness proof; the second two are economic , read from declared transcripts in the Topic 09 drill genre — cause → evidence → fix, frozen into drills.json . The lost all-reduce. A row-parallel partial already has the full output shape: batch × out. Return the partials without the sum and nothing crashes; downstream code runs on a tensor that holds one shard's contribution instead of the exact sum of all of them. This is silent corruption — the worst kind — and the element-wise proof is its designed detector: the max-abs error jumps from floating-point dust like 8.9e-16 to the scale of the activations themselves, and within_tol flips to false. The empty second GPU. A mis-sized partition contributes nothing to the join; the shape checks refuse the obvious cases, and any case that slips through shapes still fails the proof — the sum is no longer the full matmul. Both drills teach the same reflex: a join that was never proven is a join you cannot trust, which is why the proof cell precedes every sweep in the notebook. The comm-bound regression. A recorded sweep shows degrees 1, 2, 4, 8 with totals 812, 489, 402, 451 ms and compute shares 798, 401, 203, 99 ms. The knee sits at tp = 4; past it, quadrupling the compute shards (203 → 99 ms) raises the step (402 → 451 ms), because the synchronisation cost grew by about 153 ms and now dominates. On a narrow bus — PCIe next to NVLink — the same effect arrives earlier; sometimes the knee drags all the way to tp = 1. The fixes follow from the mechanism: lower the degree, shrink the exchanged bytes, or move to a faster interconnect. The straggler. One step on four GPUs with shard times 101, 103, 99, 205 ms: the max/median ratio is 2.01, past the classifier's 1.5 threshold, and the step time is 205 ms — the max, not the mean of 127 ms. Dividing compute by multiplies exposure to imbalance; balance and identical hardware are requirements, not hopes. The transcripts are captures, not live runs, and the notebook labels them as such next to the tables they produce — the same recorded-versus-fresh distinction the course has enforced since Topic 03. Transcripts run everywhere, on any CPU, with no hardware; the classification skill they teach is the reading skill, and it transfers to real clusters unchanged, where the same two failure classes arrive wearing thermal throttling and noisy neighbours instead of declared multipliers. One journal, eight hashes The lab's deliverable is a single growing journal, and by the end of an attempt it has a canonical shape. tp-plan.json — the frozen knee prediction and fit degree, written before any sweep. split-proof.json — the max-abs error rows for degrees 1, 2 and 4, each judged against the 1e-10 tolerance. sweep.json and sweep.png — one declared-engine row per degree and the observed-versus-clean curve with the knee marked. verdict.json — observed knee against the plan, with the mechanism named in one sentence. ledger.json and ledger.png — the per-GPU memory rows and the budget line. drills.json — the two classified failure transcripts. And manifest.json — the sha256 of all eight, closing the attempt. The order is not decorative: plan → proof → sweep → verdict → ledger → drills → manifest is the chapter's argument, executable. Each artifact quotes the one before it — the verdict reads the plan, the curve overlays the clean model from the plan, the manifest pins the whole chain — so an attempt is auditable end to end by someone who was not there. The teacher run of 1 November 2026 ( seminars/runs/2026-11-01-topic10-tp-sim/ ) executed all 17 code cells with 0 errors in 1.5 seconds of wall time on a plain CPU — every cell runs on free Colab too, because there are no docker guards and no GPU cells to skip. Naming provenance per row is part of the claim, the same rule as every topic before. The proof rows are real NumPy on CPU; the sweep and ledger rows are declared arithmetic with named knobs; the drill rows are recorded transcripts. A journal that mixes the three without labels is not evidence — it is decoration. Yours labels them, which is why it can be quoted. One flag, the mechanics decide In production vLLM, all of this compresses to one line of configuration: tensor_parallel_size = N . The flag starts the machinery — shards the weights, inserts the all-reduces, wires NCCL over the node's interconnect — but the flag does not decide whether the machinery helps. The knee decides. The configuration card the lab asks you to write has four fields, and each field quotes a section you have already done: flag: tensor_parallel_size — the one TP knob vLLM exposes at top level. value: 2 for the declared 8B example — the minimal fitting degree from the ledger: 16/2 + 4/2 + 1.5 = 11.5 GB ≤ 15 GiB. precondition: a fast interconnect inside one node — two all-reduce beats per block at every layer, and on a narrow bus the beats eat the gain, the comm-bound drill in data. evidence: an owner-run demonstration with a retained record — measured multi-GPU numbers enter course pages only with that provenance, and student materials carry none. The stretch placement paragraphs widen the card back into the axis map: TP for "does not fit or shorter step, inside one node"; PP for depth across devices, paying pipeline bubbles and tolerating slower links; DP for replicas when the model fits and throughput is the goal; EP for mixture-of-experts. When TP is the wrong axis, the map names it: a model that fits with a wide batch is served better by DP replicas, which pay no beats at all. The owner demonstration on a real two-GPU node is cited as a card — exactly the boundary the Topic 09 production-variant image drew — so the flag and its precondition arrive in your notes together, with the evidence status stated on the same line. What this chapter does and does not establish The lab is a declared CPU simulation, and the boundary is worth stating without varnish. The split proof is real NumPy: the errors — 0.0, 8.9e-16, 6.7e-16 against a 1e-10 tolerance — are measured on CPU, deterministic under the frozen seed. Every millisecond beyond the proof is declared arithmetic with named knobs: C = 800 ms, B = 120, b = 25 ms, straggler multipliers 1 + U(−0.10, 0.15) seeded by (2026, degree). Every byte figure is a teaching-grade 8B example: 16 GB of weights, 4 GB of KV, 1.5 GB fixed, 15 GiB of budget. Nothing here is a hardware benchmark; a student who quotes 354.6 ms as a GPU measurement has failed the reading, and the same is true of any number in this chapter taken as hardware. What needs real hardware stays with the owner: real all-reduce latencies, NCCL behaviour, thermal stragglers, the multi-GPU vLLM demonstration with tensor_parallel_size = 2 — an owner record with retained evidence, cited as a card and never quoted as student data. Out of scope, explicitly: deep PP/DP/EP mechanics (the map is one row per axis), Kubernetes and multi-node scheduling (Topic 11), NCCL tuning, cross-node tensor parallelism and training-side TP with its gradient all-reduces. What the chapter does establish is a loop that runs on any machine with Python: prove the split exact before pricing it, freeze the knee prediction before the sweep, compare shapes and name the mechanism on mismatch, decide the fit from an itemised ledger, and turn four deliberate failures into recorded diagnoses. That loop — not any particular degree, and not any particular GPU — is the transferable asset, and Topic 11 will reuse it one ladder rung higher: today you scaled one unit across the GPUs of one node with its own ledger; tomorrow a scheduler scales units across machines, and the ledger discipline moves with you. Sources, evidence status and provenance Primary sources for the mechanics: the Megatron-LM paper "Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism" (arXiv:1909.08053), which introduced the column-parallel and row-parallel splits and their all-reduce joins that this chapter and its figures follow; and the vLLM documentation on parallelism scaling , the home of the tensor_parallel_size flag on the configuration card. These are the references the lab's claims trace to, and the ones to read before disagreeing with any of them. Evidence status. The live course-side run record for this topic is the teacher simulation of 1 November 2026 ( seminars/runs/2026-11-01-topic10-tp-sim/README.md ): 17 code cells, 0 errors, 1.5 s wall on free CPU — the NumPy split proof (max-abs 8.9e-16 at tp = 2, 6.7e-16 at tp = 4) plus the declared sweep, ledger and drills, all eight artifacts hashed in the manifest. The multi-GPU vLLM demonstration ( tensor_parallel_size ≥ 2 on a real node) is an owner-run record with retained evidence, kept with the private instructor materials; its numbers enter public pages only with that provenance. Until such a record is quoted, this chapter claims an exact split, a predictable knee and an itemised ledger — not GPU serving results. Check understanding and transfer Answer before opening the explanations. Questions 2, 5 and 6 change one condition each: reproducing the notebook is not enough unless you can predict what changes next. {exercises.map(({id,title,question})=> {title}. {question} )} Reveal eight answers and their limits {exercises.map(({id,title,answer})=> {title}. {answer} )}
