Chapter 11: Kubernetes for LLM serving: GPU Operator & Helm

This chapter follows the approved Topic11 arc. The carrier is a DECLARED TEACHING MODEL OF A CLUSTER: the controllers (rolling update, probe gate, Helm revisions) are deterministic simulators that run in your browser, and the manifests carry the same fields a real Deployment would. Every number is course-inherited and named — the 165 s cold start from the T09 fleet run, the memory ledger from T10 — and nothing is invented as a benchmark. No GPU cluster is used or implied; where production practice is quoted (OpenAI, llm-d), it is cited as a source, not reproduced as a measurement. The loop you already run By the end of Topic 10 you were operating a small fleet by hand. A compose file from Topic 08 declared a gateway and llama.cpp engines with mem_limit ceilings; Topic 09 taught you what the limit means when the weights are resident (exit 137, and a restart policy that tries again); Topic 10 put shard replicas behind one address and made the fit decision from an itemised ledger. But look at what the operation itself still is: you watch, you notice the dead engine, you type the restart command, you decide when to roll the new image, and you hold the capacity math in your head while you do it. That loop works at three engines. At thirty it does not — not because any step gets harder, but because the loop does not scale with the fleet: someone must watch liveness at 3 a.m., someone must roll the new image engine by engine while the clients keep arriving, and someone must know, at every moment, how much capacity the fleet has while weights are loading. Kubernetes is the decision to stop running that loop by hand. It is not a new engine and not a new physics — it is a new relationship to the fleet you already have, and every artifact in this chapter is part of that relationship. The chapter keeps the course's honesty rules in force. The numbers you will size pods with are the ones you already measured or computed: the ledger (16 + 4)/p + 1.5 GiB is Topic 10's, and the 165 s cold start is the measured boot of the T09 fleet run. When the chapter says "the cluster waits 200 seconds for a pod", that is declared arithmetic about a teaching model — and the lab says so in its intro and its footer, the same way the Topic 10 lab said "declared CPU simulation". Desired state, not commands The inversion at the heart of Kubernetes is small to state and large to internalise: you do not tell the cluster what to do; you tell it what should exist, and controllers keep making the world match the claim. A Deployment is a declaration — replicas 3, a pod template with resource requests and limits, probes with budgets — and a reconciliation loop continuously compares the declared state to the observed state and repairs the difference. kubectl apply is not an action; it is a claim filed with a system whose job is to make the claim true. Why this suits LLM serving specifically: everything you learned so far was already declarative in spirit. The ledger is a claim about what a pod needs; the probe budget is a claim about how long the boot takes; the admission envelope of Topic 08 is a claim about how many requests the fleet will accept. Kubernetes gives those claims a format (YAML validated by a schema) and an executor (the controllers). The lab's simulators consume the same shapes — requests == limits , probe periods and thresholds, rollout parameters — so what you declare in the browser is what you would declare to a real cluster, minus the cluster. One more property matters for everything that follows: reconciliation is continuous. A crashed pod is not an incident that pages you; it is a difference between declared and observed state that the controller repairs on its next pass. The restart loop you built by hand in Topic 09 — restart until /health answers — is, in Kubernetes, somebody else's loop: the Deployment's backoff, driven by the declaration. Your job moves from doing the repairs to writing the declarations that make repairs unnecessary. The pod: your container's contract, renamed A pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share an address and a lifecycle. For this course the pod is the member container from Topic 09 with its contract renamed into Kubernetes vocabulary. The cgroup ceiling you set with mem_limit 1200m becomes resources.limits.memory ; crossing it is still OOMKilled, still exit 137 at the container level, and the restart is still there — now as the Deployment's restart policy with its backoff, not your hand on the keyboard. What the rename adds is the second number. Alongside limits — the runtime ceiling — Kubernetes asks for requests : the amount the scheduler promises to the pod when deciding which node it fits on. The pair is the pod's negotiating position: requests are what the scheduler reserves, limits are what the runtime enforces. When requests equal limits, the pod is declaring "what I reserved is exactly what I will use" — and that equality is the whole next section. Keep the physics pinned while the vocabulary moves: the weights are resident and non-negotiable; the KV cache grows with the work; the fixed overhead of the runtime does not shrink because you wished. Nothing about a pod makes memory cheaper. What a pod offers is a schedulable, replaceable, addressable unit whose appetite is declared in numbers the scheduler can read — which is exactly the ledger you already keep, in a format a machine can finally consume. The ledger becomes a manifest Topic 10's ledger makes the jump intact: weights 16 GiB and KV cache 4 GiB shard by the tensor-parallel degree, the fixed 1.5 GiB does not, and the per-pod memory is (16 + 4)/p + 1.5 GiB. At p = 1 the pod declares 21.5 GiB; at p = 2, 11.5 GiB; at p = 4, 6.5 GiB. The manifest rows are the ledger rows — nothing new is being computed, only formatted for a scheduler to read: The fixed overhead does not shard — that is lab quiz q1 and its "why" follow-up. The equality of requests and limits is what makes the pod Guaranteed, the subject of the next section. Written into a manifest, the p = 2 row reads: resources.requests.memory: 11.5Gi , resources.limits.memory: 11.5Gi , resources.limits.nvidia.com/gpu: "2" . The GPU line is vocabulary for now — slide fifteen makes it precise — but its shape already says the important thing: a GPU is a schedulable quantity exactly like memory, counted by the scheduler, requested and limited like anything else. The skill to carry out of this section is that sizing is not folklore. "Which degree fits which node" is a row in a table, computed the same way in Topic 10's stretch card and in this chapter's manifest: the sharded part divides, the fixed part stays, and the answer either fits the budget or the service does not start. A scheduler can only be as honest as the numbers it is given — under-declare and the pod lands where it cannot survive; over-declare and the cluster reserves capacity the pod never uses. The figure above is the ledger you already know; the manifest is that table wearing a schema. The one new failure mode the format introduces is a transcription error — declaring 1.5 GiB instead of 11.5 GiB — and the failure surfaces not at write time but at the first OOMKill, which is why the lab's hidden tests check the equality of requests and limits rather than trusting the shape of the YAML. QoS: Guaranteed by arithmetic Kubernetes sorts every pod into one of three quality-of-service classes, and the sorting rule is pure arithmetic. Guaranteed : requests equal limits on every container in the pod. Burstable : at least one container where requests sit below limits — cheap to schedule, first to be squeezed. BestEffort : no requests or limits at all — first out, always. The classes exist because nodes run out of memory, and when they do, the eviction order follows the classes: BestEffort pods die first, Burstable next, Guaranteed last. For an LLM pod the choice is mechanical, and the lab's hidden test enforces it by rejecting requests &lt; limits outright. The weights are resident; the engine cannot "grow into" a bigger limit the way a stateless web service might, because the memory it needs on second one is the memory it needs on day thirty. Under-promise and the scheduler will co-locate a neighbour the pod cannot survive next to; when the node runs hot, the eviction order decides who dies — and a Burstable LLM pod is evictable by design. The exam voice for this is posttest p1: what separates Guaranteed from Burstable is not a bigger number, it is the equality — requests equal limits on every container. The deeper point is the one the class system encodes: in a shared cluster, your declaration is other people's reality. The numbers you write decide where the scheduler may put you and who gets evicted when the node runs out. Guaranteed is not a luxury tier; it is the honest declaration of a pod whose appetite is known to the GiB. TP degree = pod size The ledger table hides a sentence worth making explicit: the tensor-parallel degree of the engine inside the pod determines the pod's size and its GPU count. At p = 1 the pod asks for one GPU and 21.5 GiB; at p = 2, two GPUs and 11.5 GiB; at p = 4, four GPUs and 6.5 GiB. The scaling axis you studied inside one machine in Topic 10 becomes, in the cluster vocabulary, the shape of the schedulable unit. The mechanism does not change: the weights split column- and row-parallel with all-reduce beats at the seams, and the beats demand a fast interconnect inside one node. What changes is who arranges the pieces. In Topic 10 you assembled the shards by hand in NumPy and proved the join exact; in a cluster, the engine inside the pod does the splitting, and the pod declares the resulting appetite — memory and GPU count together — as its requests. The proof discipline carries over as a deployment discipline: a pod whose engine cannot serve (weights missing, shards mismatched) must not become Ready, which is precisely the probe contract two sections ahead. This is also the right place to note what a pod is not: it is not a machine. Four pods at p = 2 are not "an 8-GPU machine"; they are four schedulable units, each demanding two GPUs and 11.5 GiB, each booting independently, each paying its own cold start. The fleet-of-pods view is what makes the rest of the chapter work — rolling updates replace pods one at a time, Services route across Ready pods, and the HPA in Topic 12 adds or removes whole pods. Everything scales in units of pods, and the pod's size is the ledger's business. Service: one address over changing pods Pods are cattle: each has an IP that dies with it. Clients cannot talk to pods directly, for the same reason Topic 08's clients did not talk to engines directly — the thing that changes must not be the thing the client addresses. A Service is the stable virtual address and a selector: it watches the fleet for pods carrying its labels, and routes to those that are Ready . The endpoint list grows and shrinks as pods come and go; the client sees one name. This is the same shape as the gateway from Topics 08–09 — one honest front door, engines behind it — promoted to cluster vocabulary. And it introduces the word this whole chapter turns on: Ready . The endpoint list tracks readiness, not liveness and not "container started". A pod that is Up but not Ready receives zero traffic; a pod that is Ready receives its share. For a stateless microservice, Ready is a formality checked in milliseconds. For an LLM pod, whose boot replays extract → weights → init → /health, Ready is 165 seconds of physics — and the next three sections give that word a definition precise enough to build on. Rolling updates are safe only because of this arrangement: the new pod is added to the endpoint list when (and only when) it is Ready; the old pod leaves the list before it dies; the client never addresses a pod at all. Hold that thought — the rolling-update section will come back to it and show exactly what happens to fleet capacity when the plan is written carelessly. The boot is physics: 165 seconds The T09 fleet run measured the boot of a member container end to end: extract the image layers, load the weights, initialise the engine, answer /health . For this course's declared 8B teaching model the number attached to that sequence is 165 seconds — a course-inherited constant, quoted from seminars/runs/2026-11-07-topic09-fleet-mac/ , not invented for this topic. In Docker you watched that number once and arranged your work around it. In a cluster, every pod boot pays it — every scale-up, every replacement, every rolling update — which is why the next hour of this chapter is about teaching the cluster to wait. Read the figure as a contract between two numbers. The blue bar is the boot: 165 seconds before the pod can serve its first token. The green bar is the cluster's patience: the startupProbe budget, whose arithmetic is the next section's whole content. The 35 seconds between them are the headroom — and the headroom is not slack. The 165 s is a median measured on one machine; the node that will host your pod next year has a different disk, and the budget must cover the tail of the boot distribution, not its median. Quiz q2's follow-up asks exactly this: why plan for more than the median? Because the median says nothing about the pod that lands on the slow node, and that pod is the one that dies if you sized the patience to the average. Three probes, three jobs Kubernetes wires three probes into a pod spec, and they answer three different questions. The startupProbe answers "has it finished booting?" — it runs first, and liveness and readiness are suspended until it passes once. The readinessProbe answers "should it receive traffic now?" — failing it removes the pod from the Service's endpoint list while the pod itself keeps living. The livenessProbe answers "is it alive at all?" — failing it kills and restarts the container. The LLM-specific discipline is keeping those questions separate. Generation latency routinely exceeds naive probe timeouts, so a liveness probe tuned for a web service will murder a healthy but busy engine — and killing it throws away the KV cache and the queued work, converting "slow" into "cold". The rule the lab encodes: a slow generation must fail readiness (stop sending new traffic to this pod) and must never fail liveness (do not restart a working engine for being busy). Posttest p2 drills exactly this distinction, and the OpenAI KubeCon talk this chapter cites reports the production incidents that come from conflating the two. The startup probe is the boot's designated waiter. Because liveness and readiness hang until it passes, the cluster's patience for the boot is expressed in exactly one place — its budget — and that is deliberate: one knob, one multiplication, auditable. The next section does the multiplication. The probe budget: one multiplication The inclusive comparison matters: exactly 165 s against a 165 s budget passes. The lab's ex2 makes you compute both sides and compare them inclusively; its hidden tests kill the off-by-one (when the threshold starts counting) and the strict-inequality bug. Read the formula as a policy, not an arithmetic exercise. Too small a budget and the cluster kills pods mid-boot, forever — the T09 crash-loop reborn at cluster scale, with the Deployment's backoff as the metronome. Too large a budget and a genuinely dead pod squats its GPU and its memory reservation for minutes before anyone gives up on it. The lab's plan — 200 s against a 165 s median — is the deliberate compromise: 21 % over the median, big enough for a slow disk, small enough that a dead pod does not hold resources for five minutes. This is also the first place the chapter's numbers meet the grader. The hidden tests of ex2 reject the plan whose budget is 100 s (5 × 20 — less than the boot), reject the plan that compares strictly (165 &lt; 165 is false, but the pod passes exactly at the line), and reject the classic off-by-one in which the first probe "doesn't count". The arithmetic is one multiplication; the discipline is that every knob has a why, and the follow-up quiz demands the why in words: headroom over the median, because the median is not the tail. Rolling update: hold the floor Now put the pieces together into the operation that makes Kubernetes worth its vocabulary: replacing the fleet's pods with a new version, in place, without stopping service. The plan is two numbers. maxSurge — how many pods above replicas may exist during the update (how fast new versions arrive). maxUnavailable — how many pods below replicas may be missing (how much capacity you are willing to lose). The floor — the guaranteed serving capacity — is replicas − maxUnavailable , and the two plans differ in exactly one of the numbers: For LLM pods the pit has a duration: the replacement only restores capacity after its boot, so a dip is not a blink — it is 165 s of degraded capacity per replaced pod. The plan maxUnavailable 0, maxSurge 1 never lets capacity leave 3: a fourth pod starts, boots, passes its startup probe, joins the Service — and only then does one old pod retire. The client never notices. The plan maxUnavailable 2, maxSurge 0 deletes two pods first and serves on one pod for the full 165 seconds the replacement spends loading weights. Same operation, same flags in the same YAML block — one flag of difference, and the difference is a capacity pit exactly as deep and as long as the boot. Walk the figure once slowly, because it is the exam. The green line is the safe plan: flat at 3 for the whole window. The red line is the honest disaster: a step down to 1 at the moment the update starts, a plateau for 165 s — the boot — and a step back. Quiz q3 asks which parameter raised the floor and the answer is "none of them — maxSurge never raises the floor"; the follow-up demands the reason: surge adds pods above the target, so the floor's formula never touches it. If you remember one inequality from this chapter, it is floor = replicas − maxUnavailable. The OpenAI lesson: surge is speed, not capacity The rolling-update failure mode has a name and a stage. At KubeCon NA 2026, OpenAI's talk "Rolling Out LLM Inference Engines on Kubernetes" reported the production form: an LLM inference rollout that looks healthy on every dashboard — the old pods keep serving, the application answers — while the rollout itself is stuck. Every new pod is booting; the first ones never became Ready, so none of the old ones may die; the deployment has been "one unavailable replica" for an hour. Nothing is on fire, which is exactly why nobody paged. The mechanism behind the stuck rollout is almost always the boot: a probe budget smaller than the real cold start, so each new pod is killed mid-load and restarts into the same trap. The stateless playbook — "replace pods; they come up in seconds" — silently assumes a boot that an LLM engine does not have. The lesson the course takes has two halves. First, the diagnosis: "application healthy + rollout stuck" is not a contradiction but a signature, and it means read the pod events, not the dashboard. Second, the arithmetic: the fix is the budget of the probe section, not a bigger surge — surge adds booting pods, and booting pods serve nothing. Cite it as a source, not a measurement: the talk is quoted for its failure taxonomy, the way this course quotes SRE literature for golden signals. The lab's fix-the-bug exercise (ex3) hands you the stuck-rollout shape in miniature — a rollout plan that eats capacity — and asks for the floor as the fix, which is the transferable half of the lesson: state the floor, then choose the flags that honour it. Helm: a release is history A chart is a template of the manifest; values are the declared numbers that fill it — the ledger row, the probe budget, the replica count. Installing a chart with values creates a release , and every helm upgrade with new values stamps a new revision into the release's history: 1, then 2, then 3. helm history lists them. Nothing is overwritten; the history only grows. The property that makes this honest is the same one that made the T08 journal trustworthy: append-only. A rollback is not a rewind — helm rollback to revision 1 from a history of [1, 2, 3] creates revision 4 whose content equals revision 1's. The old revisions stay; the new state has a new, permanent name. Posttest p3 drills the exact case, because the intuition "rollback goes back" is wrong in exactly the way that matters for audits. Every state the fleet ever ran keeps its revision number forever. A postmortem can say "revision 4 was broken" with no ambiguity about what "revision 4" refers to today. Why the course insists on this vocabulary: the runbook — this topic's milestone artifact — is written in revision numbers. "If the probe budget is wrong in revision 3, roll back to revision 1; expect revision 4 to exist afterwards; verify with helm history" is an instruction a colleague can execute at 3 a.m. without improvising. A release system whose history rewrote itself would make that sentence meaningless — you could not cite the broken state, because its name would have been recycled. Append-only is what makes the runbook quotable. The figure is from the next block's topic, and it is here for one reason: the shape. An append-only chain of records, each sealing the last, is the same discipline in the journal (T08), in Helm's revisions (here), and in the dashboards that will consume them (T13). When you meet a system that rewrites its history, you now have a reflex: ask what else it lies about. ReleaseSim: the drill The capstone class of lab 11 compresses the whole topic into one object with three methods. ReleaseSim(chart) — the constructor installs with initial values and stamps revision 1. upgrade(values) — appends the next revision; called without values, it inherits the previous revision's (a hidden test pins this). rollback(rev) — appends a new revision whose content is the named revision's; called with an unknown revision, it raises ValueError (another hidden test). The class is deliberately small: the entire vocabulary of the topic — install, upgrade, history, rollback — is three methods, and every hidden test encodes one sentence of this chapter. The drill the lab walks, and the one to rehearse mentally: install with the ledger's values (revision 1); upgrade to a better probe budget (revision 2); make it wrong — a budget of 120 s against a 165 s boot (revision 3, broken); roll back to revision 1 (revision 4 appears, with revision 1's content); verify — history is [1, 2, 3, 4], and the running values match revision 1's. Notice what the broken revision cost: nothing permanent. History absorbed the mistake, the rollback named the good state, and the fleet never served from the broken one — because the broken budget would have crash-looped the pods, which is exactly the kind of mistake you want to make against a simulator first. The transfer habit to build: after any release operation, state the history out loud. "We are on revision 5; revision 4 was the bad probe budget; rollback to 3 would create revision 6." Operators who can say that sentence from memory do not get lost in incidents; operators who cannot, guess. The lab's journal asks you to write the history after every operation for exactly this reason. GPU Operator: the dictionary Everything so far declared memory; the GPU enters as one more schedulable quantity — nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in a pod's limits — and one more piece of machinery that makes the quantity exist: the GPU Operator. Its decomposition is worth memorising as four named pieces, because production incident reports use exactly these words. The driver container loads the NVIDIA kernel driver on every GPU node (a DaemonSet — a pod on every node, which is why you never install drivers by hand). The container-toolkit makes the container runtime able to hand devices into containers. The device plugin advertises nvidia.com/gpu as a countable resource to the scheduler. The DCGM exporter publishes GPU metrics — the same exporter whose dashboards are the subject of Topic 13. The honest boundary, stated in the vision doc and repeated here: this course trains the pod-side word and names the machinery; it does not drill a real Operator installation, because there is no GPU at hand and pretending otherwise would be the lie this course does not tell. What transfers without a GPU is the structural insight: a GPU enters the system as a resource with a name, counted and scheduled like memory — and the ledger decides what fits, exactly as it did in Topic 10. Time-slicing, MIG, MPS One GPU, several pods — three arrangements with three different trade-offs, and all three are vocabulary in this course, arithmetic in none. Time-slicing : the device plugin advertises several "replicas" of the device, and pods take turns on the hardware. No memory isolation: every slice sees the whole device memory, so one pod's OOM collides with all of them. MIG (on Ampere and newer): the hardware is partitioned into slices with isolated memory and isolated fault domains — a crash stays inside its slice. MPS : multiple processes' work merges into shared GPU contexts — better utilisation than time-slicing, weaker isolation than MIG; the middle word in the dictionary. The exercise worth doing by hand is the collision of the sharing word with the ledger (exercise 7 below): four 11.5 GiB pods time-slicing one 24 GiB device do not fit, no matter what the YAML says — sharing rotates compute, it does not multiply memory. The habit this builds is the one the course has drilled since Topic 02: when someone proposes a configuration, compute the ledger before admiring the flag. The sharing words change who waits; only the ledger changes what fits. One sentence on the future, no more: DRA (Dynamic Resource Allocation) reached GA in Kubernetes 1.34 and is the direction these device words are evolving toward — a third-generation API for asking a cluster for accelerators. It changes the plumbing, not the arithmetic; the ledger discipline transfers to it unchanged. Lab 11: what you will build The lab is the topic's executable form, and it runs entirely in your browser — Pyodide, no cluster, no install, the same as every lab since the migration. Ten checkpoints carry the progress. The three quizzes come with "why" follow-ups: the numeric answer opens the door, and the checkpoint closes only after you pick the correct reason — the clamp's cost fuse, the inclusive band's anti-flap duty, the floor that surge cannot raise. The four exercises climb the ladder you know from every topic: pod_resources(p, …) — one object, the ledger as a manifest; probe_budget and goes_ready — the boot arithmetic with the inclusive comparison; fix the rollout_floor bug — a plan that eats capacity, handed to you to repair; and the capstone class ReleaseSim — three methods, four hidden sentences. Above the checkpoint count sits the star challenge, outside the score: budget the startup probe — choose period × threshold so the budget covers the 165 s boot and stays within 300 s. The page recomputes your printed result against the declared model and rejects invented numbers; the reference solution stays hidden until you pass. It is the strong-student lane, and it is also the honest-summary lane: the whole topic in one inequality. What the lab does not have is a runtime chip: no Docker, no gateway, no journal — the deterministic simulators are the point, and the honest framing ("a teaching model of a cluster") is in the intro, the footer and the next section but one. If you want the fleet itself, the Topic 08–09 runtime is still there; this topic teaches you what to say to the system that would manage it. The runbook: the milestone artifact The topic's milestone — the sentence the syllabus has carried since the vision — is "reproducible cluster deployment and rollback runbook". The runbook is one page, and every line of it quotes a section you have already done: the manifest numbers from the ledger (memory 11.5Gi at p = 2, GPU 2, requests equal limits); the probe budget with its named headroom (200 s against a 165 s median); the rollout plan and the floor it holds (0/1 keeps 3 of 3); the rollback command and the revision arithmetic (rollback to 1 from [1, 2, 3] → revision 4 exists); and the verification step (helm history, pod spec matches revision 1's values). Why a runbook and not an essay: an incident at 3 a.m. is executed by the person on call, and the person on call needs commands and expected observations, not context. The discipline of writing "what exists after the command" — revision 4, not "the old version" — is the same discipline as the lab's journal: every operation names its expected result in advance, so the drill doubles as the rehearsal. The portal's acceptance list for this topic is the runbook's rubric; the numbers come from this chapter; and the honest frame comes from the next section. What this chapter does and does not establish State the boundary without varnish. This chapter and its lab are a declared teaching model of a cluster. The simulators are deterministic Pyodide; the manifests are schema-shaped strings; no cluster was created, no GPU was scheduled, no pod booted. The numbers are course-inherited and named: 165 s from the T09 fleet run (a real measured boot, on a MacBook, of a small model — quoted, not re-measured); the ledger from T10 (declared arithmetic of a teaching 8B); the probe budget, the floor and the revision arithmetic (declared policies). Nothing here is a benchmark of Kubernetes, and a student who quotes "200 s" as what a real cluster waited has failed the reading. What stays with production, cited but not reproduced: real cluster behaviour (scheduling delays, eviction storms, multi-tenant pressure), real GPU Operator installs, real MIG partitioning, and the OpenAI and llm-d talks quoted as sources for failure taxonomies and probe designs. What stays with later topics: autoscaling the fleet's size — Topic 12 takes the declared fleet and asks who decides how many pods — and the dashboards that watch it — Topic 13, already published, reads the same signals with SLOs attached. What the chapter does establish is a vocabulary and an arithmetic that run in any browser: declare the pod from the ledger, budget the boot with named headroom, hold the rollout floor and read it off the flags, treat a release as append-only history, and write the runbook that quotes all of it in revision numbers. That bundle — not any specific YAML — is the transferable asset; a real cluster will change the numbers, and nothing else. Sources, evidence status and provenance Primary sources for the vocabulary and the policies: the Kubernetes documentation on pod QoS classes and on liveness, readiness and startup probes (with the pod lifecycle page defining the states between them) — the sorting rule and the three questions are quoted from there; the Helm documentation on helm history and helm rollback — the append-only revision rule; the NVIDIA GPU Operator documentation — the four-piece decomposition and the time-slicing/MIG/MPS dictionary; llm-d 's Model-Aware Readiness Probes — the "Ready only after the weights land" design this chapter's probe contract mirrors; and the OpenAI KubeCon NA 2026 talk "Rolling Out LLM Inference Engines on Kubernetes" — the stuck-rollout failure class and the "LLM pods live for hours" framing. Evidence status. The live course-side run record quoted in this chapter is the T09 fleet run ( seminars/runs/2026-11-07-topic09-fleet-mac/README.md ): the 165 s cold start and the boot members are its measurements, made on a MacBook with the course's small fleet — they are inputs to this topic's arithmetic, not results of it. The lab's simulators and this chapter's manifests produce no new measurements; their outputs are declared arithmetic with named knobs, and the journal records your own runs in the same honest grammar as every topic before. Until a real cluster's run record is quoted with its provenance, this chapter claims a vocabulary, an arithmetic and a runbook discipline — not cluster results. Check understanding and transfer Answer before opening the explanations. Questions 2, 5 and 7 change one condition each: reproducing the lab is not enough unless you can predict what changes when the condition moves. {exercises.map(({id,title,question})=> {title}. {question} )} Reveal eight answers and their limits {exercises.map(({id,title,answer})=> {title}. {answer} )}

Book

Chapter 12: Advanced Kubernetes: single-pod concurrency & HPA

This chapter follows the approved Topic12 arc. The carrier is a DECLARED TEACHING MODEL OF A CONTROLLER: the HPA arithmetic (formula, band, windows) is deterministic and runs in your browser in lab 12, over the T6 working point (250 tok/s per pod) and the T09 cold start (165 s) — both course-inherited and named. The compose rehearsal is prose, the production stacks (Prometheus Adapter, KEDA, llm-d) are cited as sources, and nothing here is a benchmark of any real autoscaler. One pod is already a crowd Topic 11 ended with a fleet that declares itself: pods sized from the ledger, boots budgeted by probes, releases kept as append-only history. One number in those manifests is still a human decision wearing a default: replicas . You chose 3. Why 3? Because it looked reasonable. And that is the last honest reason a human should choose it — because the honest answer changes through the day. The morning trickle needs one pod; the noon burst needs six; the night needs whatever cheap is. A static number is wrong in both directions at once: idle replicas burn GPU-hours (real money, priced in Topic 13), and a burst that outgrows the fleet produces the Topic 8 outcome — 24 arrivals met an envelope built for fewer, and the extras got honest 429s. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler — HPA — is the controller that makes that decision continuously, inside the cluster, from a metric you choose. Its entire arithmetic is one line, and one of this chapter's purposes is to earn respect for that line: by the end you will compute the decision by hand, guard it with a tolerance band and two stabilization windows, price what a wrong decision costs, and rehearse the whole loop in the lab's simulator, HPASim. The other purpose is the signal. The naive instinct — "the GPU is busy, add pods" — is wrong for LLM serving in a way that is worth internalising deeply, because it looks right and fails quietly. The chapter's first figure is that failure in one picture; everything after it is the correction. The anti-signal: GPU at 90 % Continuous batching — Topic 5's machinery — fills the engine's slots with concurrent requests so the GPU does useful work on many sequences per step. The consequence for scaling is counterintuitive: a well-served LLM engine keeps its GPU busy at loads where a naive watcher would panic. Utilization near 90 % is what a healthy engine looks like at half capacity, because the slots are full and the step is packed — utilization reports the efficiency of the batching, not the pressure of the demand. Read the figure as the topic's thesis in one window. The amber line — GPU utilization — is flat at 90 % before, during and after the burst: batching absorbed the extra arrivals without moving the needle you were tempted to watch. The blue line — queue depth per pod — is the honest one: zero until the burst, five per pod after, and it is the number the controller should read. The llm-d KubeCon NA 2026 talk compresses it into the sentence this course adopts: raw GPU utilization tells you very little about an LLM service. Posttest p2 asks you to say why, and the answer is that sentence plus one mechanism: batching. Hold the negative conclusion as firmly as the positive one: "GPU is hot" is not evidence of overload, and scaling on it adds booting pods that serve nothing while the real signal — the queue — is empty. Exercise 7 makes you write the refusal argument in two sentences, because you will need it in a design review, not in an exam. The signals that do not lie Three serving-derived signals carry the truth about demand. Queue depth per pod — how many requests are waiting at the door after the slots filled — is the most direct: it is un-served demand, measured where it accumulates. KV-cache pressure — how full the context memory is — is the Topic 02 scarcity as a gauge: near saturation, new requests will be refused or evicted no matter how idle the compute looks. TTFT — time to first token — is the client-visible promise bending under load; it is what the SLO of Topic 13 will be written about. The lab uses queue depth as its teaching signal because its arithmetic is the cleanest; the others enter as vocabulary and as the production practice of the later sections. The catch is plumbing, and it is worth naming so the lab's arithmetic stays honest about itself: the stock HPA reads CPU and memory — container metrics that say nothing about serving demand. To scale on queue depth, the metric has to be exported and fed in: the Prometheus Adapter wires custom metrics into the stock HPA; KEDA offers event-driven scalers (and scale-to-zero); llm-d's WVA weighs several serving signals into one desired-replica verdict. Different plumbing, one arithmetic — which is why the course trains the arithmetic and names the plumbing. A note on honesty that the lab keeps in its footer: queue depth "per pod" needs a denominator that only exists after pods exist, and at one pod the number is noisy. The declared teaching model uses it anyway because the controller shape is what is being taught; a production design would smooth it, aggregate it, or switch to a weighted verdict — the llm-d approach — and declare that choice too. The HPA formula The ratio measures demand against the promise (target queue 2 per pod). The ceiling refuses to round demand away — int() is the classic bug. The clamp is the cost fuse: max exists so a metric bug cannot rent the whole cluster. Compute it once by hand and the shape is yours forever. Replicas 3, queue 5 per pod, target 2: ratio 2.5, desired = ceil(3 × 2.5) = ceil(7.5) = 8, clamp [2, 10] leaves 8. The three parts do three different jobs, and each has a failure mode the lab's hidden tests hunt. Without the ceiling — int(7.5) = 7 — you quietly under-provision against fractional demand, which is exactly what bursts produce. Without the clamp, a metric bug (a doubling of the reported queue) rents the entire node pool at today's GPU prices. Without the ratio's named target, the whole thing is unmetered vibes. One reading habit the course insists on: the formula computes a recommendation , not an action. What stands between the recommendation and the fleet are the guards — the band that can refuse to act at all, and the windows that can delay acting on the way down. The next two sections are those guards. Three guards: band, ceil, clamp Guards exist because measurements are noisy and actions are expensive. The band — the tolerance — decides whether the recommendation deserves action at all: if the ratio sits inside ±10 % of 1.0, the current fleet size is within the promise's tolerance, and the correct decision is to do nothing. The ceiling decides how to act when action is due: always up, because a fraction of a pod's worth of demand still needs a whole pod. The clamp decides the boundaries of the possible: minReplicas is the floor the fleet never scales below, maxReplicas is the fuse above which no metric, however broken, may push. Walk the decision tree as the lab's walkthrough does: measure the queue; compute the ratio; if it is inside the band — hold, done; otherwise ceil, clamp, and that is the new desired count — which the controller then requests, with the actual pod creation still subject to scheduling and the 165 s boot. The guards sit before the expensive part, and their whole job is to make sure the expensive part fires rarely and honestly. The number to memorise from this section is the band's: ±10 %, inclusive on both edges. The number to understand from this section is why it is inclusive — and that deserves its own section, because it is the thermostat. The tolerance band: the thermostat Exactly 1.10 holds. Exactly 0.90 holds. The band is a closed interval on purpose: a metric parked at the boundary must not toggle the fleet. A thermostat that fires at every 0.1 degree of deviation clicks on and off all night and wears itself out. The HPA's band is the same device: between 0.9 and 1.1 times the target, the fleet is doing its job well enough that changing its size costs more than the deviation does. The inclusive edges are the whole subtlety, and quiz q2 hunts them: at ratio exactly 1.1 the correct answer is hold , because an exclusive edge would make a constant, parked ratio oscillate — scale on one tick, hold on the next — which is flapping, the disease the band exists to prevent. The follow-up asks for that reason in words, not for the number. The cost of a missing band is worth pricing once. Without it, every tick near the target is a scale event; each scale-up boots pods that pay 165 s before serving; each scale-down removes capacity that the next tick's noise asks for back. The fleet churns, the bill oscillates, and the SLO dies of indecision rather than of load. Hysteresis — the dead band — is the cheapest reliability mechanism in the chapter: it is free, and it is the difference between a controller and a mood. Up now, down carefully Scale-up window 0 s: pain is now, add capacity immediately. Scale-down window 300 s (20 ticks of 15 s): the controller takes the maximum recommendation over the trailing window — the past votes louder than the latest tick. The asymmetry is risk pricing, and both prices come from things you have already measured. Scaling up too late costs 429s and bent TTFTs immediately — the burst does not wait. Scaling down too early costs the same at the next burst, plus a boot per new pod: every capacity you release may have to be re-earned 165 seconds later, with clients queued while it loads weights. Hence: up is instant (window 0 s), down waits, and while it waits it reads the maximum of its trailing recommendations — one spike inside the window holds the fleet at the spike's size for the full 300 s, because one quiet minute is not evidence that the demand is gone. The 300 s and the 15 s tick are Kubernetes' defaults, rounded into the lab's model as exactly 20 ticks — and the rounding is declared, like every model constant in this course. The number 20 matters twice: it is the window's length in the arithmetic, and it is the hidden edge in ex3 — a window of exactly 20 ticks counts as the window, and a peak 19 ticks ago still holds the replicas. Quiz q3 asks for the division (300/15 = 20) with its why attached: the window remembers the worst recent advice, because the worst recent advice is the only proven capacity requirement on the table. The window in one picture The figure is ex3's bug and fix side by side over a spiky window: spike, quiet gap, second spike. The red line is the naive controller — follow the latest recommendation instantly. It climbs to 4 with the first spike, collapses to 1 in the quiet gap (instant down, no window), and then serves the second burst from one pod while the others boot: the SLO dies in the gap, exactly as the figure's annotation says. The green line is the windowed controller: it also climbs to 4, and then holds 4 — the maximum of its trailing twenty recommendations — until the quiet is old enough to be believed. Price the difference honestly: the green line pays for four pods through the quiet gap; the red line pays less between the spikes and catastrophically more at the second one. The window is not conservatism — it is the arithmetic of "capacity you released has to be re-earned with a boot". The lab's fix-the-bug starter implements the red line, the students implement the green, and the hidden tests pin the two edges: the exactly-20-tick window and the peak that holds. The boot makes down cautious Why does the down direction need a window at all? Because of the number this course has carried since the fleet ran: 165 s . Every pod whose capacity you release must be re-earned, on the next burst, by a boot of that length — extract, weights, init, health — with clients queued behind it. The Topic 11 startup probe budgeted that boot for one pod becoming Ready; this chapter prices it into the controller's memory. The scale-down window's 300 s is, in this reading, several boots' worth of caution — the cluster refusing to bet the fleet on one quiet minute when re-armament takes 165 s. The figure is Topic 9's startup economics; it returns here as the price tag on elasticity. The extract member, the weights delivery, the init and the health check — the same members the startup probe waits for — are what a scale-down saves and a scale-up re-pays. This is also the honest reason big-model fleets rarely scale to zero: the first client of the next burst pays the whole boot alone, in cold latency. KEDA's scale-to-zero is wonderful for small models and spiky traffic, and painful exactly in proportion to the boot — the vocabulary from the practice section, priced by this one. Fix the bug: the flutter Ex3 is the topic's fix-the-bug rung, and its starter is plausible code: a controller that reads the latest recommendation and applies it immediately. On a smooth metric it behaves. On a sawtooth — the shape of real traffic — it flaps: 1 ↔ 2 ↔ 1 on successive ticks. Two costs, both visible in the lab's report. The SLO dies on every down: each collapse is capacity removed while demand still oscillates. And the bill jerks: every up boots pods (165 s each), every down throws away warmed engines — churn that shows up in Topic 13's ledger as wasted GPU-hours. The fix is one line and one discipline: the down direction reads the maximum recommendation over the trailing 300 s (20 ticks); the up direction stays instant. The hidden tests make you honest about the edges: a window of exactly 20 ticks counts; a peak inside the window holds the replicas; the quiet between spikes proves nothing until it is twenty ticks old. When the fix passes, run the lab's report once more and read the two numbers it now shows — held ticks and unserved ticks — because that pair is the SLO's diary, and it is what the milestone asks you to write about. The transfer worth naming: hysteresis in the autoscaler is the same device as debounce in a UI, the dead band in a thermostat, and the admission envelope of Topic 8 — decisions separated from noise by an explicit, named gap. You have now met the pattern in four costumes; recognize it the fifth time without being told. HPASim: the closed loop The capstone class assembles the whole chapter into a simulator that runs in the browser. HPASim(w_ms=60, b_ms=2, cap=30, target_queue=2, window_ticks=20) — the knobs are the T6 step model (step time 60 + 2 ms per sequence, batch ceiling 30) plus this chapter's controller constants. tick(arrivals) delivers a wave of requests and returns the tick's verdict: the queue per pod, the band check, the decision, the fleet's serving rate, and the latency judgement against the working point. report() sums the run: held ticks, unserved ticks, and the trajectory of the fleet size. The per-pod capacity line comes straight from Topic 6 and is worth writing once more, because every verdict the simulator issues is measured against it: Four replicas promise 1000 tok/s; a kill drops the line to 750 for the boot — 165 s of 250 tok/s shortfall, about 41,250 tokens against the promise. The figure is the step-time economics from Topic 10's model family: the same declared knobs (W = 60 ms of weight-streaming work per step, b = 2 ms per sequence, a batch ceiling of 30) that produce the working point of 250 tok/s per pod. HPASim does not re-measure them — it consumes them as constants, which is why its latency verdicts are quotes, not measurements. The loop closes through the queue, and Topic 6's Little's law is visible inside one simulator: slow the service (a kill), and the queue grows; the growing queue trips the band; the controller scales up; the boot elapses; the queue drains. Nothing in that sentence is magic — it is the formula, the band, the windows and the capacity line running in order, which is exactly what the star challenge then asks you to tune. The failure drill The milestone's third artifact is incident notes, and the lab's drill gives them their numbers. Four replicas at the working point promise 1000 tok/s. Kill one: the line drops to 750 tok/s and stays there for the replacement's boot — 165 s of 250 tok/s shortfall, the number exercise 5 computes. The same drill at the floor — minReplicas 1 — is the honest disaster: the single pod dies, the Service has no endpoints, and clients meet a 503 window that lasts scheduling plus boot, with zero capacity behind it. Two vocabulary words guard the drill's edges, and posttest-adjacent questions like exercise 6 separate them cleanly. minReplicas is the autoscaler's floor: the HPA itself will never scale below it, so at 2 a single kill leaves a serving pod behind — degraded, not dark. PodDisruptionBudget is the drain's floor: it bounds voluntary disruptions (node upgrades, cluster maintenance — how many pods may be taken at once), and it does not protect against crashes. The crash protection is the replica count itself; confusing the two words is how teams discover that their PDB was never a safety net. Write the incident notes in the drill's grammar — what broke, what it cost in tok/s, how long the window lasted, which knob would have blunted it — because that grammar is the milestone's format and, in spirit, every postmortem you will ever file. The numbers are small on purpose: an incident you can hold in your head teaches the shape of every incident you won't. Admission and autoscaling: two envelopes Topic 8 built the admission envelope — the honest 429: when arrivals exceed what the slots and queue can hold, the gateway refuses the extras immediately, with a reason. The HPA is the second envelope, and the two compose rather than compete. Admission protects the fleet now — instant, per-request, no boot involved. Autoscaling restores and extends the envelope over minutes — it pays boots, it waits for windows. A burst that fits meets a fleet that absorbs it; a burst that exceeds meets 429s at the door and a fleet growing behind the wall; sustained demand meets a bigger steady fleet with the admission envelope resized around it. The figure is Topic 8's queue economy; reread it here and the composition is visible: the queue in front of the engines is the same queue the HPA reads. When the queue is honest and the envelope is honest, the controller's inputs are honest — garbage in any layer and the autoscaler scales a fiction. That is why this course built the layers in order: the journal (T08) made the queue provable, the probes (T11) made Ready honest, and only now does a controller get to act on them. The rehearsal the lab walks in prose — no runtime needed — repeats the T8 burst on paper: 24 arrivals against the old envelope, 16 honest 429s, then a hand "HPA tick" (you, playing the controller, doubling the replicas in the compose file), and the same burst again with fewer refusals. Do it once on paper and the division of labour is permanent: the envelope absorbs seconds, the autoscaler absorbs minutes, and neither pretends to be the other. What the wrong decision costs Both directions of a wrong replicas have a price, and the course prices them with Topic 13's declared arithmetic — cost per million output tokens = price × 1,000,000 / (throughput × 3600) — so the numbers here are quotes, not measurements. Over-provisioning pays for idle GPUs by the hour: two replicas above the demand line, at a declared 2.00 per GPU-hour, burn 4.00 per hour while serving nothing extra — 96 per day for a fleet size chosen by vibes. Under-provisioning pays in the currency of Topic 8: honest 429s and bent TTFTs, which the SLO of Topic 13 converts into a breach with a timestamp. And flapping pays in boots: every oscillation loads weights that are thrown away on the next down-tick — 165 s of disk and GPU work per churned pod, multiplied by however many times the missing band let the controller twitch. The pricing habit matters more than any single number, because it turns the guards of this chapter into line items. The tolerance band stops paying boots for noise. The clamp stops a metric bug from renting the node pool at full price. The scale-down window stops one quiet minute from triggering a fire-and-refill cycle. When Topic 13 asks you to build a cost ledger with named levers, you will discover you already own three: they were the guards, all along, and each one exists because the unguarded version of the same controller is measurably more expensive. One boundary sentence, in the course's grammar: these are declared prices on a teaching fleet — the 2.00 per GPU-hour is the same declared tier T13 uses, and the throughput line is this topic's 250 tok/s per pod. The exercise for the reader is to redo the three computations with the prices of a real quote they have at hand; the shape of the argument — guards are line items — survives every price list unchanged. And when the price list arrives, the ledger habit from Topic 10 applies to it verbatim: itemise the rows, name the knobs, and refuse any total whose components you cannot point to. Practice: what prod scales on The plumbing has three names worth carrying. The Prometheus Adapter exports serving metrics (queue depth, KV pressure, TTFT) as custom metrics the stock HPA can read — the minimal-production path for the arithmetic you already know. KEDA adds event-driven scalers — queue lengths from brokers, streams, cron — and the scale-to-zero trick, attractive for small models and spiky traffic, painful in exact proportion to the boot. llm-d's WVA weighs several serving signals into one desired-replica verdict — the "weighted verdict" approach for fleets that trust no single gauge. Around them, the vLLM production stack pairs the autoscaler with a KV-cache-aware router, so that scale events land on warmed pods instead of cold ones. The stable core under all four names is the skeleton you have built: a ratio, a band, a ceiling, a clamp, windows. When a design review produces a fifth name, ask for the skeleton — what is the metric, the target, the band, the fuse, the memory? A scaler that cannot answer those five questions is a mood, and the course has taught you to price moods in GPU-hours. One more honest boundary: everything in this section is cited practice, not executed practice — the lab's environment has no Prometheus, no KEDA, no cluster, and it says so. The arithmetic is executable in your browser; the plumbing is named so that the first time you meet it in production, it is a re-acquaintance, not a revelation. The T03 bridge: quantize the boot The bridge the posttest drills, in prose: switch the fleet to an INT4 engine. What changes? The weights member of the boot shrinks (roughly half the bytes to load), the per-pod ledger row shrinks (more replicas fit per node), and the cold scale-up's hidden cost — the 165 s of physics between a scale decision and usable capacity — shrinks with it. Elasticity got cheaper; the fleet can afford to be more elastic at the same SLO. What does not change: the policy. The HPA's formula, band and windows never mention weight precision — desired = ceil(replicas × ratio), clamped, is as true of INT4 as of fp16. The layer boundary is worth stating precisely because this course drew the same one in Topic 3: quantization changes the cost of things; the controller decides about quantities. A quantized fleet scales with the same skeleton, from the same queue, against the same promise — and the runbook's one honest edit is to re-measure the boot and re-budget the startup probe before trusting any quoted second. Exercise 8 makes you write that boundary sentence under a deliberately uncertain number — "roughly half" is a declared proportion, not a measured boot — because the course's evidence grammar applies to bridges twice over: the mechanism may be certain, and the seconds still need provenance. Lab 12: what you will build Ten checkpoints, the ladder you know. Quizzes q1–q3 with "why" follow-ups: the clamp as the cost fuse, the inclusive band as anti-flap, the window's maximum as the past voting. Exercises: desired_replicas — one line, with the int() trap in the hidden tests; hpa_step — the inclusive band, edge cases included; fix the flutter — the red line of the window figure, handed to you broken; and the capstone HPASim — the closed loop with tick and report . The posttest closes with the T03 bridge. The star challenge sits above the count, as in every lab: absorb a burst of 60 arrivals in one tick and keep the per-step time at or under 120 ms, choosing target_queue × max_replicas from a declared grid. The page replays the controller arithmetic against your printed result and rejects invented numbers; the reference stays hidden until you pass. It is the whole chapter in one trade: a tighter queue target buys latency with replicas, a bigger replica budget buys absorption with money, and the step-time budget — the T6 roof — is the wall both choices hit. What the lab has that lab 11 did not: a runtime chip is still absent — no Docker, no gateway — because the compose rehearsal is prose. But the lab's journal grammar is the same: every decision you make is recorded with its inputs, so your run can be quoted, checked and replayed by someone who was not there. That quotability is the course's quiet invariant, and it holds here too. What this chapter does and does not establish State the boundary plainly. The HPA arithmetic in this chapter is a declared teaching model of a controller: deterministic simulators in Pyodide, constants named and course-inherited — the working point 250 tok/s per pod from T6, the boot 165 s from the T09 fleet run, the windows 0/300 s from Kubernetes defaults rounded to 20 ticks, the band ±10 % from the HPA documentation. No cluster was autoscaled; no Prometheus was queried; the production stacks are cited, not run. A student who quotes "8 replicas" as what a real HPA decided has failed the reading — the lab computes recommendations for a teaching fleet, and the journal says so on every page. What stays with production, cited but not reproduced: real metric pipelines (the Adapter, KEDA, WVA plumbing), real cluster autoscaling behaviour (scheduling delays, pending pods, node pool limits), and the multi-signal verdicts of real fleets. What stays with other topics: the money — Topic 13 prices the GPU-hours this chapter's decisions burn, and turns the capacity line into a bill; the SLO — the same topic writes the promise whose violation the drill rehearsed. The two envelopes — admission and autoscaling — are this topic's composition result, and they compose honestly only because both were built on provable layers. What the chapter does establish is a controller you can carry in your head: compute the ratio, respect the band, ceil then clamp, remember the window, price the boot, drill the failure. Every production autoscaler you meet will wear a different name over exactly this skeleton — and you will recognize it, because you have run it, by hand, on a fleet you can hold in your head. Sources, evidence status and provenance Primary sources for the policy: the Kubernetes documentation on Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (with the autoscaling concepts page behind it) — the formula, the tolerance behaviour and the stabilization windows are quoted from there, including the 0/300 s defaults and the 15 s sync period the lab rounds to one tick; the llm-d KubeCon NA 2026 talk "Best Practices for LLM Autoscaling" ( llm-d.ai ) — the queue/KV/TTFT signal set and the "GPU utilization tells you very little" framing; the GKE guidance on tuning the HPA for GPU inference (JetStream's KV-cache signal); the KEDA documentation for event-driven scaling and scale-to-zero; and the vLLM production stack for the KV-cache-aware router. Each is quoted as a source for vocabulary and policy — none is reproduced as a measurement. Evidence status. The course-inherited numbers this chapter's arithmetic stands on: the T6 working point (250 tok/s per pod, from the declared step model with W = 60 ms, b = 2 ms, cap 30), the T09 fleet boot (165 s, seminars/runs/2026-11-07-topic09-fleet-mac/README.md ), and the T8 burst drill (24 arrivals, 16 honest 429s, the live gateway's journal). The lab's simulations produce no new measurements; their outputs are declared arithmetic over those constants, and the journal records your runs in the same grammar as every topic before. Until a real cluster's autoscaling record is quoted with its provenance, this chapter claims a controller you understand and a drill you have rehearsed — not autoscaling results. Check understanding and transfer Answer before opening the explanations.
