Chapter 13: LLMOps: observability, monitoring & cost control

.figure-note{font-size:.9rem;color:#4B6070;margin:.4rem 0 0;} This chapter follows the approved Topic13 arc. The carrier is a DECLARED TEACHING MODEL OF AN ON-CALL DAY: the SLO (99 %), the error budget (1 %), the burn-rate page line (8.3×) and the incident trace (p95 7.2 s for forty minutes) are declared lecture numbers; the journal semantics are the real layer-2 gateway's ( runtime/gateway/app.py ), the same hash chain lab 09 verified. Cold-start and fleet numbers cite the run record ( seminars/runs/2026-11-07-topic09-fleet-mac/README.md ). Nothing here is a benchmark of a production observability stack. 21:00: everything is green The incident that opens this chapter is deliberately boring. Every request answered 200. CI was green. The mean-latency chart — the chart everyone had agreed to watch — was flat all evening. And the users were angry, because one burst second had stretched their requests to 7.2 seconds while the fleet politely reported health. Nothing crashed. Nothing errored. The dashboard told the truth about every number it was asked to show, and it was still useless, because it had never been asked about the promise. That is the gap this chapter closes. "The server responded" and "the service kept its promise" are different statements, and production incidents live exactly in the distance between them. Topic 08 built a gateway whose journal records every outcome; Topic 09 made the unit immutable; Topics 11–12 gave the fleet declared state and a controller. All of that produced facts. This chapter is about turning facts into obligations: a promise you declare before the incident, a budget you can spend, a page that fires for the right reason, a bill with named levers, and a verdict you can reproduce. The instrument underneath all five is one you already own and have already verified with your own code: the hash-chained journal. The mean hides the tail The mean is the most popular statistic in operations and the least qualified for latency. Its failure is not subtle: it is arithmetically insensitive to the tail. Take the declared trace of this chapter — 100 requests, 96 of them at 0.8 seconds and 4 (the burst second) at 7.2 seconds. The mean is 1.06 seconds: a number a manager would call acceptable. The median is 0.8 seconds: the typical user had a fine evening. The p95 is 7.2 seconds: one user in twenty met the burst with their whole request hanging in it. Three verdicts from one trace, and only the percentile-and-window pair is falsifiable. Read the figure as the chapter's thesis in one window: the same trace yields a calm mean, a boring median and an alarming tail, and the choice of statistic is the choice of what you agree to see. Percentile scope is part of the number — "p95 TTFT over a 5-minute window" is a measurement, while "our latency is about a second" is a mood. This is why the course's rule exists: every latency statement names its percentile and its window, or it is not quoted as a number at all. Exercise 3 makes you compute both flavors of p95 on a small sample, so the nearest-rank discipline is yours before any dashboard needs it. Freeze the vocabulary before the incident Three terms carry the chapter, and they are worth freezing now, calmly, because during an incident nobody defines anything. The SLI — service level indicator — is the measured number: the thing the journal actually records, with its percentile and window as part of the number. The SLO — service level objective — is the promise you declare over that indicator: this course's working example is p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s per 5-minute window , declared before any incident, not negotiated during one. The error budget is what the promise leaves on the table: 1 − SLO. At SLO 99 % the budget is 1 % of minutes — for a 30-day month that is 432 minutes of broken promise the service is allowed to spend. The budget is the moral center of the triple, because it legalizes failure. A service that never spends its budget is over-provisioned — burning GPU-hours (real money, priced later in this chapter) for reliability nobody asked to buy. A service that spends the budget deliberately can accept a burst second, a deploy-day degradation, an experiment — inside the envelope the promise allows. The exam voice for this slide is posttest p1: an SLI is measured, an SLO is promised, and the direction matters — the promise borrows its meaning from the measured indicator, never the other way around. Four golden signals, one journal The Google SRE book's golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — sound like a monitoring-stack shopping list until you notice that this course's stack already records all four in one place. The layer-2 journal is per-request: every entry carries the timing, the sequence, the kind and the payload. Latency is the p95 of experiment entries over a window. Traffic is the sequence progression per minute. Errors are the 429s of burst entries. Saturation is the queue depth and the waits the admission envelope recorded. The discipline that makes the table honest is the source field: each signal must name the journal field that feeds it. If a signal cannot name its source, it is a vibe, not an SLI — and vibes do not survive a postmortem. This is the contract the later dashboard is held to: no tile without a source field, no number without a window. Logs you can prove Logs, metrics and traces are usually three tools and an integration bill. At course scale one artifact plays all three roles: the journal. Per-request records are the logs; aggregates over windows are the metrics; the request lifecycle from admission to final token is the trace. The reason this course can lean on one artifact so hard is a property lab 09 already proved with your own code: the journal is append-only and hash-sealed. Each entry hashes its predecessor; an edited line fails verification with a named broken_at index. The consequences are cultural before they are technical. A dashboard fed by a provable journal is ground truth: when it says the promise broke, the promise broke, and the argument moves to mitigation. A dashboard fed by editable logs is a rumor network: the most the query can say is "some process, at some point, claimed". Story 2 at the end of the chapter is the honest horror version — someone edits a log line to hide a breach — and the reason it ends badly for the editor is exactly this chain. Anatomy of an entry The journal entry is small enough to hold in your head, and every field earns its place by what breaks without it. seq orders events; a gap is a lost event, and metrics computed over silent holes are fiction. ts windows them; without it "when" is a guess and no SLO window exists at all. kind separates experiments from bursts; without it the 429 rate pollutes the latency series and every percentile becomes a mixture of two populations. payload carries the values themselves — tokens, wall time, tok/s, waits. And prev-hash seals the history; without it any rewrite passes silently. The exam voice for this section is the failure column, not the field list: a missing field is not "less convenience", it is a specific way to lie. When you build the dashboard tiles in the deliverable, the walk from real entry to tile — entry #15 of the November drill, with its 24 arrivals and its 12 rejections — is the rehearsal that makes the anatomy yours. From incident to verified fact Put the pieces together in the order the on-call actually needs. Define — the SLO existed since before the incident: p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s per 5-minute window. Query — aggregate the 21:00–21:05 window from journal entries, not from anyone's memory: p95 = 7.2 s, 3.6× over the promise. Verify — chain check over the window: ok, every one of the 15 entries seals its predecessor, so the number is a fact. Declare — the burn rate against the 1 % budget is 8.3×; page the on-call and state the breach in those terms. Mitigate — tighten the admission envelope and scale on the backlog signal, both levers the fleet already owns; the postmortem cites entries, not recollections. Notice what the walk does not contain: nobody "looked at the graphs" first, nobody argued from memory, and the declaration quantifies itself. Each step names its artifact — that habit is what the milestone deliverable asks you to keep. Burn rate: when a breach becomes a page The burn rate is the one formula that turns a promise into a page. It is a speed: how fast the error budget is being spent, relative to the pace that would exactly exhaust the budget when the period ends. Formally, for a window of T minutes containing t_bad breaching minutes at budget 1 − SLO: burn = (t_bad / T) / (1 − SLO). At burn 1× the budget lasts exactly as long as the period — a month's allowance lasts the month. The lecture's worked example: SLO 99 % → budget 1 %; a 360-minute window with 30 bad minutes gives (30/360)/0.01 = 8.33×. An evening at that pace spends a work-week's allowance. The page line at 8.3× is chosen so that such an evening wakes a human now , while a quiet 2× burn — twice the allowance, still ten hours from trouble — waits for the morning ticket. Exercise 2 makes you recompute it twice, once correctly and once with the percent trap, because the trap is the most common way this formula is broken in review. Fast and severe pages; slow and mild tickets One threshold is never enough, and the failure modes of "one threshold" are the reason the SRE Workbook pairs a fast window with a slow one. A single fast line drowns the on-call in pages: every noisy lunch trips it, and by the third swipe the real page is swiped too — alert fatigue, which is an availability problem of the channel . A single slow line goes quiet in the other direction: a slow 4× bleed never looks alarming until the budget is spent, and the discovery arrives as a bill. The pairing resolves both: the fast window (10 minutes, burn ≥ 8.3×) pages because severe-and-now deserves a human; the slow window (60 minutes, burn ≥ 3×) opens a ticket because erosion deserves a reader. Edges are inclusive — the T12 thermostat lesson, again: a metric parked exactly on the line must not toggle the policy. ok — burn &lt; 3x: silence is correct here ticket — slow burn 3x to 8.3x (60-minute window) page — fast burn 8.3x and up (10-minute window) declared policy, Topic 13 The declared on-call policy as zones. The burn rate is a speed, so the zones are speeds: above 8.3× the month evaporates in under four days and a human is woken; between 3× and 8.3× the erosion is real but readable in the morning; below 3× the correct action is none. The pairing also explains the deduplication rule the lab enforces: after a page, the slow lane is suppressed for an hour. Without it, one breach pages once and tickets five times — the channel teaches the on-call that pages come in rows, which is exactly the training that kills the sixth, honest page. Alert fatigue versus silent failure The two ways an alerting system fails are opposite, and both destroy trust. Alert fatigue is the volume failure: pages that wake nobody's action train the on-call to swipe them, and the channel dies not with a bang but with a habit. An alert must be actionable — it names the SLO, the window and the lever; if the honest response is "look at it later", the honest alert is a ticket. Silent failure is the volume failure's mirror: the mean-latency alert that stayed green through the whole 21:00 breach was not merely useless, it was an alibi — "we had alerting" turns out to mean "we had a page that never fired". A channel that only cries once a quarter is fine — provided the quarter's cry is real. The burn-rate pairing is the resolution because it prices both failures: the fast lane is expensive to wake but only fires when the promise is breaking now; the slow lane is cheap to read and catches the bleeds. Ask yourself which of the two failures your favorite service suffers from; both are common, and neither is an accident — both are policy choices someone did not make explicitly. Rules: symptoms, not causes The declared alert table of this chapter has four rows, and the last one is the design statement. Row one: burn ≥ 8.3× on p95 TTFT over the 10-minute window — page, because the promise is breaking now. Row two: burn ≥ 3× over the hour — ticket, because erosion is readable in the morning. Row three: 429 rate above 30 per minute sustained for five minutes — ticket plus a capacity review, because admission doing its job honestly is fine but a changed load shape is news. Row four: mean-latency threshold — removed . It is the anti-example: green through the incident, alibi in the postmortem, gone by design. Symptom-based alerts (the user-visible promise breaking) versus cause-based noise (CPU, restarts — those self-heal, or get their own dashboards): the rule of thumb survives contact with production because symptoms are what the promise is made of. A cause can be interesting and still irrelevant to the customer; a symptom is by definition the customer's experience. The bill: cost per 1M output tokens Observability without money is half a discipline. The bill's unit is dollars per million output tokens — output, because that is what the API bills per token on completion; prompt-cache hits save prefill work, not generation. The formula is arithmetic: price per GPU-hour P divided by sustained throughput r, scaled to the billing unit — P · 10⁶ / (r · 3600). The lecture's worked example: P = $2.00/h, r = 250 tok/s (the T6 pod model) → 2.00 · 10⁶ / (250 · 3600) = $2.22 per 1M output tokens. Two habits make the number honest. First, r is measured, not quoted : the 16 November layer-2 run measured 12.3 tok/s on a laptop engine, and quoting the pod model's 250 there would be a 20× fiction; the lab ledger substitutes your own measured rate, and the deliverable's cost ledger is judged on that substitution. Second, the denominator is sustained throughput — the number the engine holds under the day's load shape, not the burst spike a dashboard once caught. The lever catalog: name the lever, move the bar Cost work is lever work, and every lever is a named mechanism with a first risk. Batching raises sustained tok/s: the waterfall moves $2.22 → $1.39 (−37 %) and the risk is the latency of the batch — you bought speed with somebody's tail. The price tier (spot or cheaper GPU-hours) halves the base to $1.11 and the risk is availability: spot preemption is a capacity promise with a caveat. Admission — the honest 429 — keeps the SLA for the served and the risk is fairness: who is rejected, and is that policy auditable. Prompt cache skips prefill on reuse and the risk is staleness — a stale cache is a wrong-answer machine; note what it does not do: it never makes generation cheaper, and conflating those is the catalog's most common misread. The prediction discipline applies to money exactly as it applied to the knee in Topic 06: state the predicted delta before measuring, then let the lab ledger reconcile. Exercise 6 walks one full lever decision — both levers together, each alone — and asks for the order you would recommend, because the first-risk column is a decision criterion, not decoration. 429 is a cost instrument The lab 08 envelope returns wearing a finance hat. A rejection costs nothing and tells the client the truth; a late answer costs the SLA and invites retries, which amplify the load that caused them. Serving the whole burst "to be nice" spends the error budget of everyone — the tail stretch taxes every concurrent user — while rejecting the overflow honestly spends only the rejected slice. The measured drill made this concrete: 24 arrivals at 4 slots plus 4 queue seats → 8 admitted, 16 × 429 with waits the journal recorded (0.74–0.93 s); the burst second the mean chart never noticed is exactly the slice admission sheds. Fairness is a policy, not an accident. FIFO is honest to arrival order and brutal to bursty clients; the journal records every rejection, so the policy is auditable — and the audit is part of the runbook. When the cost lever says "reject more", the fairness review is what keeps the lever from becoming a filter on unpopular customers. The journal is what makes that review possible at all. The score drifts Quality claims are measurements, and measurements need controlled conditions. Run the same 100 prompts twice — batched versus isolated, warm cache versus cold — and six verdicts flip: 94/100 against 88/100, six prompts that pass in one condition and fail in the other. Batch composition changes numerics and timing; the scheduler reorders work; a warm cache hides a regression behind yesterday's answer. None of the six flips is the model "getting better or worse" — the conditions changed, not the competence. Run A — batched, warm cache: 94/100 pass Run B — isolated, cache-busted: 88/100 pass six prompts flip between the conditions — the disputed band is weather, not competence the invariant protocol (B) is the score; run A is a measurement defect to investigate The declared drift drill. Bars show pass counts under the two conditions; the colored tails mark the six disputed prompts. Averaging the two runs (91/100) is a mood — the protocol, not the average, decides which run is a score. The invariant protocol is short enough to memorize: fixed prompt order, seeded decoding, cache-busting between samples, per-sample isolation. A verdict you cannot reproduce is not a verdict — it is weather. The judge has been grading you under exactly this protocol since Round 01; the next section just makes that explicit. Judge-grade reproducibility The table that closes the evaluation block maps each requirement to the failure it kills and the place you already met it. Pinned environment (lockfile) kills "worked on my machine" — you met it in the Round 01 setup and in the Topic 09 image digest. Declared seeds kill lucky sampling — every lab journal carries one. A batch-invariant suite kills verdict weather — this topic's protocol. Snapshot at the deadline kills moving targets — round tags plus the judge's capture. Private thresholds kill overfitting the grader — that is the judge itself. None of it is new bureaucracy; it is your own world with the names filled in. The drift drill on slide 18 is the worked instance: run A (94) and run B (88), six flips, and the decision rule — B is the score because it is the invariant run; A's surplus is a measurement artifact and gets investigated, not banked. A teammate proposing the average (91/100) is proposing a mood; Exercise 7 writes the two-sentence refusal. The runbook skeleton The deliverable's capstone artifact is a runbook skeleton with four columns, and the discipline is that every row names its journal window. Symptom → query → lever → rollback: "p95 breach, burn 8.3×" → "journal window 21:00–21:05, chain verified" → "tighten queue_slots " → "widen after ten clean windows". "Bill doubles" → "cost ledger by lever" → "price tier or admission" → "revert tier, keep SLA". "Verdicts flip" → "invariant suite re-run" → "protocol B is the score" → "investigate run A's cache". "Chain verify fails" → " broken_at index" → "freeze dashboards" → "restore from the sealed backup". symptom → query → lever → rollback burn 8.3x on p95 window 21:00-21:05, verified tighten queue_slots widen after 10 clean windows bill doubles ledger by lever tier / admission revert tier, keep SLA verdicts flip invariant suite re-run protocol B is the score investigate run A cache chain verify fails broken_at index freeze dashboards restore sealed backup The skeleton the deliverable fills. Incident-ready means each row was rehearsed against a real journal window, not invented during the incident — the postmortem cites entries, never recollections. Incident-ready means each row was rehearsed, not invented. The milestone asks you to fill the skeleton for your own fleet with rows you actually ran in the lab — that is what separates a runbook from a wish list. Two failure stories, one moral Story one: the silent breach. Mean green, p95 at 7.2 seconds for forty minutes. Detection: the burn-rate page (8.3×, the fast lane). Mitigation: tighten the admission envelope, scale on the backlog signal — levers the fleet already operates. The postmortem's first line is a journal window, and every number in it was verified before it was quoted. Story two: the edited history. Someone "fixes" a log line to hide the breach. Detection: the chain names broken_at . Mitigation: dashboards read the journal only, and the hand-edited history is not a source — it is evidence of a second incident, the cover-up. The moral of the pair is the same sentence from both ends: the facts must be cheaper than the narrative . Verification makes facts cheap; that is the entire investment. What this model omits Declared simplifications, in the open: no GPU or kernel traces, no multi-node correlation, token accounting approximate, prices flat. The journal is a gateway-level view — it sees requests and tokens, not SM occupancy. A production cluster adds federation, cardinality explosions, and the observability stack's own bill, which is not zero and is itself a cost lever somebody owns. The reason the model still holds is that the method is layer-independent: SLI → SLO → burn-rate → invariant evaluation does not care how deep the instrumentation goes. Deeper traces multiply the number of fields; they do not change the discipline of naming sources, windows and percentiles. Say what the model omits before someone else discovers it — that is the honesty habit the whole course runs on. The measurement contract and the deliverable The contract in one paragraph: every number is journaled, the chain is verified, the percentile and window are named, prices are declared. A number without a source field is a mood; a source without a window is a rumor. The deliverable is your fleet under that contract: one SLO, one alert predicate with its window, one cost ledger with your measured r, and the runbook skeleton filled with rehearsed rows. These are the first four artifacts of the T16 defense story — the capstone week will ask you to defend exactly this, and the supervised agent will be aimed at exactly this surface. The lab: journal-drill versus live Lab 13 drills the whole chapter on a declared teaching journal in the gateway's canonical form: verify the chain with your own lab 09 hash walk, compute the golden signals (and watch the tampered entry's lie propagate into the error rate until verification catches it), burn the budget in quiz arithmetic, decide page/ticket/ok with inclusive edges, and run the capstone — JournalSim, a day of 10-minute buckets where the breach pages itself and both shoulders, the noisy lunch earns tickets, and one quiet evening proves the dead band. The star challenge tunes the policy: one page, zero tickets, nothing invented. When the practice runtime is connected, the same views go live against your own gateway journal — machine-local and honest; offline, the section says so and the declared fixture stays the grading surface. Where the block goes Topic 14 changes the model's voice: LoRA adapters multiply tenants over one base model, and every quality-per-tenant claim lands on the instruments you built here. Topic 15 changes the workload's shape: agent loads fork, wait on tools and reuse prefixes, and prefill and decode split into roles — your admission envelope meets a workload that breathes. Topic 16 hands you the controller's chair: the capstone asks you to supervise an optimizing agent over the lab 08 policy, and the contract you write will be judged with exactly the reproducibility discipline of this chapter. The observability layer is the block's floor; everything after this page is built on it. Keeping the journal: retention and cardinality A provable journal earns a bill of its own, and pretending otherwise is how observability stacks quietly become the second-largest line item. Three honest levers exist, and all three are policy, not accident. Retention : the raw journal is append-only, but the sealed archive — a chain whose head hash is published — can replace live entries after a retention window without breaking verification, because the verifier walks the archive and the head is pinned; the course stack simply keeps everything, and says so. Cardinality : every label you add to an entry multiplies the aggregate space — kind is three values and cheap, a per-client label is a thousand series and not cheap; the source-field discipline from the golden-signals table is also a cardinality budget. Aggregation horizon : percentiles over a minute, an hour and a day answer different questions, and computing all three forever costs three times the store; the SLO window decides which horizon is load-bearing, and that one is computed forever while the others age out. The exam voice here is the trade the lab's fixture makes visibly: the teaching journal keeps full payloads forever because the journal is the grading surface. A production journal would seal, archive and thin — and the runbook's "restore from sealed backup" row is exactly the day that decision pays for itself. Retention is not an operations footnote; it is the difference between an audit trail and a liability. Reading a dashboard critically Most dashboards are inherited, not designed — and the inheritance is worth auditing once, deliberately, with the chapter's checklist. For every tile, ask four questions. What is the source field — and can it name the journal entries that produced it? What is the window — and is it the window the SLO is written over, or a chart-convenient one? What is the percentile — and would the p50 of the same series tell the opposite story? And what action does the tile suggest — because a tile that suggests no action is decoration, and decoration costs attention that a real page will need someday. Applied to the incident that opened the chapter, the audit finds the mean-latency tile guilty on all four counts: a source nobody could name (it aggregated a proxy log, not the journal), a window nobody chose (the default of the charting tool), no percentile at all, and no action it could suggest — the mean cannot move a lever, because a mean is not a promise. The honest rebuild is small: one row per SLO, one row per alert predicate, one cost ledger, one link to the chain verifier. Four tiles, each with an answer to all four questions, beat forty tiles of inherited green. The postmortem that cites entries The postmortem is where the chapter's disciplines meet, and its quality is a diagnostic of the whole observability practice. A recollection postmortem reads like a novel — "we noticed around nine, maybe earlier" — and produces narratives. An entry-citing postmortem reads like a ledger: breach window 21:00–21:40, chain verified at declaration time; p95 by window with the tail visible from 21:04; page fired at 21:06 on the fast lane; mitigation applied 21:11; first clean window 21:52; rollback criterion met 22:02. Every timestamp is a query result, every number names its window, and the disagreement space collapses to almost nothing — what remains is the actual argument: which lever, how hard, next time what. The habit that makes this possible costs one minute during the incident: write the window down when you query it. The postmortem written from memory at midnight-plus-four will invent a coherent story, and the chain will be the only witness against it. Culture follows the instrument here: teams that verify quote, and teams that quote resolve faster — not because they are smarter, but because their disagreements are smaller. The on-call day, end to end Assemble the chapter as the shift it describes, because the pieces are easier to trust once you have watched them cooperate for twenty-four hours. The day starts quiet: the journal is appending, the verifier runs clean, the burn rate idles near 0.3×, and the correct action is none — the dead band is doing its job by doing nothing. Around ten the lunch arrives: the rolling hour accumulates erosion, the slow lane crosses 3×, and a ticket opens itself with a named window and a named lever — readable tomorrow, invisible tonight, exactly as designed. Mid-afternoon contributes one blip: a single bucket hot enough to matter for ten minutes and gone by the next; fast burn 7× — under the page line — and the slow lane never sees it accumulate. The evening is the reason the shift exists: the burst second at 21:00, the fast lane at 83×, the page, the verification that makes the declaration a fact, the admission envelope tightened, the scale decision on the backlog signal, the first clean window, the rollback criterion met by rule rather than by mood. Now replay the same day with the chapter's instruments removed. No percentile discipline: the mean says "fine" all evening. No chain: the 21:00 numbers are deniable and the denials are unfalsifiable. No pairing: either the lunch pages three times (and the real page drowns), or nothing wakes anyone at all. No cost ledger: the mitigation's price is discovered next month. No invariant protocol: the postmortem's "quality is fine" claim is weather. The day did not get harder because the fleet got worse — it got harder because the facts got expensive. Every instrument in this chapter exists to keep the facts cheap. Sources and provenance Primary sources behind the numbers: the golden signals and latency-percentile discipline are the Google SRE book's ( Monitoring Distributed Systems , 2016); the multiwindow burn-rate pairing is the SRE Workbook's "Alerting on SLOs" ( sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos , 2018); the predicate-and-window mechanics of the alert table follow the Prometheus alerting overview ; the production-grade metric surface the journal models at course scale is vLLM's production metrics ; and the agents-optimize-infrastructure frontier — the trends slide and the T16 capstone's context — is Infrathon (arXiv 2611.11995) . The in-repo sources are the layer-2 gateway journal ( runtime/gateway/app.py ), the run record seminars/runs/2026-11-07-topic09-fleet-mac/README.md for the fleet numbers quoted in comparisons, and the judge README for the reproducibility rules the course has been enforcing since Round 01.

Book

Chapter 14: Adapters & multi-tenancy: LoRA economics

This chapter follows the approved Topic14 arc. The carrier is a DECLARED TEACHING MODEL OF A MULTI-TENANT SERVING LAYER: no real LoRA training happened (adapter quality deltas are declared), the 2 ms swap cost is a declared knob, and the tenant stream is the deck's six requests. The base size (491 MB) is the real T09 course engine; the journal canonical form is the real layer-2 gateway's ( runtime/gateway/app.py ). S-LoRA and Punica are cited as the real-systems line. Nothing here is a benchmark of any production multi-tenant stack. A second team wants "its own model" The demand arrives as a compliment: your inference service is good, and now a second team wants a version tuned to its own prompts — then a third, then a product line. The naive answer is honest arithmetic in the wrong direction: a copy of the engine per tenant. On the course engine that is 491 MB per copy; by the fifth team you operate 2.5 GB of weights that drifted five ways, load five times, and disagree at the worst moment. The multiplication problem scales every bad property with the tenant count, and none of the good ones. LoRA — low-rank adaptation — collapses the multiplication. The base stays frozen; each tenant gets a small adapter, a pair of low-rank matrices per target projection, trained on the tenant's own prompts. Tenants share the base and differ by slivers. The chapter prices those slivers honestly: the rank arithmetic that sizes them, the switch that serving them costs, the routing policy that trades switches against waits, and the per-tenant measurement that keeps every promise falsifiable. Everything executable lives in lab 14 — the deck names the ideas, the lab makes them runnable in the browser, and the journal you already trust carries the tenant field that makes fairness auditable. The adapter ledger Freeze the ledger before any arithmetic — the discipline every topic here runs on. Five rows: the frozen base at 491 MB (the real T09 engine, shared by every tenant); the hidden size d = 896 (declared); the rank r = 16 (the quality/size dial); the four attention projections q, k, v, o as LoRA targets (the standard choice, declared); and the adapter's own size, which is not a row at all but the next section's computation. The ledger's point is provenance: every number is either the real course engine or a declared knob with a name. The ledger also fixes what is NOT for sale. The adapter cannot change the tokenizer, the context window, the cutoff knowledge or the T02 memory physics — those belong to the frozen base and are shared by every tenant. When a tenant asks the adapter for a longer context, they are asking the wrong layer; the honest answer is that the base contract is shared, and only the tenant delta is purchasable. Posttest p1 asks exactly this distinction, because it is the one multi-tenancy claim most often overstated. Adapter size: one multiplication A LoRA update represents the weight change of a matrix as a product of two small matrices: A of shape r × d_in and B of shape d_out × r. Storing the update means storing r × (d_in + d_out) numbers per target matrix — the r is the rank, the dial that trades expressiveness for size. With four target matrices, fp16 storage, d = 896 and r = 16: 2 × 16 × 1792 × 4 = 114 688 parameters → 229 376 bytes ≈ 0.22 MB. Two classic errors live in this formula and quiz q1 hunts both. Doubling the factor 2 twice — the "2" is fp16 bytes per parameter, not the A/B pair; the pair is already inside r × (d_in + d_out). Or dropping A/B entirely and counting only r × d — which understates the adapter by half. The exercise makes you recompute at rank 8 and rank 32, because the rank dial is the topic's version of the T10 degree: its honest setting comes from a frozen plan and a measured sweep, never from a leaderboard vibe. Read the figure as the multiplication collapsing: the 491 MB base bar dwarfs the 0.22 MB adapter slivers by three orders of magnitude. That ratio — 0.05 percent of the base per tenant — is what makes multi-tenancy affordable at all, and it is why the interesting costs of this topic are not bytes but switches. The switch: one loaded adapter at a time At serving time one adapter is resident per engine slot. Requests for tenant A run with A's weights in place; the first request for tenant B pays an adapter load. The declared teaching model prices that load at 2 ms — flat, per switch, regardless of tenant. Real systems are smarter: S-LoRA pages adapter memory so adapters swap in chunks, and Punica merges adapter compute into custom kernels so the cost shrinks further. Both are cited as the real-systems line, and both are omitted here on purpose: a flat declared cost keeps the routing arithmetic hand-checkable, which is what makes it learnable. The consequence that turns routing into economics is order-dependence. The total switch bill depends not on how many requests each tenant sent but on how their arrivals interleaved. Six requests A, B, A, B, A, B cost five switches in arrival order and one switch grouped into A, A, A, B, B, B. Same load, fivefold different bill — which means the switch count is a policy output, not a load fact. Exercise 2 makes you count it on any stream; quiz q2 counts it on the deck's worst case. The switching drill Walk the drill once slowly, because the capstone automates exactly it. Stream: A, B, A, B, A, B. FIFO: every adjacent pair differs → five swaps → 10 ms of pure switch time on six requests. Grouped: A, A, A, B, B, B → one swap → 2 ms. The fivefold difference is the switch tax collapsing under grouping. Then the honest sentence, which the ribbon of the lab figure carries: the four missing swaps did not vanish — they became waiting. The second and third A waited for the first; likewise the Bs. Grouping is not free serving; it is a trade of switching for waiting, and a policy that quotes one side of that trade without the other is lying by omission. The capstone ledger prices both sides so neither can hide. Three policies and one exchange rate FIFO: A B A B A B — 5 swaps, 0 waited W = 3: AAB | BAB → grouped [AA][B] | [BB][A] — 2 swaps, 2 waited the grouping bars show both sides: green boxes are free slots, amber boxes paid a swap or a wait The two policies side by side on the declared stream. FIFO's five amber boundaries are the switch tax; the W = 3 grouping buys two swaps at the price of two waited requests — the dial row the star challenge must reproduce. FIFO — serve in arrival order. Honest to arrivals, brutal to switches: the full tax, every tenant change priced at the declared 2 ms. The affinity window — fill a window of W arrivals, group inside it by tenant: the switch count collapses toward the tenant count per window, and the price is the wait a request pays for its group. Tenant-pinned queues — one queue per tenant, drained at will: minimal switches, real head-of-line waiting for small tenants stuck behind large ones. One exchange rate prices all three: a swap is 2 ms of engine time. The policies trade that rate against waiting, and the waiting is measured per tenant — which is the next section's discipline. There is no free policy here; the exam question is not "which policy wins" but "what does each pay with, and can you see it in the journal". The window is the dial W swaps waited declared lines: swaps ≤ 2, waited ≤ 4, W ≤ 4 1 5 0 fails swaps 2 5 0 fails swaps 3 2 2 passes both ✓ 4 3 2 fails swaps 5–6 1 3–4 fails the W ≤ 4 bound The window dial, every row priced on both sides. One W passes the declared lines inside the bound — and the page-side recompute rejects every other row, so the challenge's answer is checkable rather than arguable. The affinity window W is the tuning knob between the degenerate policies. W = 1 is FIFO: every request its own batch, all switching. W = the stream length is tenant-pinned: one batch, all waiting. Between them, W bounds the wait a request can pay (at most W − 1 arrivals ahead of it in its own group) and bounds the tenant groups per window, which bounds the switches. On the declared six-request stream: W = 1 gives five swaps and zero waited; W = 3 gives two swaps and two waited; W = 6 gives one swap and four waited. The star challenge walks this dial with declared lines — swaps ≤ 2, waited ≤ 4, W ≤ 4 — and only one W passes all three, which is what "checkable policy" means. Tenant p95: the T13 discipline, one grain finer The T13 formula — nearest-rank p95 over a named window — applied globally is the mean-vs-tail mistake again, one abstraction level up. A global p95 over two tenants reports the fast tenant's health and hides the slow tenant behind it. The honest number slices the journal by tenant first: the tenant's own entries, sorted, element ceil(0.95 × n), a measured request — then the window named on top. The small-sample caveat is honest and load-bearing: a tenant slice of 20 entries makes the p95 sensitive to a single request; short windows are noisy windows. The promise names the window anyway, because "p95 per tenant per week" is falsifiable while "our tenants are happy" is not. Lab exercise 4 computes the slice from the journal fixture; the fixture is the T13 journal shape with a tenant field added — the same hash chain, one grain finer. The verdict picture: under mixed batching tenant B sits at p95 1.6 s against the declared 1.0 s SLO — B's slice inherits A's swaps and A's slow requests inside the shared batch. Affinity grouping pulls both tenants under the SLO at the price of batch waits. Routing is not a cost-only decision; it moves per-tenant promises, and the per-tenant slice is the instrument that makes the movement visible. Quality per tenant: measured, not assumed "Our adapter is better on our prompts" is a measurement claim and must survive the T13 invariant protocol: the tenant's frozen prompt slice, fixed order, seeded decoding, cache-busting, isolation — then a delta against the frozen base. A delta you cannot reproduce is weather. The delta is also per tenant by construction: the support adapter's gain lives on support prompts; quoting it as a global improvement is the same averaging lie in a new costume. The rank dial's honest setting follows the same pattern as the T10 degree: a frozen plan, a sweep over ranks, a measured quality-per-tenant slice, a ledger row for the bytes. Rank 8 may keep most of the delta at half the bytes; rank 32 may buy two points and double the swap bytes. Neither claim is true in general — each is true or false on a measured slice, and the runbook row names the slice. 429 per tenant: fairness is auditable or it is fiction The T08 admission envelope goes one grain finer: per tenant. A noisy tenant's burst must not consume a quiet tenant's seats, and the 429 ledger must be able to prove it. Every rejection entry carries the tenant field, the rule that fired, the timestamp and the Retry-After granted — then "who was rejected, by which rule, how often" is a query, not an argument. Without the tenant field the fairness question is unanswerable; with it, the audit is part of the runbook. The T13 cost lens applies per tenant too: a tenant's cost per 1M output tokens is computed on its own measured slice — the large tenant's batching gain must not be quoted as the small tenant's bill. Weighted fair admission, where weights are declared and the weights' effect is visible in the ledger, is one honest policy among several; the auditable part is the journal, never the promise. Two failure stories, one instrument Story one: the smothered tenant. Mixed batching looks efficient globally; the global p95 is healthy; but tenant B's own slice sits at 1.6 s against a 1.0 s promise for a whole afternoon. Detection: the per-tenant slice, window named. Mitigation: affinity grouping, verified by the same slice. The postmortem cites B's entries, not the global chart that hid them. Story two: the unmeasured upgrade. Every tenant silently upgraded to rank 32; the adapters doubled; a small tenant's slot started swapping twice as often and its p95 doubled. Detection: the swap-count ledger per window — the count is a policy output, remember. Mitigation: rank back to the measured per-tenant setting; the quality claim re-run under the invariant protocol per tenant. Both stories end at the same instrument: the journal with the tenant field. What this model omits Declared simplifications, in the open: no real LoRA training happened — adapter quality deltas are declared teaching numbers; no paged adapter memory (S-LoRA's answer); no merged kernels (Punica's answer); one resident adapter per slot; switches priced flat at 2 ms; the tenant stream is six requests plus the challenge's window walk. A production stack pages adapters, overlaps adapter compute, and prices switches by bytes moved — the constants move; the ledger, the drills and the capstone arithmetic stay. Why it still holds: the method — price the sliver, count the order-dependent cost, measure promises per tenant, audit fairness from the journal — is independent of how the constant was derived. Deeper systems multiply the knobs, not the discipline of naming them. Say what the model omits before someone else discovers it. The deliverable: the routing memo The milestone artifact is one page someone else could execute: the ledger rows (rank, d, targets, adapter size at fp16); the policy you chose — FIFO, window W, or pinned queues — with its two-sided price on your own stream (swaps and waits, both counted); the per-tenant p95 table with windows named; and the fairness row — who was rejected by which rule. Checked against AdapterSim, the lab's capstone, so the memo's numbers are reproducible arithmetic, not prose. These four fields are the T16 defense story in miniature: a contract (the ledger), a policy with its price, a measurement (the per-tenant table), and an audit (the fairness row). The capstone week will ask you to defend exactly this shape at larger scale — and the supervised agent will be aimed at exactly this surface. The lab: AdapterSim and the live journal Lab 14 runs the whole chapter in your browser: quiz arithmetic on the ledger; the switching drill on the deck's stream; affinity grouping as a pure function; the tenant p95 slice on the journal fixture; and the capstone — AdapterSim, the two-sided ledger over the dial, whose every dial row you must reproduce. The star challenge tunes the window under declared lines and has exactly one passing answer. The Layer-2 section connects your own gateway: journal entries tagged with your tenant names, slices and p95s computed on real entries, the swap count being your machine's. Machine-local and honest; offline, the section says so and the declared fixture stays the grading surface. Where the block goes Topic 15 makes the workload breathe: agent loads fork, wait on tools and reuse prefixes, and the routing ledger of this chapter meets its real enemy — a stream that changes shape while you route it. Topic 16 hands over the chair: the capstone asks you to write the contract that supervises an optimizing agent over the lab 08 policy, and the artifacts you defend are the ledger, the policy price, the per-tenant table and the fairness row — the four fields of this chapter's memo, at larger scale. Worked by hand: one routing decision end to end Before trusting any simulator, do one decision with your hands — the discipline every topic here runs on. The stream is the deck's six requests; the policy under test is the affinity window W = 3; the slot starts holding adapter A; a swap costs the declared 2 ms. Window one covers arrivals 1–3: A, B, A. First-appearance order: A, then B. Group A = arrivals 1 and 3 (two requests); group B = arrival 2. Serve group A first — the slot already holds A, no swap; two requests waited behind the first A. Then group B — one swap, 2 ms; its single request waited for nothing beyond the group switch. Window two covers arrivals 4–6: B, A, B. Groups: B first (arrival 4), then A (arrivals 5–6). The slot holds B from window one — group B is free; its request waited for nothing. Group A: one swap. Waiting: two requests in group A, plus arrival 5 and 6 behind arrival 4... careful — arrival 4 is B (first of its group), arrivals 5–6 are A (two waited). Window totals: one swap, two waited. Grand total: two swaps, four waited — which is exactly the dial-table row for W = 3. The simulator must reproduce this by construction; if it disagrees with your hands, either your grouping or your carry-across rule is wrong, and the hands win. The exchange rate in practice The declared 2 ms is the chapter's fixed exchange rate between switches and waiting, and real deployments have their own. Reading it honestly means asking three questions of any number you are handed. Is it flat — one price per switch regardless of tenants — or does it scale with adapter bytes (a rank-32 swap moves twice the bytes of a rank-16 one)? Is it measured — from the serving stack's own logs, with the measurement window named — or declared? And does the price hide overlaps — S-LoRA-style paging and Punica-style merged kernels make parts of the swap run alongside compute, which is a lower effective price, not a free one. The lab's ledger keeps the rate flat and declared so the routing arithmetic is learnable; the runbook row for your own deployment replaces the constant with your measured one, window named. The exercises do not change: count swaps, group, price both sides. Only the units on the exchange line move — which is why they were named separately from the start. Capacity planning with adapters The ledger extends capacity planning by one column: per-tenant adapter bytes. The slot budget is the base plus the resident adapter plus headroom; because adapters are slivers, the resident set is nearly invariant to the tenant count — the planning question shifts from "how many copies fit" to "how many tenants share this slot before switching traffic dominates". That question has a journal answer: switches per window grow with tenant interleaving, so the slot's tenant budget is a routing property, not a memory property. A slot serving two heavy tenants alternately may pay more switch time than a slot serving five calm ones. The honest planning artifact is therefore per slot and per week: the ledger row, the observed swap count over a named window, the wait per tenant, and the rank actually deployed. One table per slot replaces the instinctive "how many models can we pack" with the measured question the topic teaches: what did each tenant's presence cost this slot, in switches and in waits, and is the routing policy still the cheapest answer. The tenant journal: retention and the fairness window Fairness claims age. A rejection audit from six weeks ago proves what the stack did then, not what it does now — so the tenant journal's retention is a policy with a name. The course stack keeps everything (the journal is the grading surface); a production stack seals archives, publishes head hashes and thins live entries. Either way the fairness window must be named wherever the fairness claim is made: "rejections per tenant over the audited window" is a number; "we are fair" is a mood. Cardinality returns at tenant grain too: the tenant field multiplies every aggregate by the tenant count. The slice-and-p95 discipline from T13 survives it — slice, sort, nearest-rank, window named — but the dashboards must compute the slices per tenant on purpose, not inherit a global aggregate and hope. Retention, cardinality and the named fairness window are the three policy lines the deliverable's runbook carries forward from T13. The on-call day for adapters Assemble the chapter as the shift it describes. Morning: the routing memo's policy is live — affinity window W = 3 on the busiest slot; the swap ledger reads two per window, the per-tenant p95 table holds both tenants under the SLO. Noon: a third tenant onboards with a rank-16 adapter; the ledger gains its sliver, the window groups it, the switches tick up one per window but hold under the line. Mid-afternoon: the noisy tenant bursts; its own queue absorbs the burst inside the window, the other tenants' slices stay under their p95s, and the 429 ledger shows the burst tenant's own rejections — fairness, visible from entries. Evening: a rank experiment for the new tenant — the frozen plan from T06 applied to the rank dial, measured on the tenant slice, ledger row updated with the bytes. Now replay the day without the chapter's instruments. No tenant field: the burst is invisible in the global p95, the fairness question unanswerable. No window dial: the swaps are whatever FIFO pays, fivefold on alternating streams. No per-tenant slice: the new tenant's quality claim is a slogan. No ledger row: the rank experiment is a vibe with bytes attached. The day got harder only because the facts got expensive — and the instruments exist to keep them cheap. Reading a multi-tenant dashboard critically The inherited multi-tenant dashboard fails an audit in four familiar places. The global p95 tile — wrong grain: promises are per tenant; the tile hides B behind A. The swap-rate tile without a window — a number that names no policy output; the swap count is a property of the routing policy over a named window, and without the window it cannot be compared across weeks. The adapter-quality banner — a claim with no slice and no protocol; quality deltas live on tenant prompt slices under the invariant protocol or nowhere. The fairness panel without the ledger link — a badge where a query should be. The honest rebuild is small and familiar from T13: one row per tenant per SLO with the slice named; one row per routing policy with its two-sided price over a named window; one cost ledger per tenant on measured slices; one link to the chain verifier. Four tiles with answers, beating forty tiles of inherited green — the T13 audit, applied one grain finer. What the adapter does not fix: the prefix Multi-tenancy tempts one more claim — "each tenant also gets its own prompt cache". The chapter refuses it, honestly: the adapter changes weights, not the KV cache layout, and a tenant's cached prefixes live in the shared cache under T05's block table. Two consequences follow. First, tenant isolation of cached state is a policy question (whose tokens may share a block), not an adapter property — the adapter neither isolates nor contaminates the cache. Second, the cache hit rate a tenant sees depends on its own prompt reuse and on eviction pressure from other tenants' prefixes: a busy new tenant can lower a quiet tenant's hit rate without either adapter changing. That coupling is measurable — hit rate per tenant, sliced from the journal like the p95 — and it belongs in the routing memo's table, because a policy that moves tenants between slots moves their cache neighborhoods too. The exam voice is a boundary statement: adapters multiply tenants over weights; the cache multiplies nothing and forgets under pressure. A tenant promising "my adapter keeps my prefixes warm" has promised the wrong instrument — the honest promise names the block table, the eviction policy and the measured hit rate per tenant, window named. This is the same refusal as the context-width claim: the adapter is a weight delta, and weight deltas do not reach the cache's ledger. Adapter versions are releases The moment a tenant retrains its adapter, the serving layer hosts a new artifact with the old tenant's name — and T09's lesson applies verbatim: a floating tag is a deferred dependency break. The honest fleet versions adapters like images: a digest or content hash on the adapter file, a release note per version naming what the training slice was, and a rollback path that restores the previous version's bytes, not just its name. The routing memo's ledger row then cites the adapter digest, and the fairness audit can prove which version served the window it audits. Version drift is the quiet failure the collapse was supposed to prevent: ten tenants with ten unversioned adapters drift as surely as ten unversioned engines — more quietly, because the base they share really is identical and the drift hides in 0.22 MB slivers. The lab's declared deltas are labeled by tenant and by rank for exactly this reason: a claim without a version is unauditable. The runbook row: "adapter B v7 → v8, digest changed, quality slice re-run under the invariant protocol, swap bytes +0.0 — the ledger row is the release note." Comparing tenants without ranking them Once promises are per tenant, someone will ask for a leaderboard of tenants — and the chapter refuses the leaderboard while keeping the comparison. The journal supports honest questions of the form "did tenant B's p95 improve after the routing change", because both sides of that sentence are measured slices with named windows. It does not support "which tenant is best", because tenants differ in domain, traffic shape and rank settings — a ranking would compare incomparable contracts and reward traffic shape over service quality. The T13 rule generalizes: a number is comparable only inside its slice and its window. The same refusal protects the fairness audit: "tenant B was rejected 30 times over the audited window by the per-tenant envelope while its weight was 1.0" is an auditable sentence; "tenant B is the worst tenant" is not a sentence the journal can prove or refute. The runbook's fairness row cites the window and the rule, exactly like every other field — because fairness that cannot cite its window is an accusation, not an audit. The shift handover for adapters The adapter era changes what a shift handover must carry, and the extra fields are all ledger fields. The outgoing shift states, per busy slot: the routing policy live (window W), the swap count over the handover window, the per-tenant p95 table with its windows, the adapter digests resident, and any rank experiment in flight with its frozen plan and its stop rule. The incoming shift can then answer the only three questions a handover exists for: is the policy the one the memo approved, are the promises holding on their slices, and is any experiment past its stop rule. Three yeses and the handover is a receipt; any no names the first incident to inspect. What the handover must not carry is the old era's cargo: a global latency chart (wrong grain), an adapter "quality" banner without a slice (an unauditable claim), or a swap count without its window and policy (a number no one can compare). The handover is a routing memo in miniature — which is why the chapter made the memo one page: if it cannot be handed over in one page, it is not yet a policy but an argument. Why agents make this worse before better The topic's forward pointer deserves its own honesty note: agentic workloads arrive burstier, longer and more prefix-dependent than human traffic, so the tenant stream this chapter routed is the calm version of the future stream. Longer sessions mean a tenant's requests hold the slot longer (more head-of-line pressure on pinned queues); tool waits mean arrivals cluster after the wait (windows fill with one tenant's post-tool fan-out); prefix reuse means the cache coupling from the earlier section grows sharper. Every one of those makes the two-sided ledger more expensive per side — which is the chapter's real gift to Topic 15: the instruments (slices, swap counts, the window dial, the two-sided ledger) are exactly what survives the workload's shape change, and the constants will move again. Migrating a tenant between policies Policies are not forever: the memo that chose W = 3 was true of the stream it measured, and streams change. Migrating a tenant from FIFO to affinity windows — or from one window to another — is a routing change with its own two-sided price, and it deserves the same freeze-then-measure discipline as any knob. Freeze the migration plan: the new W, the declared lines (swaps and waits), the window over which the comparison runs. Then measure both sides on the old policy's journal window and the new policy's live window, and reconcile them against the simulator — the same prediction-reconciliation the T06 knee and the T10 sweep ran. A migration without the old window's baseline is a policy change nobody can evaluate: the comparison needs both sides named. Two honest edge cases live at the migration's edges. A tenant mid-window when the policy flips has requests that straddle two policies — the journal must record the policy version per entry (one more field the tenant slice carries) so the comparison slices cleanly. And a tenant whose traffic shape changes between windows has moved the thing being measured — the honest memo says so: "the W = 5 row reflects the burst week" names the confound instead of hiding it. Policy versions, like adapter digests, are release notes for the routing layer. The chapter in one ledger Price the sliver: the rank arithmetic makes an adapter 0.22 MB against a 491 MB frozen base, and the rank dial is measured per tenant, never assumed. Count the swaps: they are order-dependent, fivefold between interleaved and grouped on the same load, priced at a declared 2 ms with the real-systems line cited. Measure per tenant: the promise is nearest-rank over the tenant's own journal slice, window named, small-sample caveat stated. Route with both sides priced: the window dial trades waits against swaps, the declared lines make the choice checkable, and the fairness row closes the loop — who was rejected by which rule, over which audited window. Four ledger fields, one page, one simulator to reconcile against. That is the chapter; everything after it moves the constants. Sources and provenance Primary sources: LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models ( arXiv 2106.09685 , Hu et al., 2021) for the rank arithmetic and the frozen-base idea; S-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters ( arXiv 2311.03285 , Sheng et al., 2023) for paged adapter memory — the real-systems answer to the switches our flat 2 ms prices; Punica ( arXiv 2310.18547 , Li et al., 2023) for merged kernels — the second real-systems line the declared model omits; and the SRE book's Managing Critical State for the fairness-as-policy framing. In-repo sources: the layer-2 gateway journal ( runtime/gateway/app.py ) and the T09 engine record ( seminars/runs/2026-11-07-topic09-fleet-mac/README.md (the fleet run record) ) for the base size. The judge README covers the invariant protocol the quality claims are held to.
